commonMistake: Applying a second 25% increase to 35% (giving 43.75%) instead of adding the same absolute amount of water.

optionExplanations.0: 66.25% wrongly compounds percentage increases.
optionExplanations.3: 60% overshoots; it treats both additions as fixed 25-point jumps.
optionExplanations.4: 43.75% comes from multiplying 35% by 1.25, but the second rainfall is the same volume, not the same percentage.

formulaNotes: Same volume added each week => same percentage-point increment: 28 -> 28+7=35 -> 35+7=42.

shortExplanation: The clues give Esun > Cubba > Dile (Esun longer than Cubba, Cubba longer than Dile), so Esun must be longer than Dile. Bongo only ranks below Esun, so its relation to the others is undetermined.
solutionSteps: From 'Dile shorter than Cubba': Cubba > Dile.
From 'Esun longer than Cubba': Esun > Cubba.
Chain: Esun > Cubba > Dile, therefore Esun > Dile (definitely true).
Bongo is only known to be shorter than Esun; no fixed relation to Cubba or Dile.
keyConcept: Only inequalities that follow transitively from the given chain are guaranteed.
commonMistake: Assuming Bongo's position relative to Cubba or Dile can be pinned down; it cannot.

optionExplanations.0: Bongo vs Cubba is undetermined; both could be longer.
optionExplanations.2: Dile is the shortest in the chain, so it cannot be longer than Esun.
optionExplanations.3: Cubba vs Bongo is undetermined by the clues.

shortExplanation: The pie angles imply a total of 400 votes (Peter's correct 126 gives 113.4 deg only if total = 400). Every candidate's angle matches their true vote at that total EXCEPT Kevin, whose 72 votes should give 64.8 deg but was drawn as 24.3 deg (i.e. read as 27).
solutionSteps: Angle = votes/total x 360. Test Peter: 126/400 x 360 = 113.4 deg, so the total used was 400.
Check others at total 400: Harold 100 -> 90 deg, Alison 84 -> 75.6 deg, Rachel 63 -> 56.7 deg. All match.
Kevin 72 -> 72/400 x 360 = 64.8 deg, which is NOT among the drawn angles.
Remaining angle 24.3 deg corresponds to 27 votes, so Kevin's 72 was misread as 27.
keyConcept: In a correctly summing pie chart, angle is proportional to value; the mismatched value is the error.
commonMistake: Checking angles against the true total of 445 instead of the total actually used to draw the chart (400).

optionExplanations.1: Peter's 126 gives exactly 113.4 deg at total 400, so his figure is correct.
optionExplanations.3: Alison's 84 gives exactly 75.6 deg, so hers is correct.
optionExplanations.4: Harold's 100 gives exactly 90 deg, so his is correct.

formulaNotes: angle = (votes / total) x 360; total used = 400, so Kevin's 24.3 deg implies 27 not 72.

shortExplanation: Let the tunnel be t km. The rest (16 - t) is at 60 km/h and the tunnel at 20 km/h; total time is 19 min = 19/60 h. Solving (16 - t)/60 + t/20 = 19/60 gives t = 1.5 km.
solutionSteps: Total time = 19 minutes = 19/60 hour.
Time = (16 - t)/60 + t/20 hours.
Multiply through by 60: (16 - t) + 3t = 19.
keyConcept: Total journey time is the sum of times over each speed segment (time = distance/speed).
commonMistake: Forgetting to convert 60 km/h and 20 km/h into the same time unit as the 19-minute total.

optionExplanations.1: 2.5 km would make the journey take longer than 19 minutes.
optionExplanations.3: 3.5 km overstates the slow section and exceeds 19 minutes.
optionExplanations.4: 0.5 km would leave the journey faster than 19 minutes.

formulaNotes: (16 - t)/60 + t/20 = 19/60  ->  16 + 2t = 19  ->  t = 1.5 km. The 4 km entry point is not needed for the length.

shortExplanation: The argument holds that one cold winter, caused by displaced Arctic air, does not disprove long-term global warming. Evidence that other Northern Hemisphere regions were hotter than usual shows warming continued alongside the local cold snap, strengthening the argument.
solutionSteps: Identify the conclusion: a single cold winter does not disprove global warming.
Note the given support: the cold was caused by weakened polar winds letting Arctic air escape locally.
To strengthen, find evidence that overall warming persisted even while one region cooled.
The claim that other Northern Hemisphere regions were hotter than in previous years fits: warming continued globally despite the local cold.
keyConcept: A strengthener supplies additional evidence consistent with the conclusion, here that warming continues despite a localised cold spell.
commonMistake: Choosing statements about who is making the sceptical claim, which target the objectors rather than the warming argument itself.

optionExplanations.1: One prior average winter neither confirms nor refutes a long-term warming trend.
optionExplanations.3: Where the sceptics live has no bearing on whether global warming is real.
optionExplanations.4: Saying the sceptics have further supporting evidence would weaken, not strengthen, the argument.

shortExplanation: Cash on hand is smallest when the most money is still out on loan. By the 4th Friday the Week 1 loan (maximum 3-week term) must already be repaid, but the Week 2, 3 and 4 loans can all still be outstanding: 25 + 18 + 20 = 63, leaving 120 - 63 = 57.
solutionSteps: Note that cash held = 120 - money currently out on loan, so minimise cash by maximising outstanding loans.
The Week 1 loan of 45 has a term of at most 3 weeks, so it must be repaid by the 4th Friday and returns to hand.
The Week 2 loan of 25 can be a 3-week loan due on the 5th Friday, so it can still be out.
The Week 3 loan of 18 and Week 4 loan of 20 can also still be outstanding on the 4th Friday.
Maximum outstanding = 25 + 18 + 20 = 63, so minimum cash = 120 - 63 = 57.
keyConcept: Minimum cash occurs when repayments are pushed back as far as each loan's term allows.
commonMistake: Subtracting all four loans, or forgetting that the Week 1 loan must be repaid within its 3-week limit by the 4th Friday.

optionExplanations.0: 82 assumes fewer loans are outstanding, so it does not minimise the cash held.
optionExplanations.1: 12 would require lending far more than the stated amounts.
optionExplanations.3: 100 corresponds to nearly all loans repaid, giving the largest cash rather than the smallest.

shortExplanation: The argument urges switching off motorway lighting, claiming the lights are unnecessary and even harmful. Evidence that well-lit night driving reduces concentration adds a further reason lighting is detrimental, strengthening the case for turning it off.
solutionSteps: Identify the conclusion: the government should turn off unnecessary motorway street lighting.
Note the support given: modern cars have powerful headlights, and moving from lit to unlit areas causes accidents.
A strengthener adds an extra reason that lighting itself is harmful or pointless.
The claim that driving in well-lit areas at night can cause a lack of concentration gives such a reason, supporting removal of the lights.
keyConcept: A strengthener supplies additional evidence favouring the conclusion, here that the lights themselves are detrimental.
commonMistake: Picking statements showing that unlit driving is difficult, which actually weaken the case for switching lights off.

optionExplanations.0: Daytime accident rates are irrelevant to the value of night-time lighting.
optionExplanations.2: That older drivers struggle without lighting weakens the case for turning lights off.
optionExplanations.3: That many drivers find unlit roads difficult also undermines the argument.

shortExplanation: The whole 200 g packet contains twice each per-100 g value, so dividing a packet total by the matching per-biscuit amount gives the count. Using salt, 1.04 g / 0.08 g = 13 biscuits.
solutionSteps: The packet is 200 g, so every 'per 100 g' figure is multiplied by 2 for the whole packet.
Equivalent salt per packet = 0.52 g x 2 = 1.04 g.
Each biscuit contains 0.08 g of salt.
Number of biscuits = 1.04 / 0.08 = 13.
Cross-check with energy: 510 x 2 = 1020 kcal, and 1020 / 79 is about 13.
keyConcept: Total quantity in the whole packet divided by the quantity per biscuit gives the number of biscuits.
commonMistake: Dividing the per-100 g value by the per-biscuit value and forgetting the packet is 200 g, which halves the answer.

optionExplanations.0: 22 doubles the count, for example by dividing 200 g by an incorrect mass per biscuit.
optionExplanations.1: 11 comes from using a mis-scaled total rather than the correct 1020 kcal (or 1.04 g salt) per packet.
optionExplanations.2: 6 roughly halves the true count by using the per-100 g figures instead of scaling to the 200 g packet.

figureExplanation: The panel lists values per 100 g (e.g. 510 kcal, salt 0.52 g) while the pie chart gives per-biscuit values (79 kcal, salt 0.08 g); scaling the panel to 200 g and dividing by the per-biscuit value gives 13.

shortExplanation: The owner gives reasons (protecting red squirrels, free range, low fat, low air miles). The counter-argument answers none of them and instead dismisses her as running 'a cheap publicity stunt to increase business'. That attacks her supposed motive, not her reasoning.
solutionSteps: List the owner's actual reasons: eating grey squirrels may protect the red species, and the meat is free range, low fat, low on air miles.
Look at how the argument replies: it only says the claim is 'a cheap publicity stunt' to boost business.
Note that this comment is about WHY she supposedly says it (her motive), not about whether her reasons are true.
Dismissing a claim by questioning the speaker's motive rather than engaging the reasons is the flaw (an ad hominem move).
keyConcept: Attacking the arguer's motive or character, instead of assessing their reasons, is a flaw: a bad motive does not make the reasons false.
commonMistake: Labelling it an unwarranted assumption; the flaw is not a hidden premise but the refusal to engage the reasons, dismissing the person instead.

optionExplanations.1: The argument does not assume that the red squirrel's decline justifies eating grey squirrels; it never engages that reasoning at all.
optionExplanations.2: The response does not attack the general idea of an 'ethical food'; it targets only the owner's motive, so this is not the flaw.
optionExplanations.3: That eating grey squirrels protects red ones is the OWNER's claim, not the response's assumption; the response never engages it, so it cannot be the flaw in the response's reasoning.
optionExplanations.4: The argument actually accepts that the red squirrel needs protecting, so this misreads the passage.

shortExplanation: The passage opens with its recommendation, that health services should find better ways to measure blood pressure, and then supplies the 'white coat' study and the worry about needless drugs as reasons. The conclusion is the recommendation, restated as needing more effective measurement.
solutionSteps: Separate the conclusion (the point being argued for) from the evidence (facts offered in support).
Evidence: about a third of 'hypertensive' patients read normal at home; treating people who are not really ill is worrying.
Ask what all this is offered to support: the need to measure blood pressure more accurately.
That matches 'More effective ways of measuring blood pressure are needed', which is the opening recommendation in other words.
keyConcept: The conclusion is the claim the evidence is gathered to support; a leading recommendation, even at the start, can be the conclusion.
commonMistake: Mistaking a supporting statistic or a cause mentioned in passing for the main point.

optionExplanations.0: The passage says about ONE third may be mismeasured, not two thirds, so this misstates the figure.
optionExplanations.2: Saving money is never mentioned; the argument is about measurement accuracy, not cost.
optionExplanations.3: Anxiety is offered only as the likely cause of 'white coat' readings, a supporting detail, not the conclusion, and the passage does not claim it is the most common cause of high blood pressure generally.
optionExplanations.4: Saying 'white coat' hypertension has no significance contradicts the passage, whose whole concern is that it leads to wrong treatment.

shortExplanation: In this numbering each house and the one opposite it sum to (number of houses + 1). Since 8 is opposite 11, the pairs sum to 19, so there are 19 - 1 = 18 houses.
solutionSteps: In the High Street example the opposite pairs (1 and 14, 2 and 13, ...) each sum to 15, and there are 14 houses, so pair-sum = total + 1.
On Princess Road, 8 is opposite 11, so every opposite pair sums to 8 + 11 = 19.
Therefore total houses + 1 = 19.
Total houses = 18.
keyConcept: Opposite house numbers on such a street always sum to (number of houses + 1).
commonMistake: Just adding 8 and 11 to get 19 and stopping, without subtracting 1 for the pairing rule.

optionExplanations.1: 16 would need opposite numbers summing to 17, but 8 faces 11 (sum 19).
optionExplanations.2: 20 over-counts; the pair-sum rule gives 18, not 20.
optionExplanations.4: 19 is the sum of the opposite pair, not the number of houses; the count is one less.

figureExplanation: The diagram shows one side numbered 1-7 increasing and the opposite side 14-13-...-8, so house n faces (15 - n); applying the same 'pairs sum to total + 1' rule to 8 opposite 11 gives 18 houses.

shortExplanation: Expanding each logarithm gives ln(x^2 y) = 2 ln x + ln y and 2 ln(xy) = 2 ln x + 2 ln y, so the expression collapses to 2 ln x + ln y - 2 ln x - 2 ln y + 3 ln y = 2 ln y.
solutionSteps: Write the expression: ln(x^2 y) - 2 ln(xy) + 3 ln y.
Expand the first term with the product and power rules: ln(x^2 y) = 2 ln x + ln y.
Expand the second term: 2 ln(xy) = 2(ln x + ln y) = 2 ln x + 2 ln y.
Substitute: (2 ln x + ln y) - (2 ln x + 2 ln y) + 3 ln y.
Collect the ln x terms: 2 ln x - 2 ln x = 0.
Collect the ln y terms: ln y - 2 ln y + 3 ln y = 2 ln y.
The expression is equivalent to 2 ln y.
keyConcept: Logarithms turn products into sums and powers into multiples, so a sum of log terms can be simplified by expanding each term and collecting like logarithms.
commonMistake: Applying the factor 2 in 2 ln(xy) only to ln x and not to ln y, which leaves an extra ln y and gives ln x + 2 ln y instead of 2 ln y.

optionExplanations.0: Getting 0 assumes every term cancels; the ln x terms cancel but the ln y terms sum to 2 ln y, not zero.
optionExplanations.1: The form ln x + ln y would require an ln x term to survive, but 2 ln x - 2 ln x = 0 removes all ln x.
optionExplanations.3: The form 2 ln x + 2 ln y results from adding 2 ln(xy) instead of subtracting it, a sign error.
optionExplanations.4: The form ln x + 2 ln y results from expanding 2 ln(xy) as 2 ln x + ln y, forgetting the factor 2 also multiplies ln y.

figureExplanation: The figure shows the expression ln(x^2 y) - 2 ln(xy) + 3 ln y, followed by five candidate equivalent forms: 0, ln x + ln y, 2 ln y, 2 ln x + 2 ln y, and ln x + 2 ln y. Expanding and collecting terms gives 2 ln y.
formulaNotes: ln(ab) = ln a + ln b; ln(a^n) = n ln a; k ln(ab) = k ln a + k ln b.

shortExplanation: With 2/5 of the group male and 1/3 studying mathematics, the mathematics students all fit within the males, so the overlap can range from none of them to all of them, making p range from 0 to 5/6.
solutionSteps: Take a convenient group size of 15: males = (2/5)(15) = 6 and mathematics students = (1/3)(15) = 5.
Let m = number of males who study mathematics; then p = m/6.
Minimum overlap: none of the mathematics students need be male, so m can be 0, giving p = 0.
Maximum overlap: all 5 mathematics students can be male since 5 <= 6, so m = 5, giving p = 5/6.
Therefore 0 <= p <= 5/6.
keyConcept: A conditional proportion is bounded by the overlap limits of two subgroups: the overlap runs from 0 up to the smaller subgroup size.
commonMistake: Treating the two fractions as independent and reporting a single value such as 1/3 instead of the range of possible overlap.

optionExplanations.0: The range starting at 1/3 is wrong because the overlap can be 0 when no mathematics student is male.
optionExplanations.3: The range starting at 2/5 is wrong because the mathematics students need not be male at all, so p can fall to 0.
optionExplanations.4: The range capped at 1/3 is far too low because all 5 mathematics students can be male, giving p = 5/6.

figureExplanation: The two boxed fractions in the stem are 2/5 (fraction male) and 1/3 (fraction studying mathematics); in a group of 15 these give 6 males and 5 mathematics students, whose overlap runs from 0 to 5, so p runs from 0 to 5/6.
formulaNotes: p = (males studying maths)/(males); 0 <= (males studying maths) <= min(males, maths students) = 5.

shortExplanation: R is a 72 deg rotation and S a reflection in the y-axis; tracking vertex D through each sequence, four of them return D to its original position, but RRSRSR produces a net 144 deg rotation (R squared) that moves D elsewhere.
solutionSteps: With A at the top on the y-axis, place the vertices by angle: A=90, B=18, C=306, D=234, E=162 degrees; R subtracts 72 deg, S maps angle t to 180 - t.
Track D (234 deg) through RRSRSR: 234->162->90->90->18->162->90; final 90 deg is NOT D's start, so D moves.
SR: 234->306->234 (returns to D).
SRRSRS, RSRS and RSRR each also return the point to 234 deg.
Only RRSRSR fails to leave D in place (net effect is a 144 deg rotation).
keyConcept: A sequence leaves a vertex fixed only if the composite is the identity or a reflection whose axis passes through that vertex.
commonMistake: Assuming R and S commute; the order of transformations changes the composite, so each sequence must be traced.

optionExplanations.1: SR is a reflection whose axis passes through D, so D is fixed.
optionExplanations.3: RSRS composes to the identity on D, returning it to 234 deg.
optionExplanations.4: RSRR returns the tracked point to 234 deg, leaving D in place.

formulaNotes: Model as angles: R: t -> t - 72; S: t -> 180 - t. RRSRSR sends 234 -> 90 (a net R^2 rotation).

shortExplanation: Specific heat capacity is found by energy balance: heat lost by iron = heat gained by water, m_iron*c_iron*(100 - Tf) = m_water*c_water*(Tf - 20). This needs the two masses, the water's specific heat, and the final temperature, but not the iron's thermal conductivity.
solutionSteps: Write the calorimetry balance: heat lost by iron = heat gained by water.
m_iron * c_iron * (100 - Tf) = m_water * c_water * (Tf - 20).
Rearranging for c_iron needs m_iron, m_water, c_water, the initial temps and Tf.
Thermal conductivity governs rate of heat flow, not the total energy exchanged, so it is not required.
keyConcept: Calorimetry uses conservation of thermal energy (Q = m*c*deltaT), which is independent of conductivity.
commonMistake: Confusing thermal conductivity (rate of transfer) with specific heat capacity (energy per degree per kg).

optionExplanations.0: The water's specific heat is needed to compute the heat it gains.
optionExplanations.1: The iron's mass appears directly in its heat equation.
optionExplanations.3: The final temperature sets both temperature changes and is essential.

formulaNotes: m_i*c_i*(100 - Tf) = m_w*c_w*(Tf - 20); conductivity does not appear.

shortExplanation: Melting turns solid wax to liquid, increasing molecular disorder, and the absorbed latent heat keeps temperature constant. However only weak intermolecular forces are overcome; the strong covalent C-H bonds within molecules are not broken.
solutionSteps: Statement 1: solid -> liquid increases disorder -> correct.
Statement 2: at the melting point heat is absorbed as latent heat while temperature stays constant -> correct.
Statement 3: melting breaks intermolecular forces, not intramolecular C-H covalent bonds -> incorrect.
Correct statements: 1 and 2 only.
keyConcept: A change of state breaks intermolecular forces, not the covalent bonds within molecules.
commonMistake: Believing melting breaks covalent bonds; that would be chemical decomposition, not a phase change.

optionExplanations.0: '1, 2 and 3' wrongly includes breaking C-H bonds.
optionExplanations.1: '2 and 3 only' drops correct statement 1 and keeps the false statement 3.
optionExplanations.2: '2 only' omits the correct statement about increased disorder.

shortExplanation: With zero resistance there is no heating, so no thermal effect; a solid metal has no ions free to react, so no chemical effect. A current still creates a magnetic field, so only the magnetic effect is present.
solutionSteps: Thermal effect requires resistance (P = I^2 R); with R = 0 there is no heating.
Chemical effect needs ions/electrolysis; a solid superconductor carries current via electrons, not ions.
A moving charge (current) always produces a magnetic field, so the magnetic effect remains.
Only effect 3 (magnetic) is present.
keyConcept: Superconductors carry current with zero resistance, eliminating the heating effect but not the magnetic effect.
commonMistake: Assuming any current heats the conductor; with zero resistance the Joule heating is zero.

optionExplanations.0: '1 and 3' wrongly includes the thermal effect, which vanishes at zero resistance.
optionExplanations.1: '1, 2 and 3' includes both the absent thermal and chemical effects.
optionExplanations.4: '1 only' selects the thermal effect, which does not occur in a superconductor.

formulaNotes: Joule heating P = I^2 R = 0 when R = 0; a current I still produces a magnetic field.

shortExplanation: With each capacitor equal to C, circuit 1 is three in series (C/3), circuit 2 is two in series in parallel with one (3C/2), and circuit 3 is all three in parallel (3C); increasing order is 1, 2, 3.
solutionSteps: Let every capacitor have value C.
Circuit 1 (three in series): 1/C_total = 3/C, so C_total = C/3, about 0.33C.
Circuit 2: the two series capacitors give C/2, and this is in parallel with the third: C/2 + C = 3C/2 = 1.5C.
Circuit 3 (all three between the same two nodes, in parallel): C + C + C = 3C.
Ordering smallest to largest: C/3 < 3C/2 < 3C, that is 1, 2, 3.
keyConcept: For capacitors, series connection adds reciprocally (lowering capacitance) while parallel connection adds directly (raising capacitance).
commonMistake: Applying resistor rules (series adds, parallel reciprocal), which reverses the capacitance order.

optionExplanations.0: '3, 2, 1' reverses the order; the all-series circuit (1) is the smallest, not the largest.
optionExplanations.1: '1, 3, 2' wrongly ranks the all-parallel circuit (3C) below the series-parallel one (1.5C).
optionExplanations.2: '2, 1, 3' places the series circuit (C/3) second, but it is actually the smallest.

figureExplanation: Circuit 1 shows three capacitors in a single line (series); circuit 2 shows two capacitors in series on the top branch bridged by a third capacitor (that branch is in parallel with the pair); circuit 3 shows three capacitors all spanning the same two nodes (fully parallel).
formulaNotes: Series: 1/C = 1/C1 + 1/C2 + ...  Parallel: C = C1 + C2 + ...

shortExplanation: Velocity, weight (a force), electric field and acceleration all have direction and are vectors. Electric charge has only magnitude and sign but no direction, so it is a scalar.
solutionSteps: A vector has both magnitude and direction.
Velocity, acceleration and electric field are directional -> vectors.
Weight is a force (mass x g) acting downward -> vector.
Electric charge is a scalar quantity with no direction.
keyConcept: Scalars have magnitude only; vectors also have direction.
commonMistake: Confusing electric charge with electric field; the field is a vector, the charge is not.

optionExplanations.0: Velocity has magnitude and direction, so it is a vector.
optionExplanations.1: Weight is a downward force, a vector.
optionExplanations.3: Electric field points in a definite direction, so it is a vector.

shortExplanation: Total contact area = 10000 nails x 1.0 mm^2 = 10000 mm^2 = 0.01 m^2. The man's weight is 75 x 10 = 750 N, so pressure = 750 / 0.01 = 7.5 x 10^4 Pa.
solutionSteps: Weight W = mg = 75 x 10 = 750 N.
Total area = 10000 x 1.0 mm^2 = 10000 mm^2.
keyConcept: Pressure = force / area; the force spreads over the combined area of all nail tips.
commonMistake: Using one nail's area, or mishandling the mm^2-to-m^2 conversion (factor 10^-6).

optionExplanations.0: 7.5 x 10^6 Pa uses the area of a single nail, not all 10000.
optionExplanations.2: 7.5 x 10^3 Pa uses too large a total area.
optionExplanations.4: 7.5 x 10^5 Pa results from a 10x conversion error in the area.

shortExplanation: Transcription copies a DNA template into RNA, so its direct product is mRNA. Producing insulin or antibodies or a protein's primary structure requires the further step of translation.
solutionSteps: Transcription: DNA -> mRNA (RNA polymerase reads the template).
The immediate product of transcription is therefore mRNA.
Protein products (insulin, antibodies, primary structure) come only after translation.
So the direct product is mRNA.
keyConcept: Transcription yields RNA; protein appears only after the separate step of translation.
commonMistake: Jumping to the final protein product and skipping the mRNA intermediate.

optionExplanations.0: Insulin is a protein, made by translation, not directly by transcription.
optionExplanations.3: A protein's primary structure requires translation of the mRNA.
optionExplanations.4: A replicated DNA molecule is the product of replication, not transcription.

shortExplanation: The heart, pulmonary vessels and alveoli lie in the thorax above the diaphragm. The liver sits in the abdomen, just below the diaphragm.
solutionSteps: The diaphragm separates the thoracic cavity (above) from the abdominal cavity (below).
Heart, pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein and alveoli are thoracic -> above.
The liver is an abdominal organ -> below the diaphragm.
keyConcept: The diaphragm divides thoracic organs (heart, lungs) from abdominal organs (liver, stomach).
commonMistake: Placing lung-associated vessels below the diaphragm; they are all thoracic.

optionExplanations.0: The heart lies in the thorax, above the diaphragm.
optionExplanations.1: The pulmonary vein is part of the thoracic circulation.
optionExplanations.4: Alveoli are in the lungs, within the thorax.

shortExplanation: Cell membranes contain proteins, enzymes and antibodies are proteins, and viruses have a protein coat, so all contain amino acids. Amylose is a polymer of glucose (a polysaccharide) with no amino acids.
solutionSteps: Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins.
Cell membranes contain membrane proteins; enzymes and antibodies are proteins; viruses have a protein capsid.
Amylose is a chain of glucose units (starch component), a carbohydrate.
Therefore amylose contains no amino acids.
keyConcept: Amino acids build proteins; polysaccharides like amylose are built from monosaccharides.
commonMistake: Assuming any large biological molecule contains amino acids; carbohydrates do not.

optionExplanations.0: Membranes include embedded and peripheral proteins made of amino acids.
optionExplanations.2: Viruses have a protein coat (capsid) containing amino acids.
optionExplanations.3: Enzymes are proteins, so they are made of amino acids.

shortExplanation: Ribosomes carry out translation (protein synthesis) in the cytoplasm and on rough ER, and contain rRNA. They do NOT carry out transcription, which is performed by RNA polymerase in the nucleus.
solutionSteps: Ribosomes are the site of translation, assembling proteins from mRNA.
They occur free in the cytoplasm and bound to rough endoplasmic reticulum.
They contain ribosomal RNA (rRNA), so RNA is associated with them.
Transcription (DNA -> mRNA) is done by RNA polymerase, not ribosomes -> that statement is false.
keyConcept: Ribosomes translate mRNA into protein; transcription is a separate, polymerase-driven process.
commonMistake: Confusing translation (ribosomes) with transcription (RNA polymerase).

optionExplanations.0: Ribosomes are indeed involved in protein synthesis; this statement is correct.
optionExplanations.1: Free ribosomes are genuinely found in the cytoplasm.
optionExplanations.2: Ribosomes do bind rough endoplasmic reticulum, so this is correct.

shortExplanation: The complementary strand of ACG-GCT-GGT-TCC is TGC-CGA-CCA-AGG, which contains a CGA triplet, so the first statement is correct. With adenine pairs worth 2 H bonds and guanine pairs worth 3, each triplet of the given strand totals 8, so the second statement is correct. The third statement is wrong: transcribed with this strand as template, the mRNA gains one uracil per template adenine, and this strand has only one adenine, not three.
solutionSteps: Build the complementary strand using A-T and G-C pairing: ACGGCTGGTTCC pairs with TGCCGACCAAGG.
Split the complement into triplets aligned with the original: TGC, CGA, CCA, AGG, so a CGA triplet is present and the first statement is correct.

Count hydrogen bonds per triplet of the given strand using 2 for each A-T pair and 3 for each G-C pair: ACG = 2+3+3 = 8, GCT = 3+3+2 = 8, GGT = 3+3+2 = 8, TCC = 2+3+3 = 8, so every triplet totals 8 and the second statement is correct.

For the mRNA, a uracil is placed opposite each adenine in the template strand; the given strand contains only one adenine, so the transcript from it carries one uracil, not three, and the third statement is incorrect.
The correct statements are the first and the second only.
keyConcept: Complementary base pairing (A-T, G-C) fixes both the opposite sequence and the hydrogen-bond count, and each mRNA uracil is placed opposite an adenine in the template strand.
commonMistake: Counting the three thymines in the given strand as the number of uracils; a uracil is placed opposite each template adenine, of which there is only one here.

optionExplanations.0: Choosing the first statement only drops the correct hydrogen-bond statement.
optionExplanations.1: Choosing the second and third statements includes the false uracil-count statement.
optionExplanations.2: Choosing the third statement only selects the incorrect statement and discards the two correct ones.
optionExplanations.3: Choosing the second statement only drops the correct complementary-triplet statement.

formulaNotes: Hydrogen bonds per pair: A-T = 2, G-C = 3. Each triplet of this strand sums to 8. mRNA uracils = number of adenines in the template = 1.

shortExplanation: Two unaffected parents cannot pass on a dominant disease allele, so an inherited sex-linked dominant condition cannot explain an affected son; every other option is possible.
solutionSteps: Both parents are unaffected, boy C is affected, and his sisters are unaffected.
Sex-linked recessive works: a carrier mother (X^A X^a) passes X^a to a son (X^a Y), who is affected, while daughters receive the father's normal X and are unaffected.
Autosomal recessive, i.e. both parents carriers (Aa x Aa), can give an affected aa child - possible.
A new mutation in boy C alone explains why nobody else is affected - possible.

Sex-linked dominant: an individual carrying the dominant allele would itself be affected, but both parents are unaffected and so carry no such allele to pass on - so this cannot explain it (other than by a fresh mutation, which is a separate option).
keyConcept: A dominant condition requires an affected parent (or a new mutation); it cannot be silently carried by unaffected parents and inherited by a child.
commonMistake: Assuming 'sex-linked' automatically fits an affected boy, without checking that a dominant allele must come from an affected parent.

optionExplanations.1: Sex-linked recessive works: a carrier mother passes the recessive X-linked allele to her son.
optionExplanations.3: Autosomal recessive works: two carrier parents can produce an affected homozygous child.
optionExplanations.4: A new mutation can produce a single affected individual from unaffected parents.

figureExplanation: The pedigree shows two unaffected parents (unfilled circle and square) with four children, only boy C shaded (affected); unaffected parents cannot transmit a dominant disease allele, which rules out sex-linked dominant inheritance.

shortExplanation: Antibodies, T cells, B cells and phagocytes are all part of the immune defence. Beta cells are pancreatic cells that secrete insulin and have no role in fighting infection.
solutionSteps: Antibodies neutralise pathogens; B cells produce them; T cells coordinate/kill infected cells; phagocytes engulf pathogens.
Beta cells are located in the pancreatic islets and secrete insulin.
Insulin regulates blood glucose, not immune defence.
So beta cells are not involved in defending against infection.
keyConcept: Immune defence involves lymphocytes, antibodies and phagocytes; beta cells are endocrine, not immune.
commonMistake: Confusing pancreatic beta cells with B cells (lymphocytes) because of the similar name.

optionExplanations.0: Antibodies directly neutralise and tag pathogens.
optionExplanations.1: T cells are central to the adaptive immune response.
optionExplanations.4: Phagocytes engulf and destroy invading microbes.

shortExplanation: Glycolysis produces pyruvate without releasing CO2, and mammalian anaerobic respiration converts pyruvate to lactate with no CO2. Only the Krebs cycle releases CO2, so CO2 is produced in stage 3 only.
solutionSteps: Glycolysis: glucose -> 2 pyruvate; no CO2 released.
Anaerobic respiration in mammals: pyruvate -> lactate; no CO2 released.
Krebs cycle: decarboxylation steps release CO2.
Therefore CO2 is released in stage 3 (Krebs cycle) only.
keyConcept: In mammals CO2 comes from the link reaction and Krebs cycle; glycolysis and lactate fermentation release none.
commonMistake: Assuming lactate fermentation gives off CO2; that occurs in yeast (ethanol) fermentation, not mammalian.

optionExplanations.1: '1 and 2 only' wrongly attributes CO2 to glycolysis and mammalian anaerobic respiration.
optionExplanations.2: '1 only' credits glycolysis, which does not release CO2.
optionExplanations.3: '2 and 3 only' includes lactate fermentation, which produces no CO2 in mammals.

shortExplanation: By Chargaff's rule guanine pairs with cytosine and adenine with thymine, so if guanine is 32% then cytosine is also 32%, leaving 36% split equally between adenine and thymine, giving thymine = 18%.
solutionSteps: Guanine pairs with cytosine, so C = G = 32%.
Together G + C = 64% of the bases.
The remaining 100 - 64 = 36% is shared by adenine and thymine.
Since A = T, thymine = 36 / 2 = 18%.
keyConcept: Chargaff's base-pairing rules: %A = %T and %G = %C.
commonMistake: Assuming thymine simply equals guanine (32%) instead of applying the complementary pairing rule.

optionExplanations.0: 32% would be the amount of cytosine (which pairs with guanine), not thymine.
optionExplanations.2: 23% does not result from any correct application of the pairing rules to a 32% guanine value.
optionExplanations.3: 34% ignores that A and T must split the leftover 36% equally.

shortExplanation: The mitotic sequence is prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, so telophase immediately follows anaphase.
solutionSteps: Recall the ordered phases of mitosis: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase.
Anaphase is when sister chromatids separate to opposite poles.
The next stage, where chromosomes decondense and nuclear envelopes reform, is telophase.
keyConcept: Order of mitosis: Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase (PMAT).
commonMistake: Choosing cytokinesis, which overlaps with telophase but is division of the cytoplasm, not the next mitotic phase.

optionExplanations.1: Interphase is the growth stage between divisions, not immediately after anaphase.
optionExplanations.3: Prophase begins mitosis and comes long before anaphase.
optionExplanations.4: Cytokinesis is cytoplasmic division that accompanies/follows telophase, not the mitotic phase directly after anaphase.

shortExplanation: A phenotype can rise in frequency through an advantageous mutation, greater reproductive success of individuals carrying it, or an environmental change that favours it, so all three are possible causes.
solutionSteps: An advantageous mutation can introduce or boost a beneficial trait (statement 1 valid).
Greater reproductive success of individuals with that phenotype passes it on more often (statement 2 valid).
A change in environment can make the phenotype more favourable, increasing its frequency (statement 3 valid).
All three mechanisms can independently raise phenotype frequency.
keyConcept: Allele/phenotype frequencies change through mutation, selection, and environmental pressures.
commonMistake: Excluding environmental change, forgetting that the environment determines which phenotypes are favoured by selection.

optionExplanations.0: '3 only' wrongly rejects the roles of mutation and differential reproductive success.
optionExplanations.1: '1 and 2 only' ignores that environmental change drives selection.
optionExplanations.4: '1 only' omits selection and environmental factors, both valid causes.

shortExplanation: ATP is produced during the light reactions of photosynthesis and during cellular respiration, making it the molecule common to both processes.
solutionSteps: Photosynthesis generates ATP in the light-dependent reactions.
Respiration generates ATP in glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation.
Therefore ATP is synthesised in both processes.
keyConcept: ATP is the universal energy currency made in both photosynthesis and respiration.
commonMistake: Picking glucose or oxygen, which are products of photosynthesis but reactants (consumed) in respiration.

optionExplanations.0: Glucose is produced in photosynthesis but broken down, not made, in respiration.
optionExplanations.1: Reduced NADP (NADPH) is specific to photosynthesis; respiration uses NADH/FADH2.
optionExplanations.4: Oxygen is released by photosynthesis but consumed in aerobic respiration, not made.

shortExplanation: Mitochondria are found only in eukaryotes and so identify the cell as eukaryotic; ribosomes occur in prokaryotes too, and during metaphase the nuclear envelope has already broken down, so a distinct nucleus is not present.
solutionSteps: Ribosomes are present in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, so they cannot identify a cell as eukaryotic (statement 2 rejected).
During metaphase the nuclear envelope has disassembled, so there is no intact nucleus at this stage (statement 3 rejected).
Mitochondria are membrane-bound organelles unique to eukaryotes (statement 1 valid).
Only mitochondria confirm eukaryotic status here.
keyConcept: Membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria are diagnostic of eukaryotic cells.
commonMistake: Counting the nucleus, forgetting that during metaphase the nuclear membrane is broken down so no intact nucleus exists.

optionExplanations.1: '2 and 3 only' includes ribosomes (also in prokaryotes) and a nucleus that is absent during metaphase.
optionExplanations.2: '1 and 3 only' still relies on a nucleus that has broken down in metaphase.
optionExplanations.4: '1, 2 and 3' includes ribosomes, which are non-diagnostic, and the absent nucleus.

shortExplanation: Gas to solid is called deposition, not freezing; freezing is the liquid-to-solid change, so this pairing is the incorrect one.
solutionSteps: Match each stated change to its correct name.
Solid to liquid = melting (correct); solid to gas = sublimation (correct).
Liquid to gas = evaporation (correct); gas to liquid = condensation (correct).
Gas to solid is deposition; calling it freezing is wrong, since freezing is liquid to solid.
keyConcept: Gas to solid = deposition; liquid to solid = freezing.
commonMistake: Confusing deposition (gas to solid) with freezing (liquid to solid).

optionExplanations.0: Solid to liquid = melting is correctly named.
optionExplanations.2: Solid to gas = sublimation is correctly named.
optionExplanations.4: Gas to liquid = condensation is correctly named.

shortExplanation: HBr adds across the C=C double bond of propene (addition), the bromide is then replaced by cyanide (nucleophilic substitution), and the nitrile is finally reduced to a primary amine (reduction).
solutionSteps: Stage 1: CH3CH=CH2 becomes CH3CHBrCH3. HBr adds across the C=C double bond, so this is addition.
Stage 2: CH3CHBrCH3 becomes (CH3)2CHCN. The Br is replaced by the CN group, so this is nucleophilic substitution.
Stage 3: (CH3)2CHCN becomes (CH3)2CHCH2NH2. The nitrile C≡N gains hydrogen to become CH2NH2, so this is reduction.
keyConcept: Identify addition (across a double bond), substitution (one group swapped for another) and reduction (gain of hydrogen) from the structural change at each stage.
commonMistake: Calling stage 3 hydrolysis; hydrolysis of a nitrile gives a carboxylic acid, whereas forming the amine requires reduction.

optionExplanations.0: Stage 1 adds HBr across a double bond, so it is addition, not substitution.
optionExplanations.3: Stage 2 swaps Br for CN, which is substitution, not a second addition.
optionExplanations.4: Stage 3 forms an amine, which is reduction; hydrolysis would instead give a carboxylic acid.

figureExplanation: The scheme propene to 2-bromopropane to (CH3)2CHCN to isobutylamine shows an added HBr, then a Br-for-CN swap, then a C≡N to CH2NH2 gain of hydrogen.
formulaNotes: C=C + HBr -> C-C with H and Br added; R-Br + CN^- -> R-CN + Br^-; R-CN + 4[H] -> R-CH2-NH2.

shortExplanation: Isomers must share the same molecular formula and have different structural formulae; their physical properties are generally different, not similar, so only statements 1 and 3 are necessarily correct.
solutionSteps: Isomers have the same molecular formula by definition (statement 1 correct).
Different arrangements of atoms mean different structural formulae (statement 3 correct).
Different structures give different physical properties such as boiling point (statement 2 incorrect).
Only 1 and 3 must be true.
keyConcept: Isomers: same molecular formula, different structures, and generally different properties.
commonMistake: Assuming isomers have similar physical properties; different structures usually produce measurably different properties.

optionExplanations.0: '1 and 2 only' wrongly claims similar physical properties and omits the different structures.
optionExplanations.1: '1, 2 and 3' incorrectly includes the false claim of similar physical properties.
optionExplanations.3: '1 only' omits the essential requirement of different structural formulae.

shortExplanation: Carbon-carbon bond length increases from the triple bond to the double bond to the single bond; a double bond is less than twice as strong as a single bond; and a triple bond does share six electrons. All three statements are correct.
solutionSteps: Bond length: higher bond order pulls the atoms closer, so the triple bond is shortest, the double bond longer, and the single bond longest, meaning length increases in the order triple, double, single, so the first statement is correct.

Bond strength: a double bond is stronger than a single bond but not twice as strong, because the second (pi) overlap is weaker than the first (sigma) bond, so the double-bond strength is less than twice the single-bond strength and the second statement is correct.
Electron count: a carbon-carbon triple bond consists of three shared pairs of electrons, that is six electrons, so the third statement is correct.
All three statements are correct.
keyConcept: Higher bond order means shorter bonds and more shared electrons, but bond strength does not scale exactly with bond order because the pi contributions are weaker than the sigma bond.
commonMistake: Assuming a double bond must be exactly twice as strong as a single bond, when the extra pi overlap contributes less than a full second bond.

optionExplanations.0: Excluding the bond-length statement is wrong, since length does increase from triple to double to single.
optionExplanations.1: Excluding the bond-strength statement is wrong, since a double bond is genuinely less than twice as strong as a single bond.
optionExplanations.3: Excluding the six-electron statement is wrong, since a triple bond genuinely shares six electrons.
optionExplanations.4: Choosing the six-electron statement alone ignores the two correct statements about length and strength.

formulaNotes: Shared electrons: single bond = 1 pair (2 electrons), double bond = 2 pairs (4 electrons), triple bond = 3 pairs (6 electrons). Approximate strengths: single ~347, double ~614, triple ~839 kJ/mol, so the double bond is less than twice the single.

shortExplanation: Gallium is in group 13 and forms Ga3+, so gallium carbonate must be Ga2(CO3)3, not GaCO3; the other formulae correctly balance their ionic charges.
solutionSteps: Carbonate is CO3 2-; balancing with Ga3+ requires the formula Ga2(CO3)3.
GaCO3 would need Ga2+, which gallium does not form, so it is incorrect.
Check the others: Cs+ with NO3- gives CsNO3; Be2+ with SO4 2- gives BeSO4.
Sn4+ with S2- gives SnS2; Ba2+ with two HCO3- gives Ba(HCO3)2. All correct.
keyConcept: Ionic formulae must balance total positive and negative charge, using group position to assign ion charge.
commonMistake: Assuming gallium behaves like a +2 metal; group 13 metals typically form 3+ ions.

optionExplanations.1: CsNO3 correctly pairs Cs+ with NO3-.
optionExplanations.2: BeSO4 correctly pairs Be2+ with SO4 2-.
optionExplanations.4: Ba(HCO3)2 correctly pairs Ba2+ with two HCO3- ions.

shortExplanation: Assigning oxygen as -2 and the halogens as -1, nitrogen is +3 in NOCl and KNO2, +4 in NO2, and +5 in NO2Cl and Ca(NO3)2, so the oxidation numbers shown are 3, 4 and 5.
solutionSteps: The distinct oxidation numbers are 3, 4 and 5.
keyConcept: Oxidation numbers are found by fixing O at -2 and halogens at -1, then solving for the neutral or ionic total.
commonMistake: Miscounting NO2Cl as +4 by forgetting the chlorine contributes -1, which raises nitrogen to +5.

optionExplanations.0: '3, 4, 5, 6' includes +6, which nitrogen never reaches in these compounds.
optionExplanations.1: '2, 3, 4, 5' includes +2, which does not appear here.
optionExplanations.3: '4, 5, 6' omits the +3 seen in NOCl and KNO2 and adds a non-existent +6.

formulaNotes: Sum of oxidation numbers = overall charge; O = -2, Cl = -1, K = +1, Ca = +2.

shortExplanation: Balancing potassium gives b = 2, and balancing sulfur gives a = 6; matching hydrogen atoms (12 from acid plus 30 from ethanol equals 20 in acetic acid plus 2c) yields c = 11, which also balances oxygen.
solutionSteps: Potassium: 4 K on the left equals 2b on the right, so b = 2.
Sulfur: a must equal 4 (MnSO4) + 2 (K2SO4) = 6, so a = 6.
Hydrogen left: 6*2 (H2SO4) + 5*6 (ethanol) = 12 + 30 = 42.
Hydrogen right: 5*4 (acetic acid) + 2c = 20 + 2c.
Set 42 = 20 + 2c, giving c = 11.
Check oxygen: left 16 + 24 + 5 = 45; right 16 + 8 + 10 + 11 = 45, balanced.
keyConcept: Balance a redox equation by conserving each element in turn, then confirm with hydrogen and oxygen.
commonMistake: Forgetting the 6 H per ethanol molecule when counting hydrogen, which throws off the water coefficient.

optionExplanations.0: 21 overcounts water; it does not satisfy the hydrogen balance of 42 total H atoms.
optionExplanations.2: 16 does not balance hydrogen (would require 52 H atoms on the left).
optionExplanations.3: 17 gives too many H atoms on the right, breaking the balance.

formulaNotes: With a = 6, b = 2: H balance 12 + 30 = 20 + 2c gives c = 11.

shortExplanation: Ethane (C2H6) has molar mass 30 g/mol, so 3000 g is 100 mol; each molecule has 6 hydrogen atoms, giving 600 mol of H atoms, which is 600 * 6.0*10^23 = 3.6*10^26 atoms.
solutionSteps: Molar mass of C2H6 = 2*12 + 6*1 = 30 g/mol.
Moles of ethane = 3000 g / 30 g/mol = 100 mol.
Each ethane has 6 H atoms, so moles of H = 100 * 6 = 600 mol.
keyConcept: Number of atoms = moles of substance x atoms per molecule x Avogadro constant.
commonMistake: Forgetting to convert kilograms to grams, or omitting the factor of 6 hydrogen atoms per ethane molecule.

optionExplanations.2: 6.0*10^25 corresponds to only 100 mol of atoms, ignoring the 6 H per molecule.
optionExplanations.3: 3.6*10^23 is off by a factor of 1000, treating the mass as grams not kilograms scaled wrongly.
optionExplanations.4: 6.0*10^22 is far too small, equivalent to only 0.1 mol of atoms.

formulaNotes: N = n * N_A, with n(H) = (mass / molar mass) * 6.

shortExplanation: The passage sets the economic and personal benefits of workforce mobility against the growing costs of caring for isolated elderly people, so the balanced conclusion is that the benefits must be weighed against those costs.
solutionSteps: The passage lists benefits of mobility: more opportunities and a stronger economy.
It then lists costs: elderly people without nearby family and increased state care funding.
A valid conclusion must reflect both sides rather than favour one prescription.
The statement weighing benefits against costs captures exactly this balance.
keyConcept: A conclusion must follow from and summarise the balance of reasons given, not add new prescriptions.
commonMistake: Choosing a prescriptive option (e.g. people should stay near home) that goes beyond what the balanced passage supports.

optionExplanations.2: 'People should find work close to home' is a recommendation the passage never argues for.
optionExplanations.3: 'The state should provide care to make mobility possible' picks one side and adds an unstated policy claim.
optionExplanations.4: 'People should prioritise caring for parents over work' contradicts the acknowledged benefits of mobility.

shortExplanation: The argument rests on drug companies fearing imitators who could copy disclosed information; if strong patent laws stop competitors from using that information to make rival drugs, the fear is removed and the argument collapses.
solutionSteps: The conclusion is that companies will stop introducing new drugs for fear of imitators.
This depends on rivals being able to exploit the disclosed manufacturing details.
If strong patent laws prevent rivals from using that information, there is no real threat of imitation.
So this statement most directly undermines the reasoning.
keyConcept: Weaken an argument by removing the assumption its conclusion depends on.
commonMistake: Choosing a statement that supports the companies' secrecy concern instead of neutralising the fear of imitation.

optionExplanations.0: 'Enough drugs already exist' addresses need, not the fear-of-imitators mechanism the argument uses.
optionExplanations.1: 'Secrecy is vital for survival' actually strengthens the companies' concern.
optionExplanations.2: 'People may avoid drugs when better informed' is a different issue unrelated to imitators.

shortExplanation: All the reasons about strict laws, high costs, and the willingness to use cheaper methods build toward the point that the law must change to save these buildings.
solutionSteps: The passage states buildings are doomed without a change in the law.
It supports this by noting current laws make renovation too expensive or impractical.
It notes people would maintain them if allowed cheaper modern methods.
These reasons converge on the conclusion that a legal change is needed to preserve the buildings.
keyConcept: The main conclusion is the claim all the other statements are given to support.
commonMistake: Selecting a supporting reason (e.g. current laws make renovation too expensive) rather than the overall conclusion it backs.

optionExplanations.0: 'Nothing wrong with changing character' is an intermediate value claim, not the overall point.
optionExplanations.1: 'Buildings need strict-rule renovation' contradicts the passage's call for looser rules.
optionExplanations.3: 'Existing laws make buildings too expensive' is a supporting reason, not the conclusion.

shortExplanation: The passage argues against assuming foreign travel is uniquely valuable and ends by asserting that projects within one's own society can be just as rewarding, which is its main conclusion.
solutionSteps: The passage challenges the belief that foreign travel is inherently or uniquely beneficial.
It notes downsides of global travel and the value of home-based projects.
The final claim is that working within our own society can be equally rewarding.
This is the conclusion the other points support.
keyConcept: Identify the claim that the rest of the passage is marshalled to establish.
commonMistake: Picking a narrower supporting point about confidence and independence instead of the broad equal-reward conclusion.

optionExplanations.0: 'Foreign projects must include community work' is a condition the passage never states.
optionExplanations.1: 'Foreign travel is not the only way to gain confidence' is a supporting sub-point, not the main claim.
optionExplanations.3: 'There is inherent benefit in going abroad' is the belief the passage argues against.

shortExplanation: The argument only suggests success and motivation may share a common cause in aptitude; it never assumes you must have special aptitude in order to be motivated, so that statement is not a flaw of the argument.
solutionSteps: Identify the argument's flaws: it treats feeling successful/motivated as being so, and overgeneralises to all learning.
It also fails to rule out successful learners who lacked motivation, and rests on only adult learners.
The claim about assuming motivation requires special aptitude misdescribes the text, which only says both may be due to aptitude.
So that statement is NOT a flaw the argument commits.
keyConcept: A 'NOT a flaw' answer must be something the argument does not actually do.
commonMistake: Overlooking that the passage says aptitude 'may' cause both, so it never assumes aptitude is required for motivation.

optionExplanations.0: Assuming felt success equals real success is a genuine flaw the argument makes.
optionExplanations.1: Assuming felt motivation equals real motivation is likewise a genuine flaw.
optionExplanations.2: Failing to rule out successful learners who lacked motivation is a real gap in the reasoning.

shortExplanation: The argument overturns a nationwide finding using a survey taken only in a heavy-traffic area, whose respondents are unlikely to represent the whole population, which is the key flaw.
solutionSteps: The nationwide survey found most people would not give up their cars.
The rebuttal uses a survey limited to a heavy-traffic area where 76% favoured public transport.
People in heavy-traffic areas have atypical motivations, so this sample is not representative.
Concluding the national findings are wrong from an unrepresentative sample is the flaw.
keyConcept: A conclusion about a whole population needs a representative sample, not a special subgroup.
commonMistake: Focusing on missing implementation detail (how to improve transport) instead of the sampling flaw.

optionExplanations.0: Not specifying which transport to improve is a detail gap, not the core reasoning error.
optionExplanations.1: 'Counter arguments not explained' is vague and not the specific flaw.
optionExplanations.3: Ignoring the 24% is minor; the real problem is the whole sample's non-representativeness.

shortExplanation: Total capacity is 700 spaces; the system admits up to 90% of that (630 cars), and with 4 road-level spaces reserved for staff, the maximum number of public cars is 630 - 4 = 626.
solutionSteps: Each of the top seven levels holds 2*15 + 6*10 = 90 cars, so 7*90 = 630.
The road level holds 2*15 + 4*10 = 30 + 40 = 70 cars.
Total capacity = 630 + 70 = 700.
The system stops at 90% of capacity: 0.9*700 = 630 cars admitted.
Subtract the 4 staff-reserved spaces: 630 - 4 = 626 public cars.
keyConcept: Compute total capacity, apply the percentage cap, then subtract unavailable reserved spaces.
commonMistake: Reporting 630 (the 90% cap) without deducting the 4 staff-reserved spaces.

optionExplanations.0: 644 exceeds even the 90% admission cap of 630.
optionExplanations.2: 696 ignores the 90% limit and the reserved staff spaces.
optionExplanations.3: 630 is the 90% cap but does not subtract the 4 staff spaces.

formulaNotes: Public max = 0.9 * total capacity - reserved staff spaces = 0.9*700 - 4 = 626.

shortExplanation: The regular jar costs 4.50/0.25 = 18.00 per kg and the large jar costs 6.30/0.40 = 15.75 per kg, so the large jar is 18.00 - 15.75 = 2.25 cheaper per kilogram.
solutionSteps: Regular jar price per kg = 4.50 / 0.250 kg = 18.00 per kg.
Large jar price per kg = 6.30 / 0.400 kg = 15.75 per kg.
keyConcept: Compare value for money by converting each price to a common unit (price per kilogram).
commonMistake: Comparing the jar prices directly instead of normalising to price per kilogram.

optionExplanations.0: 3.60 does not match the 2.25 per-kg difference from the correct division.
optionExplanations.1: 6.00 overstates the saving and matches no correct calculation.
optionExplanations.3: 3.15 misapplies the figures and is not the per-kg difference.

formulaNotes: Price per kg = cost / mass in kg; saving = 18.00 - 15.75 = 2.25.

shortExplanation: Turning the watch over reverses the four digits left-to-right and rotates each one 180 degrees. Only 15:51 (3.51pm) maps back onto itself, so it reads the same either way.
solutionSteps: Upside down, the four digits reverse in order and each rotates 180 degrees: 0->0, 1->1, 2->2, 5->5, 8->8, 6->9, 9->6, while 3, 4 and 7 become unreadable.
For the display to look identical, the first digit must equal the rotation of the fourth, and the second must equal the rotation of the third.
Convert 3.51pm to 24-hour time: 15:51, digits 1, 5, 5, 1.
Reverse to 1, 5, 5, 1 and rotate each digit, which leaves 1, 5, 5, 1 = 15:51 - identical.
The example confirms the rule: 10:50 reversed and rotated becomes 05:01, which is one minute past five.
keyConcept: A 180-degree turn of a digital display both reverses the digit order and rotates each digit, so only 0, 1, 2, 5, 8 (and the 6/9 pair) survive.
commonMistake: Rotating each digit in place while forgetting that the whole display also reverses left-to-right.

optionExplanations.0: 5.51am is 05:51; reversed and rotated it reads 15:50, a different time.
optionExplanations.2: 1.01am is 01:01; reversed and rotated it reads 10:10, not the same time.
optionExplanations.3: 3.21pm is 15:21; reversed and rotated it reads 12:51, not the same time.

figureExplanation: The worked example shows the display 10:50 read upside down becoming 05:01 (one minute past five), which fixes the reverse-and-rotate rule used to test each option.

shortExplanation: With 350 votes it is impossible for two other candidates to each exceed 350 (that would need over 700 votes plus the candidate's 350), so this candidate must be in the top two and therefore either won or came second.
solutionSteps: A second ballot happening means no one exceeded 500 in the first ballot.
For the candidate to miss the top two, two others must each beat 350 votes.
Two candidates each above 350 need more than 700 votes, leaving under 300 for our candidate, contradicting their 350.
So the candidate is guaranteed a top-two place and reaches the second ballot.
In the second ballot they either win or finish second.
keyConcept: Use vote totals to bound how many candidates can outscore a given tally.
commonMistake: Assuming 350 votes could leave the candidate third, which is arithmetically impossible out of 1000 total votes.

optionExplanations.0: Third place is impossible, so an option allowing third is wrong.
optionExplanations.2: This claims the candidate did not win, but winning the second ballot is possible.
optionExplanations.3: Coming third cannot happen given the vote arithmetic.

shortExplanation: The 1904 winning time of 21.6 seconds was the fastest Olympic time until it was beaten by 21.2 in 1932, a span of 28 years, which is the longest any record stood unbroken.
solutionSteps: Track the fastest time so far (the Olympic record) as years progress.
21.6 set in 1904 was not beaten in 1908, 1912, 1920, 1924 (a tie, not a break), or 1928.
It was finally beaten by 21.2 in 1932, so it stood from 1904 to 1932 = 28 years.
The next long spell, 20.7 (1936) beaten by 20.62 (1960), is 24 years, which is shorter.
The longest unbroken period is therefore 28 years.
keyConcept: An Olympic record stands until a strictly faster time is achieved; a tie does not break it.
commonMistake: Counting the 1924 tie (21.6) as breaking the record, which would wrongly shorten the span.

optionExplanations.1: 16 years matches no correct record-to-record gap here.
optionExplanations.2: 24 years is the 1936-1960 span (20.7 to 20.62), which is not the longest.
optionExplanations.4: 20 years does not correspond to any record standing period in the data.

shortExplanation: The whole argument is built to show that the orbital deviations cannot tell us whether Planet X exists, because the calculated orbits are probably wrong regardless of any extra planet.
solutionSteps: The passage explains the deviations would occur even if the orbits were wrongly predicted.
It argues old, inaccurate data make the calculated orbits probably wrong.
So the deviations do not distinguish between a real Planet X and simple calculation error.
The main conclusion is that these deviations cannot tell us whether Planet X exists.
keyConcept: The main conclusion is the claim the reasoning ultimately supports, not a supporting premise.
commonMistake: Selecting 'the calculations are probably wrong', which is a supporting reason, not the final conclusion.

optionExplanations.0: The passage does not claim Planet X cannot exist, only that the deviations are uninformative.
optionExplanations.1: This contradicts the argument, which casts doubt on the undiscovered-planet inference.
optionExplanations.3: 'Calculations are probably wrong' is a premise supporting the main conclusion, not the conclusion itself.

shortExplanation: The argument treats a correlation between the name John and university attendance as if the name causes attendance, when both are more plausibly linked to underlying social factors, so it confuses correlation with cause.
solutionSteps: The evidence is that people named John attend university more often than those named Wayne.
The argument leaps to the claim that naming a child John improves his chances.
But the name is likely a marker of background factors, not a cause of attendance.
This mistakes a correlation for a causal relationship.
keyConcept: A correlation between two variables does not establish that one causes the other.
commonMistake: Labelling it a hasty generalisation instead of the correlation-causation error at its core.

optionExplanations.0: Drawing a general conclusion from specific evidence does not capture the causal error here.
optionExplanations.1: Necessary/sufficient confusion is not what the argument does; it is about causation.
optionExplanations.2: The argument does cite evidence (records), so 'no evidence' is inaccurate.

shortExplanation: The passage's points about poor literacy and employer expectations all support the recommendation that students must be helped to recognise how important good writing skills are.
solutionSteps: The passage notes low literacy among science undergraduates and that good writing matters.
It notes employers expect graduates to communicate fluently and accurately.
These reasons support the call to make students recognise the importance of literacy.
That recommendation is the main conclusion.
keyConcept: The main conclusion is the recommendation the supporting facts are given to justify.
commonMistake: Choosing a factual premise (e.g. many graduates cannot write correctly) rather than the recommendation it supports.

optionExplanations.0: 'Education is failing' is a broad claim the passage does not set out to prove.
optionExplanations.2: 'Many graduates cannot write correctly' is a supporting premise, not the conclusion.
optionExplanations.3: 'Employment depends on literacy' is a reason offered, not the overall point.

shortExplanation: The packet holds 24 full scoops of powder. Using only three-quarters of a scoop per wash makes the fixed amount of powder last longer: 24 divided by 3/4 gives 32 washes.
solutionSteps: Total powder in packet = 24 scoops (24 full-scoop washes).
Each wash now uses 3/4 of a scoop.
Number of washes = 24 / (3/4) = 24 * 4/3 = 32.
keyConcept: Dividing a fixed total by a smaller per-use amount increases the number of uses.
commonMistake: Multiplying 24 by 3/4 (giving 18) instead of dividing by 3/4.

optionExplanations.1: 18 comes from taking three-quarters of 24, which reduces washes rather than increasing them.
optionExplanations.3: 26 has no arithmetic basis in the given quantities.
optionExplanations.4: 30 does not result from 24 / (3/4).

shortExplanation: The argument concludes two-year engineering degrees are unrealistic because attainment is already low after two years of a three-year course. This only holds if the two-year course would not simply pack in more teaching each year.
solutionSteps: The reasoning compares progress after two years of a normal three-year course.
It assumes a two-year degree delivers the same yearly teaching, not compressed extra content.
If a two-year course had far more teaching per year, the low-attainment point would collapse.
Therefore the unstated assumption is equal teaching per year.
keyConcept: An assumption is an unstated premise the conclusion needs in order to follow.
commonMistake: Choosing a plausible background fact that the argument does not actually rely on.

optionExplanations.1: Whether school exams are easier is a possible cause but is not required for the conclusion.
optionExplanations.2: The relative importance of maths and physics over time is not something the argument depends on.
optionExplanations.4: Student motivation is never invoked by the reasoning.

shortExplanation: The passage stresses that tiredness evidence is not conclusive while drink-driving evidence is. The natural conclusion is that prosecuting sleep-related cases will be harder than prosecuting drink driving.
solutionSteps: Identify the key contrast: inconclusive evidence for falling asleep vs conclusive evidence for drink driving.
A conclusion must follow from this stated contrast.
Weaker evidence means harder proof in court.
So prosecution for falling asleep will be less easy than for drink driving.
keyConcept: A valid conclusion follows directly from the evidence actually stated.
commonMistake: Picking a strong causal or policy claim that the passage never establishes.

optionExplanations.0: The passage does not compare the overall scale of the two problems.
optionExplanations.1: Long working hours as a cause is not stated or supported.
optionExplanations.2: Reducing driving hours is a policy recommendation the passage does not make.

shortExplanation: Apply the 0.20 packet reduction first (1.60 to 1.40), then the 10% off the whole bill applies to that item too, giving 1.40 * 0.9 = 1.26.
solutionSteps: Marked price of pasta = 1.60 - 0.20 = 1.40.
Bill exceeds 10, so 10% off applies to every item.
keyConcept: A fixed discount and a percentage discount are applied in sequence to reach the final price.
commonMistake: Applying 10% to the original 1.60 before subtracting the 0.20.

optionExplanations.1: 1.24 would need a slightly larger fixed discount than 0.20.
optionExplanations.2: 1.30 ignores the 10% discount entirely.
optionExplanations.3: 1.12 applies 20% instead of the 0.20 then 10% sequence.

formulaNotes: Final = (list - fixed_discount) * (1 - 0.10).

shortExplanation: The passage argues that whether happiness is set by genes or by a soul, 'either way, you're born as you are', so we may as well accept that it is decided at birth to some extent.
solutionSteps: Locate the summarising line: 'Either way, you're born as you are.'
The writer downplays the fear of genetic influence.
The point being argued for is acceptance that potential happiness is partly set at birth.
That is the main conclusion, not the twin-study statistic used to support it.
keyConcept: The main conclusion is the claim the rest of the passage is trying to persuade you of.
commonMistake: Selecting the supporting statistic (half of happiness is genetic) instead of the point it supports.

optionExplanations.0: This is the study's finding used as evidence, not the conclusion drawn from it.
optionExplanations.2: The passage presents soul and genes as examples, not an exclusive either/or claim.
optionExplanations.3: 'No control at all' is stronger than the passage's 'to some extent decided at birth'.

shortExplanation: Because BetaAir's plane (60 min) is faster than AlphaAir's (90 min), Johnston overtakes AlphaAir planes that departed earlier. Matching positions shows he passes the AlphaAir flights that left at t=0, t=-10 and t=-20, so he passes 3 before landing.
solutionSteps: Let an AlphaAir plane depart Rome at t=0; Johnston departs at t=5 and lands at t=5+60=65.
Express positions along the route: an AlphaAir plane leaving at time a is at (t-a)/90; Johnston is at (t-5)/60.
Set the positions equal: (t-5)/60 = (t-a)/90, which gives t = 15 - 2a at each meeting.
AlphaAir departure times are multiples of 10: a=0 gives t=15, a=-10 gives t=35, a=-20 gives t=55, all within the flight window [5, 65].
a=-30 gives t=75 (after Johnston lands) and a=10 gives t=-5 (before either takes off), so both are excluded.
Johnston therefore passes exactly 3 AlphaAir planes.
keyConcept: Relative-motion overtaking: a faster plane catches slower ones that departed earlier, provided the crossing falls within its own flight time.
commonMistake: Counting only planes that depart after Johnston, or forgetting the earlier AlphaAir planes still airborne ahead of him.

optionExplanations.0: 0 ignores that BetaAir (60 min) is faster than AlphaAir (90 min) and so overtakes several planes.
optionExplanations.2: 2 misses one of the three qualifying earlier departures.
optionExplanations.4: 4 wrongly includes the plane that left at a=-30, whose crossing time t=75 is after Johnston has landed.

formulaNotes: Meeting time t = 15 - 2a, from (t-5)/60 = (t-a)/90.

shortExplanation: The final 60 miles equal the fraction left after 60% is done and then 60% of the remainder: that is 0.4 * 0.4 = 0.16 of the whole, so total = 60 / 0.16 = 375 miles.
solutionSteps: Let total distance = T. Completed so far = 0.60T, remaining = 0.40T.
Next he does 60% of the remainder: 0.60 * 0.40T = 0.24T.
Distance still left = 0.40T - 0.24T = 0.16T.
This equals 60 miles, so T = 60 / 0.16 = 375 miles.
keyConcept: Sequential percentages compound multiplicatively on the remaining amount.
commonMistake: Treating the last 60 miles as 40% of the journey (giving 150) instead of 16%.

optionExplanations.1: 250 miles does not satisfy 0.16T = 60.
optionExplanations.2: 300 comes from mishandling the second 60% step.
optionExplanations.3: 225 miles does not give 60 miles as its remaining 16%.

shortExplanation: The 4cm side walls reduce the internal floor to 48-8 = 40cm by 44-8 = 36cm; the thicker 8cm base only reduces internal height, not the floor dimensions.
solutionSteps: External width 48cm minus two 4cm walls = 48 - 8 = 40cm.
External depth 44cm minus two 4cm walls = 44 - 8 = 36cm.
The 8cm base affects height only, so the internal base measures 40cm x 36cm.
keyConcept: Wall thickness is subtracted twice (both sides) from each in-plane dimension.
commonMistake: Using the 8cm base thickness to shrink the base's length and width instead of the height.

optionExplanations.0: 40cm x 40cm subtracts too little from the 44cm depth.
optionExplanations.1: 36cm x 36cm subtracts 8cm from both, wrong for the 48cm width.
optionExplanations.2: 40cm x 32cm over-subtracts from the depth.

shortExplanation: The single hand is fixed pointing straight up, so each dial reads whatever mark it has brought to the top. Because each dial is numbered opposite to its own rotation, the hour dial reads 8 and the minute dial reads 40, giving 8:40.
solutionSteps: The one hand is fixed pointing up, so the time is whichever mark each dial has rotated to the top.
The hour dial turns clockwise, so for time to advance correctly its hour marks must be numbered anticlockwise around the face.
Its large '12' dot sits at the lower-left (about the 8 o'clock position), so the mark now at the top is the 8, and the hour is 8.
The minute dial turns anticlockwise, so its minute marks must be numbered clockwise.
Its large '0/60' dot sits at the lower-right (about the 4 o'clock position), so the mark now at the top is the 40, and the minutes are 40.
Therefore the time is 8:40.
keyConcept: With a fixed pointer, each dial must be numbered opposite to its direction of rotation so that time reads forward; the value shown is whatever mark sits under the pointer at the top.
commonMistake: Reading each dial as an ordinary clockwise clock, which gives 3:40 or 3:20 instead of 8:40.

optionExplanations.0: 9:20 reads the minute dial the wrong way (giving 20 instead of 40) and also places the hour one division off (9 instead of 8).
optionExplanations.1: 3:20 misreads both dials as ordinary clockwise clocks.
optionExplanations.3: 3:40 reads the hour dial as a clockwise clock; because its numbering runs the other way, the hour is 8, not 3.
optionExplanations.4: 8:20 reads the minute dial the wrong way; with clockwise minute numbering the top mark is 40, not 20.

figureExplanation: The large hour dot lies at the lower-left (about the 8 o'clock position) and the large minute dot at the lower-right (about the 4 o'clock position), with the hand straight up. Allowing for the stated opposite rotations, the marks at the top read 8 hours and 40 minutes.

shortExplanation: Only the United States shows both a fall in unemployment (6.1 to 5.9) and a rise in inflation (+0.3 to +0.4) from February to March.
solutionSteps: 'Unemployment has fallen' means March unemployment below February: United States (5.9 < 6.1), Germany (9.2 < 9.3) and UK (9.1 < 9.2) qualify.
'Rise in the inflation rate' means March inflation above February: United States (+0.4 > +0.3) and France (+0.3 > 0.0) qualify.
Both conditions together: only the United States appears in both lists.
keyConcept: Apply two separate conditions and find the single item that satisfies both simultaneously.
commonMistake: Checking only one of the two conditions, or reading a lower inflation figure as if it were a fall in unemployment.

optionExplanations.1: The UK's unemployment fell but its inflation dropped (+0.5 to +0.2), so inflation did not rise.
optionExplanations.2: France's inflation rose but its unemployment was unchanged at 12.6, so unemployment did not fall.
optionExplanations.4: Germany's unemployment fell but its inflation stayed at +0.1, so inflation did not rise.

figureExplanation: In the table the United States row shows unemployment 6.1 to 5.9 (a fall) and inflation +0.3 to +0.4 (a rise), the only country meeting both conditions.

shortExplanation: The argument blames the great nations for relying on trucks instead of helicopters. This only makes sense if those nations actually had helicopters that could reach Haiti within the week.
solutionSteps: The conclusion is that the great nations should be ashamed of failing to deliver aid by helicopter.
Blame requires that the better option was actually available to them.
So the argument assumes they had helicopters capable of reaching Haiti in that time.
Without that assumption the criticism collapses.
keyConcept: Blaming someone for not acting assumes the action was genuinely possible for them.
commonMistake: Choosing a fact about Haiti's roads or food supply that the criticism does not depend on.

optionExplanations.0: Whether trucks specifically could be imported is not what the shame claim rests on.
optionExplanations.2: Total food availability inside Haiti is a separate issue from the delivery-method criticism.
optionExplanations.4: The passage states images were seen worldwide, so this contradicts the text rather than being an assumption.

shortExplanation: The Inca Empire was centred on Cusco in modern-day Peru, from which it expanded along the Andes.
solutionSteps: Recall the Inca heartland and capital city, Cusco.
Cusco lies in present-day Peru.
Therefore the civilization was centred in Peru.
keyConcept: The Inca capital Cusco is in Peru, the core of the empire.
commonMistake: Confusing the empire's outer reaches (Ecuador, Bolivia, Chile) with its centre.

optionExplanations.0: Chile held only the empire's far southern frontier.
optionExplanations.3: Ecuador was a northern part of the empire, not its centre.
optionExplanations.4: Bolivia lay within the empire but was not its core.

shortExplanation: A placebo is an inactive substance or sham treatment given for its psychological effect, with no pharmacological action of its own.
solutionSteps: Define placebo: a dummy treatment lacking active ingredients.
Its effects arise from expectation, not chemistry.
So it is best described as an inactive drug or treatment.
keyConcept: A placebo has no active therapeutic ingredient; it is a control or expectation-based treatment.
commonMistake: Assuming a placebo is a real but weak drug rather than an inactive one.

optionExplanations.0: A painkiller has genuine analgesic action, unlike a placebo.
optionExplanations.1: A local anaesthetic actively blocks nerve signals.
optionExplanations.4: A sedative is a pharmacologically active depressant.

shortExplanation: Hannibal, the Carthaginian general, famously led his army, including elephants, across the Alps to invade Italy during the Second Punic War.
solutionSteps: Recall the celebrated Alpine crossing with war elephants.
This was Hannibal of Carthage in 218 BC.
So the answer is Hannibal.
keyConcept: Hannibal's crossing of the Alps is the classic feat associated with this question.
commonMistake: Confusing Hannibal with his father Hamilcar or with Roman leaders.

optionExplanations.0: Octavius (Augustus) was a Roman leader, not the Alpine crosser.
optionExplanations.2: Hamilcar was Hannibal's father and did not make this crossing.
optionExplanations.3: Augustus was Rome's first emperor, unrelated to this feat.

shortExplanation: The World Health Organisation has its headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland.
solutionSteps: Recall that many UN specialised agencies are based in Geneva.
The WHO's main headquarters is in Geneva.
So Geneva is correct.
keyConcept: WHO headquarters are located in Geneva, Switzerland.
commonMistake: Assuming WHO is based in Washington DC or Rome like other agencies.

optionExplanations.0: Nairobi hosts UN environment offices, not WHO headquarters.
optionExplanations.1: Washington DC hosts bodies like PAHO and the World Bank, not WHO's HQ.
optionExplanations.2: Rome hosts the FAO, not the WHO.

shortExplanation: Galileo studied pendulums and improved the telescope, thermometer and microscope, but he did not design an electric battery; that was Alessandro Volta, much later.
solutionSteps: Review Galileo's contributions: pendulum timing, telescope, thermoscope, early microscope.
The electric battery was invented by Volta around 1800, after Galileo's era.
So the electric battery is the thing Galileo did NOT do.
keyConcept: The electric battery is attributed to Volta, not Galileo.
commonMistake: Assuming all listed instruments belong to Galileo because he was a prolific experimenter.

optionExplanations.0: Galileo did observe that a pendulum's period is regular.
optionExplanations.1: Galileo notably improved and used the telescope for astronomy.
optionExplanations.3: Galileo built an early thermoscope, a forerunner of the thermometer.

shortExplanation: Start from centre-radius form (x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 = r^2 with centre (-1.5, 0.5) and r = 3, expand, then double every term to clear the halves. This gives 2x^2 + 6x + 2y^2 - 2y - 13 = 0.
