keyConcept: Magnetic repulsion occurs only between two magnets with like poles; unmagnetised magnetic materials are only ever attracted.
commonMistake: Thinking any magnetic or charged bar could be repelled, when only a permanent magnet with a like pole is repelled.

optionExplanations.0: Unmagnetised soft iron is magnetised by induction and attracted, not repelled.
optionExplanations.1: Unmagnetised cobalt is ferromagnetic and would be attracted.
optionExplanations.2: A charged copper bar is attracted to a magnet via induced charge, not repelled.

shortExplanation: A single 4 ohm resistor is in series with two parallel 4 ohm resistors, giving 4 + 2 = 6 ohm total, so the main-line current is 12/6 = 2.0 A (ammeter Y). This splits equally between the branches, so the ammeter in one branch reads 1.0 A (X), and the voltmeter across the series resistor reads 2.0 x 4 = 8.0 V (Z).
solutionSteps: The two 4 ohm resistors in parallel give 4 x 4 / (4 + 4) = 2 ohm.
Add the series 4 ohm resistor: total resistance = 4 + 2 = 6 ohm.
Main-line current from the 12 V supply: I = 12 / 6 = 2.0 A, which is what ammeter Y in the main line reads.
The identical parallel branches split this current equally, so the ammeter in one branch (X) reads 1.0 A.
The voltmeter (Z) sits across the single series resistor and reads 2.0 A x 4 ohm = 8.0 V.
keyConcept: Series resistances add, the main-line current splits equally between identical parallel branches, and a voltmeter reads only the potential drop across the component it spans.
commonMistake: Treating the branch ammeter as the full current, or reading the voltmeter as the supply voltage instead of the drop across its series resistor.

optionExplanations.0: A main-line current of 0.0 A is impossible in a complete circuit carrying current, and 12 V across the series resistor ignores the parallel section.
optionExplanations.3: Currents of 3.0 A and 6.0 A require a far smaller total resistance and ignore the series resistor.
optionExplanations.4: The two currents are right, but 6.0 V misreads the voltmeter; it spans the series resistor and reads 8.0 V.

figureExplanation: One 4 ohm resistor sits in the main line with voltmeter Z across it; ammeter X is in one of two parallel 4 ohm branches, and ammeter Y is in the main line near the battery.
formulaNotes: V = I R; parallel resistance = (R1 R2)/(R1 + R2); series resistances add.

shortExplanation: Falling oestrogen, maximal LH and FSH, and rising progesterone all coincide with the mid-cycle LH surge that triggers ovulation, so the stage is the few days just before and including ovulation.
solutionSteps: Oestrogen peaks just before ovulation and then falls, so it is on the way down around the surge.
The LH and FSH surge reaches its maximum at this point and triggers ovulation.
Progesterone begins to rise as the corpus luteum starts to form at ovulation.
The stage that satisfies all three conditions at once is the window from a few days before ovulation up to the time of ovulation.
keyConcept: The mid-cycle LH and FSH surge coincides with declining oestrogen and the very start of the progesterone rise as ovulation occurs.
commonMistake: Placing peak LH and FSH in the luteal phase, when in fact both hormones fall sharply after ovulation.

optionExplanations.0: At the start of menstruation all of these hormones are low, not maximal, and oestrogen is not yet falling from a peak.
optionExplanations.1: At the end of menstruation FSH is rising but LH is not at its peak and progesterone is not yet rising.
optionExplanations.3: After ovulation LH and FSH have already fallen sharply, so they are not maximal in the luteal phase.
optionExplanations.4: Between the end of menstruation and four days before ovulation oestrogen is rising, not falling, and LH and FSH have not yet peaked.

shortExplanation: The correct ordered subsequence is calcium release, exposure of binding sites, power stroke releasing ADP and phosphate, then detachment of the myosin head, which is 5, 1, 2, 4.
solutionSteps: Calcium ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (event 5).
Calcium binding shifts tropomyosin so the myosin-binding sites on actin are uncovered (event 1).
Myosin binds and performs the power stroke as ADP and phosphate are released from the myosin head (event 2).
A new ATP molecule binds and the myosin head detaches from actin (event 4).
This gives the order 5, 1, 2, 4.
keyConcept: The cross-bridge cycle runs: calcium release, binding-site exposure, power stroke with ADP and phosphate release, then ATP-driven detachment.
commonMistake: Placing detachment of the head before ADP and phosphate are released, or exposing binding sites before calcium is released.

optionExplanations.0: Placing detachment (4) before the power-stroke release of ADP and phosphate (2) reverses the correct order.
optionExplanations.1: Releasing ADP and phosphate (2) before the binding sites are uncovered (1) is impossible, since myosin has not yet bound.
optionExplanations.2: Starting with binding sites uncovered (1) before calcium release, and ending with sodium channels opening (3), is out of order.
optionExplanations.4: This omits calcium release before site exposure and ends with detachment before the ADP and phosphate release, so it is out of order.

shortExplanation: A dihybrid cross QqRr x QqRr with complete dominance gives the classic 9:3:3:1 phenotype ratio, which is 4 distinct phenotypes.
solutionSteps: Each gene has two phenotypes under complete dominance: dominant or recessive.
Two independent genes give 2 * 2 = 4 phenotype combinations.
These appear in the 9:3:3:1 ratio, confirming 4 phenotypes.
keyConcept: For two independently assorting genes with complete dominance, the number of phenotypes is 2 x 2 = 4.
commonMistake: Reporting 9 (the number of genotypes) or 16 (the number of offspring boxes) instead of the number of phenotypes.

optionExplanations.0: 16 is the number of squares in the Punnett grid, not the phenotype count.
optionExplanations.3: 8 does not correspond to genotype or phenotype counts here.
optionExplanations.4: 9 is the number of distinct genotypes, not phenotypes.

formulaNotes: Number of phenotypes (complete dominance) = 2^(number of genes) = 2^2 = 4.

shortExplanation: The radioactive strand marks the original DNA. After three semiconservative replications there are 8 molecules, and only 1 still carries the radioactive strand (12.5%), so the other 7 are completely non-radioactive (87.5%).
solutionSteps: Only the radioactive strand can be tracked as the original DNA, since new and old non-radioactive strands are indistinguishable.
Semiconservative replication conserves each parental strand, so the one radioactive strand always ends up in exactly one molecule.
Three rounds of replication produce 2^3 = 8 double-stranded molecules.
Molecules still carrying the radioactive (original) strand: 1 of 8 = 12.5%.
Molecules with no radioactive strand at all: 7 of 8 = 87.5%. These figures match row 1.
keyConcept: In semiconservative replication a parental strand is never lost, only distributed among an ever-larger number of molecules.
commonMistake: Treating replication as conservative, or forgetting that only the radioactive strand is trackable, which distorts the fractions.

optionExplanations.0: 87.5% original and 12.5% non-radioactive simply swaps the two correct percentages.
optionExplanations.3: 50% and 50% would apply after a single replication, not three.
optionExplanations.4: 25% and 75% miscount the number of molecules produced after three rounds.

figureExplanation: The starting molecule has one radioactive strand and one non-radioactive strand; only the radioactive strand serves as the trackable original after replication.
formulaNotes: Number of molecules after n replications = 2^n; the single radioactive strand stays in exactly one molecule.

shortExplanation: Photolysis splits water as 2H2O -> O2 + 4H+ + 4e-, directly producing oxygen and protons. Carbon dioxide is not involved.
solutionSteps: Write the photolysis reaction: 2H2O -> O2 + 4H+ + 4e-.
Identify the direct products: oxygen, protons (H+) and electrons.
Carbon dioxide is a reactant of the Calvin cycle, not a photolysis product.
So only oxygen (1) and protons (3) are directly produced.
keyConcept: Photolysis of water in the light reactions yields oxygen, protons, and electrons.
commonMistake: Including carbon dioxide, confusing photolysis with the carbon-fixing Calvin cycle.

optionExplanations.0: 1 only omits the protons that photolysis also releases.
optionExplanations.1: 2 and 3 only wrongly includes carbon dioxide and drops oxygen.
optionExplanations.3: 1 and 2 only wrongly pairs oxygen with carbon dioxide.

shortExplanation: A heterozygous cell that has not replicated its DNA is Aa. At the start of both mitosis and meiosis I the DNA has already been copied in S phase, so each allele exists as two sister chromatids, giving AAaa. This is Aa, AAaa, AAaa.
solutionSteps: A cell just beginning to specialise is in the unreplicated diploid state, so its alleles are simply Aa.
Mitosis is preceded by S phase, so at its start each chromosome carries two identical sister chromatids: A, A, a, a = AAaa.
Meiosis I is also preceded by S phase, so that cell likewise starts as AAaa.
The combination Aa, AAaa, AAaa is the correct row.
keyConcept: DNA replication in S phase duplicates every allele into sister chromatids before both mitosis and meiosis I begin.
commonMistake: Forgetting that meiosis I is also preceded by replication, and so writing Aa instead of AAaa at its start.

optionExplanations.1: This places the replicated state (AAaa) on the unreplicated specialising cell and the unreplicated state on the start of mitosis.
optionExplanations.3: This lists Aa at the start of mitosis, ignoring the preceding DNA replication.
optionExplanations.4: This gives AAaa at the start of mitosis but Aa for meiosis I, ignoring that meiosis I is also post-replication.

figureExplanation: The three situations are an unreplicated specialising cell, the start of mitosis, and the start of meiosis I; the latter two are both post-replication.
formulaNotes: A replicated heterozygous locus has two chromatids per homologue: A, A, a, a (AAaa).

shortExplanation: The central carbon carries an amino group, a carboxylic acid group, a hydrogen and a side chain. The variable R group is the CH3 (label 2) and the acidic group is the COOH (label 3).
solutionSteps: Identify the four groups on the central carbon: H2N (amino), COOH (carboxyl), H, and CH3.
The variable R group is the side chain that differs between amino acids: here CH3, labelled 2.
The acidic group is the carboxyl COOH, labelled 3.
So variable group = 2 and acidic group = 3.
keyConcept: Every amino acid shares an amino group, a carboxyl group and a hydrogen on the alpha carbon, differing only in the R side chain.
commonMistake: Confusing the basic amino group (NH2) with the acidic carboxyl group (COOH).

optionExplanations.0: This calls the hydrogen (label 4) the R group; the hydrogen is not the variable side chain here.
optionExplanations.1: This misassigns the amino group as acidic; COOH is the acidic group.
optionExplanations.3: This picks the amino group (label 1) as the R group, but the amino group is common to all amino acids.

figureExplanation: Label 1 points to H2N, label 2 to CH3, label 3 to COOH and label 4 to H around the central carbon.
formulaNotes: Amino acid general form: H2N-CHR-COOH.

shortExplanation: Osteocytes are mature bone cells, so in a shoulder joint they are found in bone tissue.
solutionSteps: Recall that osteocytes are the mature cells of bone.
Of the listed tissues, only bone tissue contains osteocytes.
Select bone tissue.
keyConcept: Osteocytes are bone cells housed in the lacunae of bone tissue.
commonMistake: Confusing osteocytes with chondrocytes, which are the cells of cartilage.

optionExplanations.1: Ligaments are dense connective tissue with fibroblasts, not osteocytes.
optionExplanations.2: Cartilage contains chondrocytes, not osteocytes.
optionExplanations.4: Skin contains keratinocytes and other epidermal/dermal cells, not osteocytes.

shortExplanation: A probe fluoresces only if it is complementary to a region of the sample TGGTCAAGATTAT. ACCAGT is complementary to the sample's TGGTCA and CTAATA is complementary to its GATTAT, so those two spots bind and light up.
solutionSteps: Hybridisation requires the probe to be complementary (A-T, G-C) to a region of the sample, not identical to it.
Sample start TGGTCA pairs with ACCAGT: T-A, G-C, G-C, T-A, C-G, A-T.
Sample region GATTAT pairs with CTAATA: G-C, A-T, T-A, T-A, A-T, T-A.
The probes TGGTCA and GATTAT are identical to sample regions, so they cannot base-pair with them.
Only the spots carrying ACCAGT and CTAATA fluoresce.
keyConcept: Probe hybridisation depends on complementary base pairing, not on matching the sample's exact sequence.
commonMistake: Marking probes whose sequences are identical to the sample, which actually cannot hybridise because identical strands do not base-pair.

optionExplanations.0: Not all four bind; the probes identical to sample regions cannot hybridise.
optionExplanations.2: The probe GATTAT is identical to a sample region, not complementary, so its spot does not fluoresce.
optionExplanations.3: Both GATTAT and TGGTCA are identical to sample sequences, so neither of those spots binds.

figureExplanation: The table lists probes GATTAT, CTAATA, ACCAGT, TGGTCA; comparing each with the sample shows only ACCAGT and CTAATA are complementary.
formulaNotes: Complement rule along the sample: A pairs with T, G pairs with C.

shortExplanation: Period X is at the very start, during atrial contraction and ventricular filling. The atrium empties so its blood volume decreases, ventricular pressure is well below aortic pressure so the semilunar valve is closed, and the ventricle wall is still relaxed.
solutionSteps: Locate X at the beginning of the cycle, before ventricular pressure rises steeply.
This is atrial systole and late ventricular diastole: the atrium contracts and pushes blood into the ventricle, so the volume of blood in the atrium decreases.
Ventricular pressure is far below aortic pressure, so the aortic semilunar valve stays closed.
The ventricle has not yet contracted, so its wall muscle is relaxed.
Decreases, closed, and relax together identify the correct row.
keyConcept: The aortic semilunar valve opens only when ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure, which has not happened during early filling.
commonMistake: Assuming the ventricle is already contracting or the aortic valve is open at the very start of the cycle.

optionExplanations.0: This says the aortic valve is open, but it stays closed while ventricular pressure is below aortic pressure.
optionExplanations.1: This says the atrial volume increases and the ventricle contracts, the opposite of atrial emptying with a relaxed ventricle.
optionExplanations.3: This has an open valve and a contracting ventricle, which describes ejection, not the filling phase at X.

figureExplanation: During X the left-ventricle trace is still low and flat while the atrial trace shows its contraction bump, and aortic pressure stays well above ventricular pressure, keeping the aortic valve shut.
formulaNotes: The aortic valve opens when P(ventricle) > P(aorta); before that it is closed.

shortExplanation: During mitosis the valid order is: chromosomes line up at the equator (metaphase), spindle fibres shorten (anaphase), nuclear envelope reappears (telophase), then the cytoplasm divides (cytokinesis). The row reading 'chromosomes line up at the equator - spindle fibres shorten - nuclear envelope reappears - cytoplasm divides' is the only correct sequence.
solutionSteps: Recall the ordered stages: DNA condenses, nuclear envelope breaks down, chromosomes align at the equator, spindle fibres shorten to pull chromatids apart, nuclear envelope re-forms, cytoplasm divides.
Test each row as a left-to-right subsequence of that order.
The row 'chromosomes line up at the equator -> spindle fibres shorten -> nuclear envelope reappears -> cytoplasm divides' follows the true order exactly.
Reject rows where DNA condenses after the chromosomes align, or where spindle fibres shorten before the chromosomes line up.
keyConcept: Mitotic events occur in a fixed order: condensation -> alignment -> separation -> envelope reforms -> cytokinesis.
commonMistake: Placing 'spindle fibres shorten' before 'chromosomes line up at the equator' - alignment (metaphase) must come first.

optionExplanations.0: The row starting 'nuclear envelope disappears -> spindle fibres shorten -> chromosomes line up' separates chromatids before the chromosomes have aligned, which is impossible.
optionExplanations.1: The row placing 'DNA starts to condense' after the chromosomes have already lined up reverses the true order.
optionExplanations.3: The row 'DNA condenses -> nuclear envelope disappears -> spindle fibres shorten -> chromosomes line up' has alignment happening after the spindle has already shortened.

figureExplanation: Reading each row left to right, only the row 'chromosomes line up at the equator, spindle fibres shorten, nuclear envelope reappears, cytoplasm divides' matches the metaphase-anaphase-telophase-cytokinesis order.

shortExplanation: Glucagon is a peptide hormone, not a carbohydrate. Amylose, ribose, amylopectin and maltose are all carbohydrates.
solutionSteps: Recall that carbohydrates are sugars, starches and related molecules.
Ribose (a monosaccharide), maltose (a disaccharide), amylose and amylopectin (starch polysaccharides) are all carbohydrates.
Glucagon is a protein/peptide hormone, despite the similar-sounding name.
Select glucagon as the non-carbohydrate.
keyConcept: Glucagon is a peptide hormone; do not confuse it with glucose-based carbohydrates.
commonMistake: Assuming 'glucagon' is a sugar because it resembles 'glucose'.

optionExplanations.1: Amylose is a starch polysaccharide, so it is a carbohydrate.
optionExplanations.2: Ribose is a five-carbon monosaccharide, a carbohydrate.
optionExplanations.3: Amylopectin is a branched starch polysaccharide, a carbohydrate.

shortExplanation: Blocking voltage-gated sodium channels prevents the sodium influx needed for depolarisation, so it becomes harder to depolarise the neuron and fire an action potential.
solutionSteps: Depolarisation depends on sodium entering through voltage-gated Na+ channels.
If these channels open less easily, sodium influx is reduced.
Reaching the threshold and depolarising becomes more difficult.
Therefore it is harder to depolarise the neuron.
keyConcept: Voltage-gated sodium channels drive the rising (depolarising) phase of the action potential.
commonMistake: Thinking sodium channels control repolarisation; repolarisation is driven mainly by potassium channels.

optionExplanations.0: The threshold is effectively harder to reach, not lowered.
optionExplanations.1: Repolarisation depends on potassium efflux, not the blocked sodium channels.
optionExplanations.4: The resting potential and Na+/K+ pump are largely unaffected; the effect is on triggering, not maintaining rest.

shortExplanation: In a sperm cell the nucleus (the head) is largest, the mitochondria (in the midpiece) are next, and ribosomes are by far the smallest: 2, 1, 3.
solutionSteps: The sperm nucleus forms the head and is several micrometres across, the largest structure listed.
Mitochondria are around a micrometre, smaller than the nucleus.
Ribosomes are only tens of nanometres, the smallest.
Descending order: nucleus (2), mitochondria (1), ribosome (3).
keyConcept: Typical size order is nucleus > mitochondrion > ribosome.
commonMistake: Ranking the mitochondrion above the nucleus; the nucleus is the larger organelle.

optionExplanations.0: 1, 2, 3 wrongly places mitochondria above the larger nucleus.
optionExplanations.1: 1, 3, 2 places the tiny ribosome above the nucleus, which is wrong.
optionExplanations.3: 2, 3, 1 places the ribosome above the mitochondrion, which is wrong.

shortExplanation: Prokaryotes have no membrane-bound organelles, so transcription occurs in the cytoplasm only; they lack mitochondria, and ribosomes carry out translation, not transcription.
solutionSteps: Prokaryotic DNA is free in the cytoplasm, where transcription takes place.
Prokaryotes have no mitochondria, so option 2 is impossible.
Ribosomes perform translation, not transcription, so option 3 is excluded.
Therefore transcription occurs in the cytoplasm only.
keyConcept: In prokaryotes transcription happens in the cytoplasm because there is no nucleus or membrane-bound organelle.
commonMistake: Assuming ribosomes transcribe; ribosomes translate mRNA, they do not make it.

optionExplanations.0: 3 only wrongly assigns transcription to ribosomes, which translate.
optionExplanations.1: 1 and 3 only adds ribosomes, which do not transcribe.
optionExplanations.3: 1 and 2 only includes mitochondria, which prokaryotes do not have.

shortExplanation: Splitting the mutated DNA ATCTTGCGG into ATC, TTG, CGG, the tRNA anticodon has the same base sequence as this DNA strand but with U replacing T, giving AUC, UUG, CGG. From the key these are the open square, open circle and open diamond, matching the open-square/open-circle/open-diamond sequence.
solutionSteps: Divide the mutated DNA into triplets: ATC, TTG, CGG.
The mRNA is complementary to the DNA, and each tRNA anticodon is complementary to the mRNA, so the tRNA anticodon equals the original DNA triplet with uracil in place of thymine.
Convert: ATC -> AUC, TTG -> UUG, CGG -> CGG.
Look up in the key: AUC = open square, UUG = open circle, CGG = open diamond.
Match to the option showing open square, open circle, open diamond.
keyConcept: tRNA is RNA, so its triplets contain U not T; two rounds of complementary base pairing return the DNA base sequence with T replaced by U.
commonMistake: Leaving thymine in the tRNA triplet (choosing ATC or TTG) - a real tRNA anticodon can never contain T.

optionExplanations.0: This uses the filled square (ATC), which still contains thymine and so cannot be a tRNA triplet.
optionExplanations.1: The middle symbol here is the filled circle (GAA), which does not correspond to the TTG->UUG conversion.
optionExplanations.4: Both the filled square (ATC) and filled diamond (TTG) contain thymine, impossible for tRNA.

figureExplanation: The key assigns AUC = open square, UUG = open circle, CGG = open diamond; the T-containing entries (ATC, TTG) are distractors because tRNA cannot contain thymine.

shortExplanation: Evolution can produce all three: changes in allele frequency (the definition of evolution), speciation, and increased biodiversity.
solutionSteps: Evolution is fundamentally a change in allele frequency in a population (2).
Sustained divergence can lead to new species, i.e. speciation (1).
The formation of new species and traits can increase biodiversity (3).
All three are possible outcomes.
keyConcept: Evolution ranges from shifts in allele frequency up to speciation and greater biodiversity.
commonMistake: Treating speciation or biodiversity as separate from evolution, when they are among its outcomes.

optionExplanations.0: 2 and 3 only omits speciation, a clear outcome of evolution.
optionExplanations.1: 1 only ignores allele-frequency change and biodiversity.
optionExplanations.4: 1 and 2 only leaves out increased biodiversity, which evolution can also produce.

shortExplanation: The compound is 0.60 g carbon and 0.15 g hydrogen, giving a C:H mole ratio of 0.05:0.15 = 1:3, so the empirical formula is CH3 and a valid molecular formula is C2H6.
solutionSteps: Mass of hydrogen = 0.75 - 0.60 = 0.15 g.
Mole ratio C:H = 0.05 : 0.15 = 1 : 3, empirical formula CH3.
The molecular formula must keep a 1:3 ratio: C2H6 (2:6) fits.
keyConcept: Convert masses to moles, simplify the ratio to the empirical formula, then match a molecular formula with the same ratio.
commonMistake: Forgetting to find the hydrogen mass by difference before computing moles.

optionExplanations.0: C3H8 has a C:H ratio of 3:8, not 1:3.
optionExplanations.1: C2H4 has a ratio of 1:2, not 1:3.
optionExplanations.3: CH4 has a ratio of 1:4, not 1:3.

formulaNotes: moles = mass / Ar; empirical ratio from smallest whole-number mole ratio.

shortExplanation: 24.6 g of 1-bromopropane is 0.20 mol, so the theoretical yield of propan-1-ol (Mr 60) is 12.0 g. The actual 8.00 g gives a yield of 8.00/12.0 = 66.7%.
solutionSteps: Moles of C3H7Br = 24.6 / 123 = 0.20 mol.
The 1:1 stoichiometry gives 0.20 mol of propan-1-ol theoretically.
Theoretical mass = 0.20 * 60 = 12.0 g.
keyConcept: Percentage yield = (actual mass / theoretical mass) * 100, using stoichiometry from moles of the limiting reactant.
commonMistake: Comparing masses directly (8.00/24.6) instead of using moles and the product's molar mass.

optionExplanations.0: 57.1% would come from an incorrect molar mass or mole calculation.
optionExplanations.1: 93.0% overstates the yield and does not match the mole arithmetic.
optionExplanations.3: 33.3% comes from dividing by the wrong theoretical value.

formulaNotes: moles = mass/Mr; theoretical mass = moles * Mr(product); yield% = actual/theoretical * 100.

shortExplanation: Pure water always contains equal concentrations of H+ and OH-, so statement 1 is true. Because self-ionisation is endothermic, heating shifts the equilibrium forward, raising [H+] and lowering the pH (statement 2 true), while the extra ions increase, not decrease, conductivity (statement 3 false).
solutionSteps: In pure water every ionisation event produces one H3O+ and one OH-, so [H+] = [OH-] at every temperature: statement 1 is true.
The reaction is endothermic, so by Le Chatelier's principle an increase in temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right, increasing Kw.
A larger Kw means a larger [H+]; since pH = -log[H+], the pH falls as temperature rises: statement 2 is true.
More ions in solution carry more charge, so electrical conductivity increases with temperature: statement 3 is false.
Therefore statements 1 and 2 only are correct.
keyConcept: Heating endothermic self-ionisation increases Kw, so pure water stays neutral ([H+] = [OH-]) but its pH drops below 7.
commonMistake: Thinking a falling pH means the water becomes acidic; it stays neutral because [H+] and [OH-] rise together.

optionExplanations.0: Statement 3 is wrong because producing more ions raises conductivity rather than lowering it.
optionExplanations.2: Statement 1 alone is incomplete: the endothermic shift also makes the pH fall, so statement 2 is true as well.
optionExplanations.4: Statement 2 is true but so is statement 1: pure water always has equal H+ and OH- concentrations.

shortExplanation: Neutral Al (Z = 13) is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p1. Forming Al2+ removes the two highest-energy electrons, first the 3p electron and then one 3s electron, leaving 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1.
solutionSteps: Write the ground-state configuration of neutral aluminium (13 electrons): 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p1.
A 2+ ion has lost 2 electrons, leaving 11 electrons.
Electrons are removed from the outermost (highest-energy) subshells first: the single 3p electron goes first, then one of the 3s electrons.
The result is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1.
keyConcept: Cations form by removing electrons from the outermost occupied subshell of the neutral atom.
commonMistake: Removing three electrons (giving the noble-gas core 1s2 2s2 2p6), which is Al3+, not Al2+.

optionExplanations.0: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p1 has 13 electrons and is the neutral aluminium atom.
optionExplanations.2: 1s2 2s2 2p6 has only 10 electrons, corresponding to Al3+, not Al2+.
optionExplanations.4: 1s2 2s2 2p5 3s2 wrongly removes electrons from the inner 2p subshell instead of the outermost electrons.

shortExplanation: A formula XY2 requires X2+ combined with two Y- ions. Atomic number 12 (magnesium, group 2) forms 2+ ions and atomic number 9 (fluorine, group 17) forms 1- ions, giving MgF2.
solutionSteps: For an ionic compound XY2, the charges must balance: X must be 2+ and each Y must be 1-.
X = 12 is magnesium, a group 2 metal that loses 2 electrons to form Mg2+.
Y = 9 is fluorine, a group 17 non-metal that gains 1 electron to form F-.
Mg2+ with two F- gives the neutral formula MgF2, matching XY2.
keyConcept: Ionic formulas follow from balancing the group-determined ion charges (group 2 gives 2+, group 17 gives 1-).
commonMistake: Pairing a 1+ metal with a 2- non-metal (like Na and S), which gives X2Y, the reverse of the required XY2.

optionExplanations.0: Sodium (11) forms 1+ ions and sulfur (16) forms 2- ions, so they combine as Na2S (X2Y), not XY2.
optionExplanations.1: Lithium (3) is 1+ and chlorine (17) is 1-, giving LiCl (XY), not XY2.
optionExplanations.3: Carbon (6) does not form simple ionic compounds; it bonds covalently.

shortExplanation: The two isomers have the same molecular mass, so the difference comes from London dispersion forces: the straight-chain pentane has a larger contact surface area between molecules, giving stronger instantaneous/induced dipole attractions and a higher boiling point.
solutionSteps: Both compounds are C5H12, so their relative molecular masses are identical.
Both are non-polar alkanes, so the only intermolecular forces are instantaneous (spontaneous) dipole - induced dipole attractions (London dispersion forces).
Pentane is a straight chain, allowing molecules to lie close together over a large surface area; 2,2-dimethylpropane is compact and near-spherical, so molecules touch over less area.
Greater contact area means stronger dispersion forces for pentane, so more energy is needed to separate its molecules: its boiling point (36 C) is higher than that of the branched isomer (10 C).
keyConcept: Among alkane isomers, less branching means more intermolecular contact and stronger dispersion forces, hence a higher boiling point.
commonMistake: Attributing the difference to molecular mass; isomers have exactly the same molecular mass.

optionExplanations.0: It is pentane, the higher-boiling isomer, that has the stronger intermolecular forces, not 2,2-dimethylpropane.
optionExplanations.1: Isomers share the same molecular formula, so their relative molecular masses are equal.
optionExplanations.3: Pentane is a non-polar alkane; it has no permanent dipoles, only instantaneous/induced dipoles.

shortExplanation: With N = -3 and 4 H at +1, the ammonium ion NH4 carries a +1 charge; with Cr = +6 and 4 O at -2, chromate CrO4 carries a -2 charge. Two NH4+ ions balance one CrO4 2-, giving the neutral formula (NH4)2CrO4.
solutionSteps: Charge on NH4: (-3) + 4(+1) = +1, so the ion is NH4+.
Charge on CrO4: (+6) + 4(-2) = -2, so the ion is CrO4 2-.
A neutral compound needs total charge zero: 2(+1) + (-2) = 0.
Therefore the correct formula is (NH4)2CrO4 with no overall charge shown.
keyConcept: Sum of (oxidation number x number of atoms) over all atoms must equal zero for a neutral compound.
commonMistake: Writing brackets with an overall charge around a complete compound, or using the wrong ratio of ammonium to chromate.

optionExplanations.0: A complete ionic compound is neutral; it cannot carry an overall + charge.
optionExplanations.1: NH4Cr2O7 has total charge (+1) + (-2) = -1 with the given oxidation numbers; the dichromate salt would need two NH4+ ions.
optionExplanations.4: (NH4)3CrO4 has total charge 3(+1) + (-2) = +1, so it is not neutral.

shortExplanation: Propanal is the three-carbon aldehyde, so it ends in the -CHO group: CH3CH2CHO.
solutionSteps: The suffix -al indicates an aldehyde, whose functional group is -CHO on a terminal carbon.
The prefix propan- indicates a three-carbon chain.
Placing -CHO at the end of a three-carbon chain gives CH3CH2CHO.
keyConcept: Aldehydes (-al) carry the -CHO group at the end of the carbon chain.
commonMistake: Confusing the aldehyde -CHO with the ketone C=O in the middle of the chain (CH3COCH3 is propanone).

optionExplanations.0: CH3CH2CH2OH contains an -OH group and is propan-1-ol, an alcohol.
optionExplanations.2: CH3COCH3 has the carbonyl on the middle carbon, so it is propanone, a ketone.
optionExplanations.3: CH3CH2CO2H contains the -COOH group and is propanoic acid.

shortExplanation: Propan-1-ol is C3H7OH (C3H8O). Balancing its complete combustion gives 2 C3H8O + 9 O2 -> 6 CO2 + 8 H2O, so CO2 : H2O = 6 : 8 = 3 : 4.
solutionSteps: Write the formula of propan-1-ol: C3H7OH, i.e. C3H8O.
Each molecule contains 3 C atoms, so it produces 3 CO2, and 8 H atoms, so it produces 4 H2O.
Balance oxygen: right side has 3(2) + 4(1) = 10 O; the alcohol supplies 1, so O2 supplies 9/2, giving C3H8O + 9/2 O2 -> 3 CO2 + 4 H2O (or doubled: 2 C3H8O + 9 O2 -> 6 CO2 + 8 H2O).
The ratio CO2 : H2O is 3 : 4.
keyConcept: In complete combustion, moles of CO2 equal the C atoms and moles of H2O equal half the H atoms per molecule of fuel.
commonMistake: Forgetting the oxygen atom already present in the alcohol when balancing, or miscounting the 8 hydrogens of C3H7OH.

optionExplanations.0: 4 : 7 does not match the atom counts; propan-1-ol has only 3 carbons, so 3 CO2 form per molecule.
optionExplanations.1: 3 : 8 doubles the water; 8 H atoms give 4 H2O per molecule, not 8.
optionExplanations.2: 2 : 7 corresponds to neither the carbon count nor the hydrogen count of C3H7OH.

shortExplanation: At 80 C, 50 g of water dissolves 60 g of KNO3. At 25 C the whole 60 g would need 120 g of water (50 g per 100 g), so 120 - 50 = 70 g of water must be added.
solutionSteps: Solubility at 80 C is 120 g per 100 g water, so 50 g of water dissolves 60 g of KNO3 when saturated.
On cooling to 25 C, solubility is 50 g per 100 g water, so the 50 g of water keeps only 25 g dissolved; 60 - 25 = 35 g of solid separates out.
To hold all 60 g in solution at 25 C requires 60 / (50/100) = 120 g of water.
The mixture already contains 50 g of water, so the minimum extra water is 120 - 50 = 70 g.
keyConcept: Solubility scales proportionally with the mass of water: required water = total solute / (solubility per gram of water).
commonMistake: Calculating the water needed for only the 35 g of crystals while forgetting the 50 g of water present is already saturated and can dissolve nothing more.

optionExplanations.0: 20 g is far too little; it would dissolve only 10 g more KNO3 at 25 C, leaving most of the 35 g of solid undissolved.
optionExplanations.1: 140 g would be needed for 70 g of solute; here only 60 g of KNO3 is present in total.
optionExplanations.2: 120 g is the total water required at 25 C, not the extra amount to add on top of the 50 g already present.

shortExplanation: CO and NO are neutral oxides that do not react with water, so they give no acidic solution; CO2 forms carbonic acid and SO2 forms sulfurous acid.
solutionSteps: CO2 dissolves in water to give H2CO3 (carbonic acid): acidic.
SO2 dissolves in water to give H2SO3 (sulfurous acid): acidic.
CO and NO are classed as neutral oxides: they do not react with water to form acids.
The two non-acidic oxides are therefore CO and NO.
keyConcept: Most non-metal oxides are acidic, but CO and NO are neutral oxides that do not form acids in water.
commonMistake: Assuming every non-metal oxide is acidic; CO and NO are the classic neutral exceptions.

optionExplanations.0: SO2 is acidic, forming sulfurous acid in water, so this pair is wrong.
optionExplanations.1: CO2 is acidic, forming carbonic acid in water, so this pair is wrong.
optionExplanations.3: CO is neutral but CO2 dissolves to give an acidic solution.

shortExplanation: Sodium carbonate is the salt of a strong base (NaOH) and a weak acid (carbonic acid); the carbonate ion hydrolyses to produce OH-, making the solution basic with pH > 7.
solutionSteps: A salt of a strong base and a weak acid gives a basic solution because the anion accepts protons from water.
In Na2CO3 solution: CO3 2- + H2O <-> HCO3- + OH-, generating excess OH-, so pH > 7.

Check the others: NaI comes from a strong acid and strong base (neutral, pH 7); NH4Cl contains the weakly acidic NH4+ (pH < 7); AlBr3 gives the acidic hydrated Al3+ ion (pH < 7); CH3CO2H is itself a weak acid (pH < 7).
Only the sodium carbonate solution is basic.
keyConcept: Salt hydrolysis: anion of a weak acid makes a solution basic; cation of a weak base (or a small highly charged metal ion) makes it acidic.
commonMistake: Treating every sodium salt as neutral; the carbonate anion is a base and raises the pH.

optionExplanations.0: Hydrated Al3+ is acidic because the highly charged ion polarises water and releases H+, giving pH < 7.
optionExplanations.1: NaI is the salt of a strong acid (HI) and a strong base, so its solution is neutral, not basic.
optionExplanations.2: NH4+ is a weak acid that donates a proton to water, giving pH < 7.

shortExplanation: The fire explanation predicts that carbon loss was greatest close to the Sun, where hot oxygen atoms were most plentiful. Evidence that carbon abundance in the asteroid belt increases with distance from the Sun matches exactly this predicted gradient, strengthening the argument.
solutionSteps: Identify the conclusion: the Earth's carbon deficit is more likely due to burning (carbon combining with hot oxygen atoms) than to carbon boiling away.
Note the mechanism's key prediction: because oxygen atoms were fewer further from the Sun, less carbon should have burned at greater distances, leaving more carbon there.
The statement that carbon abundance in the asteroid belt increases with distance from the Sun confirms this predicted pattern.
Confirming a distinctive prediction of the fire hypothesis strengthens the argument.
keyConcept: A claim is strengthened by independent evidence that matches a specific prediction of its proposed mechanism.
commonMistake: Choosing a statement that merely attacks the boiling theory again instead of positively supporting the burning mechanism.

optionExplanations.0: Carbon arriving later from an asteroid concerns the carbon Earth does have; it does not support the burning explanation of the deficit.
optionExplanations.3: Carbon-rich Earth-like planets elsewhere say nothing about why our inner solar system lost carbon.
optionExplanations.4: The argument already rejects the boiling account because temperatures were too low; adding that oxygen would also boil away does not support the fire mechanism and even undercuts it.

shortExplanation: Only cards at least 6 cm wide, at least 8 cm high and with a photo qualify. The cheapest such type costs 1.50 standard and 1.95 deluxe, so the extra is 0.45 per card, i.e. 0.45 x 50 = 22.50.
solutionSteps: Apply the constraints: width >= 6, height >= 8, photo required.
Eliminate the 6x6 and 7x7 cards (height under 8) and the 6x10 card without a photo.
Qualifying types and prices (standard/deluxe): 6x10 photo+greeting 1.75/2.15; 7x10 photo 1.50/1.95; 7x10 photo+greeting 1.60/2.15; 10x10 photo 2.25/2.95.
The cheapest qualifying type is the 7x10 photo card at 1.50 standard.
Its deluxe version costs 1.95, an extra 1.95 - 1.50 = 0.45 per card.
For 50 cards the total extra is 50 x 0.45 = 22.50.
keyConcept: Filter the table by all stated constraints first, then compare prices only among qualifying rows.
commonMistake: Including the 6x10 card without a photo (cheapest overall at 1.00) even though Tom requires a photo.

optionExplanations.0: 30.00 would need a 0.60 per-card difference, which does not match the cheapest qualifying type.
optionExplanations.1: 20.00 corresponds to a 0.40 per-card difference, e.g. the 6x10 photo+greeting card, which is not the cheapest qualifying type.
optionExplanations.2: 25.00 would come from a 0.50 difference per card, which no qualifying type has.

shortExplanation: The passage sets up the view that Earth being the only planet with intelligent life would be an amazing coincidence, then argues that this rests on a fallacy, concluding that it would not be such a coincidence after all.
solutionSteps: Locate the claim the author opposes: that it would be an amazing coincidence if Earth were the only planet with intelligent life.
Identify the author's move: 'This objection, however, rests on a fallacy... so it wouldn't be such a coincidence.'
The observation selection effect (observers necessarily come from successes) is the supporting reason, not the conclusion.
The main conclusion is therefore that there would be no amazing coincidence if Earth turned out to be the only planet with intelligent life.
keyConcept: The main conclusion is the claim everything else supports; here it is signalled by 'so it wouldn't be such a coincidence'.
commonMistake: Selecting one of the supporting premises (the selection effect or the non-random sample point) instead of the claim they are used to establish.

optionExplanations.0: That our planet is not a randomly selected sample is a reason given for the conclusion, not the conclusion itself.
optionExplanations.1: The guarantee that observers arise where intelligent life arose is the premise explaining the selection effect, not the final claim.
optionExplanations.4: This is the view the argument attacks, the opposite of its conclusion.

shortExplanation: The walls minus the window give 67 m2, the ceiling adds 24 m2, and the 20% wooden wall area needs a second coat adding about 13.4 m2, for roughly 104.4 m2 in total. At 24 m2 per can that requires 4.35 cans, so 5 cans must be bought.
solutionSteps: Wall area: two walls of 4 x 3.5 = 14 m2 each and two of 6 x 3.5 = 21 m2 each, total 2(14) + 2(21) = 70 m2.
Subtract the window: 1.5 x 2 = 3 m2, leaving 70 - 3 = 67 m2 of wall (the door is painted, so it stays included).
Ceiling area: 4 x 6 = 24 m2.
Second coat on wood: 20% of the 67 m2 wall area = 13.4 m2 extra.
Total area to cover: 67 + 24 + 13.4 = 104.4 m2.
Cans needed: 104.4 / 24 = 4.35, so round up to 5 cans.
keyConcept: Compute total coverage area including repeat coats, then always round the number of cans up.
commonMistake: Rounding 4.35 down to 4 cans, or forgetting to add the second coat for the wooden 20% of the walls.

optionExplanations.0: 4 cans cover only 96 m2, less than the 104.4 m2 required once the second coat on the wood is included.
optionExplanations.1: 6 cans would be needed only if the area exceeded 120 m2, well above the actual total.
optionExplanations.4: 3 cans cover just 72 m2, not even enough for the walls and ceiling with a single coat.

shortExplanation: The case for spreading the initiative depends on the events actually creating an interest in gardening. If children enjoy the events but gain no interest in gardening, the first link of the causal chain fails, so the recommendation loses its support.
solutionSteps: Map the argument: events -> interest in gardening -> interest in learning about food -> deterred from junk food -> spread the initiative.
To weaken it, attack a necessary link in this chain.
The statement that most children enjoyed the events but did not gain an interest in gardening breaks the very first link.
Without that interest, none of the later benefits follow, so the conclusion to support and spread the initiative is undermined most.
keyConcept: An argument built on a causal chain is weakened most by evidence that an early link does not hold.
commonMistake: Picking a practical obstacle (some schools lack gardens) rather than evidence that the claimed effect does not occur.

optionExplanations.1: Junk food stalls at the events are an ironic detail but do not show the initiative fails to create interest in gardening.
optionExplanations.2: Schools without gardens limit where the scheme can run but do not weaken the claim that it works where it does run.
optionExplanations.3: Older people currently dominating gardening says nothing about whether children can be won over by the events.

shortExplanation: Both halves cover equal distance, so on a distance-time graph the bend sits at half the total distance. The slow uphill first half is a shallow line taking more time, and the fast downhill second half is a steeper line taking less time, with distance never decreasing.
solutionSteps: The two halves cover equal distance, so the corner on the distance-time graph is at half the total distance (halfway up the vertical axis).
The first half at 5 km/h is slow, giving a shallow slope that takes more time.
The second half at 15 km/h is fast, giving a steeper slope that takes less time.
Distance only increases as Leroy travels toward work, so the line never falls back.
The graph that rises gently to the halfway height and then steeply on to the top fits all of this.
keyConcept: On a distance-time graph a steeper slope means a higher speed, and equal distances put the corner at half the total distance.
commonMistake: Choosing a graph that rises and then falls back toward zero, which would mean the distance travelled decreases, as if Leroy returned to the start.

optionExplanations.0: This line rises steeply first and then shallowly, which is fast then slow, the reverse of slow uphill then fast downhill.
optionExplanations.1: The corner sits well below the halfway distance, so the shallow slow part covers less than half the journey instead of an equal half.
optionExplanations.2: The line rises to a peak and then falls back to zero, implying Leroy returns to the start, which does not happen.
optionExplanations.3: This line also rises to a peak and then falls back to zero, meaning the distance from home decreases, which cannot happen on the trip to work.

figureExplanation: The correct graph is a continuously rising line whose corner is at half the total distance, shallow before the corner (slow uphill) and steeper after it (fast downhill).

shortExplanation: The conclusion that fluoridation should not take place rests entirely on the campaigner's reported experiences. That evidence only counts against fluoridation if one assumes the symptoms were actually caused by fluoride in the water.
solutionSteps: Identify the conclusion: 'Even so, fluoridation should not take place.'
Identify the only evidence offered: the campaigner's and her son's symptoms in a fluoridated area, which disappeared after leaving.
For this anecdote to support the conclusion, the unstated link must be that fluoride in the water caused those symptoms.
Without that causal assumption the evidence is irrelevant, so it is the underlying assumption.
keyConcept: An assumption is the unstated claim needed to connect the evidence to the conclusion.
commonMistake: Choosing a broader value claim (mass medication is always wrong) that the argument never needs, instead of the causal link it does need.

optionExplanations.0: The argument opposes this particular measure on health grounds; it does not need the sweeping claim that all mass medication is wrong.
optionExplanations.1: Whether other fluoride sources exist is irrelevant to the reasoning from the reported symptoms.
optionExplanations.4: The argument opposes fluoridation everywhere, so it cannot be assuming it is only needed in deprived areas.

shortExplanation: The passage argues for acting on suspicion of harm now rather than waiting for conclusive research, citing past mistakes and a growing threat. The terrorist example mirrors this exactly: arrest on suspicion, because waiting for conclusive evidence caused past harms and the threat has grown.
solutionSteps: Extract the structure: where there is good reason to suspect harm, act now instead of waiting for conclusive proof; past experience of delayed action warns us; the scale of the risk has grown.

Test the terrorist option: arrest at once on suspicion (act before proof), past waiting led to atrocities (past mistakes forewarn), and the threat of terrorism has grown (growing scale). All three elements match.
The other options either demand checks before acting, respond to established rather than suspected harm, or concern testing frequency, so they do not share the precautionary structure.
keyConcept: Matching reasoning questions compare argument structure, here the precautionary pattern: suspicion plus past mistakes justify acting before conclusive evidence.
commonMistake: Matching the surface topic (safety, danger) instead of the structural move of acting on suspicion without waiting for proof.

optionExplanations.0: Requiring checks before adoption is the opposite move: it demands evidence before acting rather than acting on suspicion.
optionExplanations.2: Closing substandard homes responds to harm already established, not to suspected but unproven harm.
optionExplanations.3: The cyclist example argues from lack of conclusive evidence to withholding confidence, which reverses the passage's precautionary logic.

shortExplanation: With first digit 4 and a two-digit total, the three odd numbers must have tens digits 4, 1 and 2, and the only unit digits that keep all eight digits different are 3, 5 and 9, giving a sum of 87. The last digit is therefore 7.
solutionSteps: The reference is three 2-digit odd numbers followed by their sum; 6 digits plus a 2-digit sum makes 8 digits, so the sum is between 10 and 99.
The first number is 4 followed by an odd digit, so it is at least 41; hence the other two numbers together are at most 99 - 41 = 58, forcing their tens digits to be small.
Try tens digits 1 and 2 for the other numbers: the sum is 40 + 10 + 20 + (units) = 70 + (sum of the three odd unit digits).
The unit digits must be odd, distinct, and different from 4, 1, 2; candidates are 3, 5, 7, 9.
If the units are 3, 5, 9 their sum is 17, giving a total of 87; digits used are 4,1,2,3,5,9,8,7 - all eight different and no zero. (Example: 43 + 15 + 29 = 87.)
Other unit choices fail: units 3,5,7 give total 85, repeating 5; units 3,7,9 give 89, repeating 9; units 5,7,9 give 91, repeating 9 and 1. Tens digits 1,3 or 2,3 push the total over 99.
The sum is 87, so the last digit of the reference is 7.
keyConcept: Use the size constraint on the two-digit sum to pin down the tens digits, then enforce the all-digits-different condition on the units.
commonMistake: Forgetting that the digits of the sum itself must also differ from the six digits of the three numbers.

optionExplanations.0: A last digit 3 would need a total of 83, i.e. unit digits summing to 13, impossible with three distinct odd digits from 3,5,7,9.
optionExplanations.1: A last digit 5 would require unit digits summing to 15 (total 85), which forces a repeated 5.
optionExplanations.2: A last digit 9 would require a total of 89, repeating the digit 9 already used as a unit.

shortExplanation: The argument dismisses fears about Arctic migrating animals purely on the evidence of great tits adapting in Oxfordshire. That inference only works if one assumes Arctic migrating animals can adapt to climate change as successfully as those birds.
solutionSteps: Identify the conclusion: the Greenland scientists' fears about caribou and other migrating animals are unfounded.
Identify the evidence: great tits in Oxfordshire adapted their egg-laying by two weeks to match food availability.
The gap: evidence about small resident birds in Oxfordshire is applied to migrating Arctic mammals.
The unstated bridge is that Arctic migrating animals can adapt as successfully as the great tits; without it the analogy fails.
keyConcept: Arguments from analogy assume the compared cases are relevantly similar in adaptive capacity.
commonMistake: Confusing the assumption with a comparison of the scientists' expertise or of climate scale, which the argument never relies on.

optionExplanations.1: The argument needs caribou to be as adaptable as birds, not birds to be more adaptable than mammals.
optionExplanations.3: Nothing in the reasoning compares the researchers' expertise; it compares the animals' responses.
optionExplanations.4: The argument does not require identical scales of climate change, only that the adaptive success transfers.

shortExplanation: The cat's ratio is 5.3 g / 3500 g = 0.00151. The mouse gives 0.09 / 58 = 0.00155, which is far closer to the cat than any other species.
solutionSteps: Convert the cat's body mass: 3.5 kg = 3500 g, so ratio = 5.3 / 3500 = 0.00151.
Compare each to 0.00151; the mouse (difference 0.00004) is closest.
keyConcept: Compare ratios by dividing cerebellum mass by body mass in consistent units (grams).
commonMistake: Forgetting to convert the cat's 3.5 kg into 3500 g before forming the ratio.

optionExplanations.0: Pigeon's ratio 0.00080 is about half the cat's, one of the least similar.
optionExplanations.1: Squirrel's ratio 0.00429 is nearly three times the cat's, the furthest away.
optionExplanations.2: Dog's ratio 0.00171 is close but its difference from the cat is about five times larger than the mouse's.

figureExplanation: Using the tabulated masses, cerebellum/body ratios are computed for each species and the mouse (0.00155) lies nearest the cat's 0.00151.

shortExplanation: The passage says sports are played either for exercise or for competition, and that pool is unlikely to be played for exercise. It follows that pool players are more likely to be motivated by competition than football players, for whom exercise is also a live motive.
solutionSteps: Premise 1: sports are played either for exercise or for competition.
Premise 2: pool involves little physical activity, so it is unlikely to be played for exercise; by elimination pool is mostly played for competition.
Premise 3: football involves much running, so exercise is a realistic motive for football players.
Therefore a pool player is more likely than a football player to be playing for the competition, which is the supported conclusion.
keyConcept: With an exhaustive either/or premise, ruling out one motive for a group licenses the conclusion that the other motive dominates.
commonMistake: Drawing a value judgement (which sport is better, or what counts as a sport) that the neutral premises never support.

optionExplanations.0: The passage compares motives, not the merit of the sports; 'better' is unsupported.
optionExplanations.2: The passage says some people are more motivated to run in a game; it draws no general claim that exercising is easier within another activity.
optionExplanations.4: The passage states two possible reasons for playing sport and never says exercise is the main one, so pool's status as a sport is untouched.

shortExplanation: Mounting the plate upside down is a 180 degree rotation, and seeing it in the mirror adds a left-right flip; combined they equal a single top-to-bottom flip of 'S308 CNH', which keeps the left-to-right order and flips each character top-to-bottom. Only the S and the N are not symmetric top-to-bottom, so they reverse while the others stay the same.
solutionSteps: The front plate reads 'S308 CNH' when correctly mounted.
Mounting it upside down rotates the whole plate by 180 degrees.
Viewing that plate in the rearview mirror reflects it left-to-right.
A 180 degree rotation followed by a left-right reflection is equivalent to one top-to-bottom flip, which preserves the left-to-right order of the characters.
Under a top-to-bottom flip, characters symmetric about a horizontal axis are unchanged: 3, 0, 8, C and H all stay the same.
The S and the N are not symmetric about a horizontal axis, so each becomes its top-to-bottom mirror: the S turns into a reversed S (resembling a 2) and the N into a reversed N.
Keeping the original order, the result is reversed-S, 3, 0, 8, space, C, reversed-N, H.
keyConcept: A 180 degree rotation combined with a mirror reflection equals a single top-to-bottom flip, which keeps character order but flips each glyph about a horizontal axis.
commonMistake: Applying only one transformation (just the rotation or just the mirror), or reversing the left-to-right order as a pure 180 degree rotation would.

optionExplanations.0: Here the S is left upright while the 3 and the C are reversed, so the wrong characters are changed; a top-to-bottom flip reverses only the S and the N.
optionExplanations.1: The S is correctly reversed, but the C is also reversed and the N is left upright, so the wrong set of characters is flipped.
optionExplanations.2: The N is correctly reversed, but the S is left upright and the 3 is reversed, again flipping the wrong characters.
optionExplanations.4: The N is reversed, but the S is left upright and the C is reversed, so it changes the wrong characters.

figureExplanation: The plate 'S308 CNH' is shown top-to-bottom flipped: a reversed S (looking like a 2), unchanged 3, 0 and 8, an unchanged C, a reversed N, and an unchanged H, all in the original left-to-right order.

shortExplanation: Everything in the passage - the persistence of congestion and the increased danger - is offered as reasons for the opening claim that raising the limit to 150 km/hr would not be a good thing, which is therefore the main conclusion.
solutionSteps: Spot the position statement at the start: 'such an increase would not be a good thing'.
Check the role of the other claims: the persistence of speeding, the unchanged congestion at higher speed, and the increased tailgating danger are all reasons supporting that position.
A main conclusion is the claim supported by the rest; here it is that raising the speed limit to 150 km/hr would not be a good thing.
keyConcept: Distinguish the overall evaluative conclusion from the intermediate factual claims that support it.
commonMistake: Choosing the intermediate result about congestion, which is itself only a reason for the final judgement.

optionExplanations.0: The cause of bunching is background explanation supporting the congestion point, not the argument's target claim.
optionExplanations.1: The claim that all drivers would drive faster is a premise for the danger point, not the conclusion.
optionExplanations.3: That raising the limit would not reduce congestion is an intermediate conclusion used to support the overall judgement, not the main conclusion itself.

shortExplanation: The argument's principle is that a whole population should not be subjected to an intervention when only an identifiable affected group needs it; those individuals should instead be identified and advised. Rejecting water fluoridation in favour of dentists advising patients with tooth problems applies the same principle.
solutionSteps: Extract the principle: do not impose a blanket measure on everyone when the benefit applies only to an identifiable group; target that group with advice instead.
The fluoride option mirrors this: instead of medicating everyone's water, dentists should advise the specific patients with tooth problems.
The other options endorse population-wide compulsion, punishment, or general education, none of which match the targeted-advice-over-blanket-measure structure.
keyConcept: Underlying-principle questions ask for a new case governed by the same general rule, here targeted intervention instead of mass measures.
commonMistake: Matching the topic (health measures) rather than the rule of targeting only the affected group.

optionExplanations.1: The seatbelt example accepts a universal compulsory measure, the opposite of the argument's principle.
optionExplanations.3: Extending a smoking ban into homes broadens a blanket restriction rather than targeting only those affected.
optionExplanations.4: General alcohol education for all pupils is a population-wide approach, not advice targeted at an affected group.

shortExplanation: The hovercraft arrives after 50 minutes, waits 20, and starts back at minute 70; setting the ferry's outward position equal to the hovercraft's return position gives a meeting at minute 80, so the ferry has been sailing 1 hour 20 minutes.
solutionSteps: Take the crossing distance as 1 unit. The ferry covers it in 100 minutes, so its position at time t is t/100.
The hovercraft covers it in 50 minutes, docks from minute 50 to 70, then returns; on the way back its position (measured from Sandpoint) is 1 - (t - 70)/50.
Set the positions equal: t/100 = 1 - (t - 70)/50.
Multiply by 100: t = 100 - 2(t - 70) = 240 - 2t, so 3t = 240 and t = 80 minutes.
Check the window: the meeting at t = 80 lies between 70 and 120, so it happens during the hovercraft's return leg.
The ferry left at t = 0 and has been sailing continuously, so it has sailed 80 minutes = 1 hour 20 minutes.
keyConcept: Model each vessel's position as a linear function of time, including the port stop, and equate positions to find the meeting time.
commonMistake: Forgetting the 20-minute port stop and starting the hovercraft's return at minute 50, which gives a meeting near 1 hour 7 minutes.

optionExplanations.1: 1 hour 7 minutes results from ignoring the hovercraft's 20-minute stop in Genville.
optionExplanations.2: At 1 hour 30 minutes the two would already have passed each other; positions are equal at exactly 80 minutes.
optionExplanations.4: 1 hour 10 minutes does not satisfy the position equation: at t = 70 the hovercraft is only just leaving Genville while the ferry is at 0.7 of the crossing.

shortExplanation: The seven gaps total 1075 cm and each 2.4 m (240 cm) rail can supply pieces summing to at most 240 cm, so at least ceil(1075/240) = 5 rails are needed, and 5 is achievable.
solutionSteps: Each rail is 240 cm, so the minimum possible number is ceil(1075/240) = ceil(4.48) = 5.
All seven gaps are covered by cutting pieces from just 5 rails.
keyConcept: Cutting-stock minimum: total length divided by rail length rounded up, checked against a feasible packing.
commonMistake: Assuming one rail is needed per gap (7 rails) instead of cutting single rails to serve several short gaps.

optionExplanations.1: Three rails give at most 720 cm, far below the 1075 cm required.
optionExplanations.2: Four rails give at most 960 cm, still less than 1075 cm, so 4 is impossible.
optionExplanations.3: Six rails work but are not the smallest number, since 5 already suffice.

figureExplanation: The seven labelled gaps (115, 90, 120, 180, 210, 150, 210 cm) sum to 1075 cm; packing them into 240 cm rails needs a minimum of 5.

shortExplanation: The argument concedes that the officers' offences prevent worse crimes but insists this is beside the point: a breach of the law remains wrong whatever good it achieves. That is precisely the principle that the end does not justify the means.
solutionSteps: Note the concession: undercover offences help convict dangerous criminals and prevent serious crime.
Note the pivot: 'But that is not really the point. A breach of the law is a breach of the law... Preventing a crime does not make it right to commit another crime.'
The general rule doing the work is that a good outcome cannot legitimise a wrongful act - the end does not justify the means.
keyConcept: The underlying principle is the general rule the specific case instantiates; here, outcomes cannot legitimise unlawful acts.
commonMistake: Selecting the crime-prevention value the argument explicitly sets aside rather than the rule it asserts.

optionExplanations.0: The argument says the officers' acts are breaches of the law regardless of their reasons, the opposite of defining crime by criminal intent.
optionExplanations.1: Preventing serious crime by any reasonable means is the position the argument rejects, not its principle.
optionExplanations.3: The passage notes some of these offences do have victims, but the argument's force does not rest on denying victimless crime.

shortExplanation: Starting from the FULL tank on 2 June, all fuel added afterwards (37 + 25 + 21 + 34 + 18 = 135 litres) approximates the fuel used over 25,454 - 23,508 = 1946 km, giving about 6.9 litres per 100 km, so the best estimate offered is 6.8 litres / 100 km.
solutionSteps: Begin the estimate at a known tank state: on 2 June the tank was FULL at 23,508 km.
Sum all petrol added after that point, which approximates the petrol consumed since then: 37 + 25 + 21 + 34 + 18 = 135 litres.
Find the distance over the same period: 25,454 - 23,508 = 1946 km.
Compute consumption: 135 / 1946 x 100 = about 6.9 litres per 100 km.
The closest figure offered is 6.8 litres / 100 km.
keyConcept: A fuel-log estimate must begin at a moment when the tank level is known (a FULL entry); fuel added after that point approximates the fuel used.
commonMistake: Dividing the small 5-litre top-up on 2 June by the following distance, which gives the absurdly low figure of about 1.7 litres / 100 km.

optionExplanations.0: 9.9 litres / 100 km comes from dividing the 117 litres added between 6 and 23 June by only the 1184 km from 23,805 to 24,989, an inconsistent pairing of fuel and distance.
optionExplanations.1: 7.7 litres / 100 km does not follow from any consistent pairing of fuel added and distance covered in the log.
optionExplanations.2: 1.7 litres / 100 km uses only the 5-litre top-up on 2 June, which mostly replaced fuel used before the record begins.
optionExplanations.4: 8.0 litres / 100 km counts the full 135 litres but measures distance only from the 6 June fill (1649 km), double-counting the 37 litres that themselves filled the tank.

shortExplanation: The 1 m clearance shrinks the usable floor to a 4 m by 4 m square, and the nine rigid 1.5 m cases each need a straight edge at least 1.5 m long. Only the tall arch both fits that square and offers exactly nine such edges.
solutionSteps: Start with the room. It is 6 m by 6 m, and you must leave 1 m clear all the way around the tables. That 1 m border on every side leaves a 4 m by 4 m square in the middle for the four tables.

Now the cases. There are nine of them, each a rigid 1.5 m long. A case can only lie along a straight stretch of table edge that is at least 1.5 m long, so you need nine such straight stretches in total.
So a good layout must clear two hurdles at once: fit inside the 4 m by 4 m square, AND expose at least nine straight runs of 1.5 m.
Check the tall arch. It is a 4 m wide top bar with a 2 m tall leg hanging under each end, so it measures 4 m across and 3 m tall. That fits inside the 4 m by 4 m square.
Count its outer runs. Top of the bar (4 m long): 2 cases. Left outer edge (3 m): 2 cases. Right outer edge (3 m): 2 cases.
Count its inner runs. The gap under the bar, between the legs (2 m): 1 case. The inner face of each leg (2 m tall): 1 case each, so 2 more.
Add them up: 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 9. It fits the square and holds all nine cases, so this is the satisfactory arrangement.
keyConcept: A layout works only if it clears both hurdles at once: it fits the 4 m by 4 m usable square, and its edges provide at least nine separate straight runs of 1.5 m for the nine rigid cases.
commonMistake: Checking only whether the tables fit and forgetting the second hurdle. The neat 3 m by 3 m pinwheel fits easily, but its four 3 m sides give only eight 1.5 m runs, so the ninth case has nowhere to go.

optionExplanations.0: The pinwheel fits as a tidy 3 m by 3 m square, but its four 3 m sides each hold only two 1.5 m cases: eight in all, one short of nine.
optionExplanations.1: Four tables in one row stretch 8 m long. That cannot even fit the 4 m usable width, let alone leave the 1 m clearance.
optionExplanations.3: The solid 4 m by 2 m block fits, but only its outside edges are usable: two 4 m sides (2 cases each) and two 2 m sides (1 each) give just six runs.
optionExplanations.4: The right shape but stretched too wide, about 6 m across, so it cannot leave the 1 m clear border in a 6 m room.

figureExplanation: The five pictures are: a pinwheel of four tables (a 3 m by 3 m square), a single 8 m row, a tall arch (a 4 m wide bar with a 2 m leg under each end, so 4 m by 3 m), a solid 4 m by 2 m block, and a wider stretched arch. Trace the tall arch's edges to see why it wins: the 4 m top holds 2 cases, each 3 m outer side holds 2, the 2 m gap under the bar holds 1, and the 2 m inner face of each leg holds 1, giving nine in all, while its 4 m by 3 m footprint still fits the 4 m by 4 m usable square. The pinwheel gives only 8 runs, the block only 6, and the row and the wide arch are too long to leave the 1 m clearance.

shortExplanation: Max Weber is a founding figure of sociology, not pedagogy, so that scholar/field pairing is the incorrect one.
solutionSteps: Check each pairing against the scholar's recognized field.
Amartya Sen is a Nobel-winning economist, Konrad Lorenz founded ethology, Doris Lessing won the Nobel in Literature, and Wittgenstein was a philosopher.
Max Weber is famous for sociology (e.g. 'The Protestant Ethic'), not pedagogy.
The mismatched pair is Max Weber with Pedagogy.
keyConcept: Match major scholars to the discipline they are actually associated with.
commonMistake: Assuming a broad social-science thinker like Weber belongs to education/pedagogy rather than sociology.

optionExplanations.0: Amartya Sen is genuinely an economist (welfare economics, Nobel 1998), so this pair is correct.
optionExplanations.1: Konrad Lorenz is a founder of ethology, so this pair is correct.
optionExplanations.4: Ludwig Wittgenstein was a philosopher of language and logic, so this pair is correct.

shortExplanation: Mahatma Gandhi was never awarded the Nobel Peace Prize despite several nominations; the other four figures were.
solutionSteps: Recall the Peace Prize laureates among the listed figures.
Aung San Suu Kyi (1991), Nelson Mandela (1993), Willy Brandt (1971) and Martin Luther King Jr. (1964) all received it.
Gandhi was nominated multiple times but never won.
Therefore Gandhi is the one who was NOT awarded the prize.
keyConcept: Knowledge of prominent Nobel Peace Prize laureates.
commonMistake: Assuming such an iconic peace figure as Gandhi must have received the prize.

optionExplanations.0: Aung San Suu Kyi received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1991.
optionExplanations.1: Nelson Mandela shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993.
optionExplanations.4: Martin Luther King Jr. received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964.

shortExplanation: From 2 log10(x) - 3 = log10(y), write 2 log10(x) = log10(x^2) and 3 = log10(1000), so log10(x^2) - log10(1000) = log10(y), giving y = x^2/1000.
solutionSteps: Use the power law: 2 log10(x) = log10(x^2).
Write the constant as a log: 3 = log10(1000).
Substitute: log10(x^2) - log10(1000) = log10(y).
Apply the quotient law: log10(x^2 / 1000) = log10(y).
Equate the arguments: y = x^2 / 1000.
keyConcept: Logarithm laws: a*log(x) = log(x^a), a constant k = log(10^k), and log(a) - log(b) = log(a/b).
commonMistake: Treating the '3' as subtracting 3 from x^2 rather than as log10(1000), leading to y = x^2 - 3.

optionExplanations.2: Dividing by 3 instead of 1000 misreads the constant term, since 3 = log10(1000) not log10(3).
optionExplanations.3: Writing y = x^2 - 3 subtracts 3 outside the logarithm, ignoring that the whole equation is in log form.
optionExplanations.4: Using 2x instead of x^2 misapplies the power law, which turns the coefficient 2 into an exponent.

figureExplanation: The correct expression is y = x^2 / 1000, obtained by converting 2 log10(x) to log10(x^2) and 3 to log10(1000).

shortExplanation: Solving the system gives x = 4 and y = 3, so x + y = 7.
solutionSteps: From 2x - y = 5, write y = 2x - 5.
Substitute into x + 3y = 13: x + 3(2x - 5) = 13.
Expand: x + 6x - 15 = 13, so 7x = 28 and x = 4.
Then y = 2(4) - 5 = 3, giving x + y = 4 + 3 = 7.
keyConcept: Solve simultaneous linear equations by substitution.
commonMistake: Sign slip when substituting -y, which flips the value of y.

optionExplanations.1: 8 does not match the solved values x = 4, y = 3.
optionExplanations.2: 6 comes from an arithmetic slip; the exact solution gives 7.
optionExplanations.3: 9 would require different x, y values than the system yields.

shortExplanation: Since a + b + c = 24, the four new numbers sum to 36, giving a mean of 9.
solutionSteps: Mean of a, b, c is 8, so a + b + c = 3 * 8 = 24.
Sum of the new four numbers: (a+1) + (b+2) + (c+6) + 3 = (a+b+c) + 12.
That equals 24 + 12 = 36.
keyConcept: Total = mean * count; track the added constants separately.
commonMistake: Dividing the added constants by 3 instead of using all four values.

optionExplanations.0: 7 ignores part of the added constants or divides incorrectly.
optionExplanations.1: 11 would come from dividing 24 by 3 then adding, mishandling the count of four.
optionExplanations.4: 27 is 24 + 3, forgetting to divide the total by 4.

shortExplanation: Using difference of squares, 27^2 - 23^2 = 200 and 14^2 - 6^2 = 160, summing to 360.
solutionSteps: Apply a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b).
keyConcept: Factor differences of squares to avoid squaring large numbers.
commonMistake: Computing (27 - 23)^2 + (14 - 6)^2 instead of the difference of squares.

optionExplanations.0: 1680 overcounts, e.g. treating the products incorrectly.
optionExplanations.2: 80 = 4^2 + 8^2, the error of squaring the differences.
optionExplanations.3: 840 is double 420 and does not match the correct 360.

shortExplanation: Both V/R1 and Q/t have units of electric current (amperes), so their sum is dimensionally consistent as a current.
solutionSteps: V/R equals current by Ohm's law (V = IR), giving amperes.
Q/t is charge per time, which is also amperes.
Adding two currents yields a current, so units match on both sides.
The other options add quantities of different dimensions.
keyConcept: An equation is dimensionally consistent only if every added term shares the same units.
commonMistake: Adding terms that look physical but differ in dimension, such as energy plus power.

optionExplanations.0: mv^2 is energy but Fv is power (energy per time), so the sum mixes dimensions.
optionExplanations.1: R1 and R2 are ohms but 1/R3 and 1/R4 are inverse ohms, so terms differ.
optionExplanations.3: vt^2 has units of m*s while F/m is an acceleration, so they cannot be added.

formulaNotes: V = IR so V/R = I; I = Q/t. Both give amperes.

shortExplanation: For uniform circular motion the resultant force is centripetal: F = m v^2 / r = 1000 x 30^2 / 50 = 18000 N = 18 kN. It points toward the centre of the circle, which in the diagram is the direction labelled R.
solutionSteps: At constant speed around a circle the resultant force is centripetal, given by F = m v^2 / r.
Substitute the values: F = 1000 x (30)^2 / 50 = 1000 x 900 / 50.
The acceleration and resultant force point toward the centre of the circle, which is the direction labelled R.
The row giving 18 kN and direction R is correct.
keyConcept: Uniform circular motion requires a net centripetal force of m v^2 / r directed toward the centre of the circle.
commonMistake: Concluding the resultant force is zero because the speed is constant; the velocity direction keeps changing, so there is a centripetal acceleration.

optionExplanations.0: A resultant force of 0 kN ignores that changing direction requires a net centripetal force.
optionExplanations.1: The magnitude 18 kN is right, but direction Q is along the motion (tangential); the acceleration points toward the centre.
optionExplanations.4: 30 kN comes from an incorrect calculation, and direction Q is tangential rather than toward the centre.

figureExplanation: The car sits at the left of the circle with the centre to its right; R points toward that centre, Q points forward along the motion, and P points outward away from the centre.
formulaNotes: F = m v^2 / r = 1000 x 30^2 / 50 = 18000 N = 18 kN, directed toward the centre (R).

shortExplanation: Specific heat capacity is c = Q / (m * deltaT) = 9000 / (2.5 * 4). The expression with 9000 divided by (2.5 x 4) is correct.
solutionSteps: Start from Q = m c deltaT.
Rearrange for c: c = Q / (m * deltaT).
Substitute Q = 9000 J, m = 2.5 kg, deltaT = 4 K.
keyConcept: Q = m c deltaT rearranges to c = Q / (m deltaT).
commonMistake: Placing mass and temperature change in the numerator (e.g. 9000 x 2.5 x 4), inverting the correct rearrangement.

optionExplanations.0: 9000 x 2.5 x 4 multiplies everything instead of dividing energy by (m deltaT).
optionExplanations.1: (2.5 x 4)/9000 inverts the whole expression, giving 1/c not c.
optionExplanations.2: 9000 x 2.5 / 4 puts mass in the numerator instead of the denominator.

figureExplanation: Only the expression 9000 / (2.5 x 4) correctly places energy over the product of mass and temperature rise.

shortExplanation: A couple is two equal, opposite, non-collinear forces; its torque equals F times the perpendicular separation d between them. The diagram with one force up at one end and the equal force down at the other end, separated by d, correctly gives torque = F x d.
solutionSteps: Identify a couple: two equal-magnitude forces that are antiparallel and act along different lines (not collinear).
Reject diagrams with both forces in the same direction (no rotation) or acting along the same line (no couple).
The remaining valid couples have one force up at one end and one force down at the other, separated by distance d.
The torque of a couple about any point equals F times the separation d, so torque = F x d.
Select the diagram that both shows this up/down couple and states torque = F x d.
keyConcept: The moment of a couple is F times the perpendicular distance between the two forces and is the same about any point.
commonMistake: Halving the torque to (F x d)/2, as if only one force or half the arm contributed - the full separation d applies.

optionExplanations.0: This shows a genuine couple but states torque (F x d)/2, understating the true moment F x d.
optionExplanations.1: The two forces act along the same line (both along the beam axis), so they form no couple and produce no rotation.
optionExplanations.2: Both forces point up (parallel, same direction), giving a net force rather than a couple.

figureExplanation: The correct diagram has an upward F at one end and a downward F at the other, a perpendicular separation d, and the stated torque F x d.
formulaNotes: Torque of a couple = F x d, where d is the perpendicular distance between the two equal antiparallel forces.

shortExplanation: Ribosomes are built from rRNA and protein and contain RNA but no DNA.
solutionSteps: List organelles that hold DNA: nucleus/nucleolus region, mitochondria and chloroplasts all contain DNA.
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum has little characteristic nucleic acid content and is not the RNA-only structure sought.
Ribosomes consist of ribosomal RNA plus proteins, with no DNA.
So the RNA-containing but DNA-free organelle is the ribosome.
keyConcept: Ribosomes are ribonucleoprotein particles: rRNA plus protein, no DNA.
commonMistake: Choosing the nucleolus, which is associated with the DNA of ribosomal gene regions.

optionExplanations.0: The nucleolus forms around DNA (the nucleolar organizer regions), so it is associated with DNA.
optionExplanations.1: Mitochondria contain their own DNA as well as RNA.
optionExplanations.2: Chloroplasts contain their own DNA as well as RNA.

shortExplanation: Mitosis produces two cells genetically identical to the diploid parent, so each cell keeps both homologous chromosomes (two DNA molecules carrying the two linked genes), each molecule bearing one allele of each gene. Depending on the parent's linkage phase this is either E and R on one molecule with e and r on the other, or E and r on one with e and R on the other, so rows 6 and 7 are both possible.
solutionSteps: In mitosis DNA replicates and sister chromatids separate, so each daughter cell is identical to the parent and stays diploid.
The cell therefore contains both homologous chromosomes, i.e. two DNA molecules carrying these two linked genes.
Because both genes lie on the same molecule, each molecule must carry one allele of each gene (never just one gene).
For a heterozygote in coupling (cis): one molecule has E and R, the other has e and r (row 6).
For a heterozygote in repulsion (trans): one molecule has E and r, the other has e and R (row 7).
Since the phase is unspecified, both row 6 and row 7 are possible.
