Supply and demand is an economics concept, Bayes' theorem is due to Thomas Bayes, and the uncertainty principle is Heisenberg's.
So the correct association is the normal distribution curve.
keyConcept: The normal distribution is synonymously called the Gaussian distribution, after Carl Friedrich Gauss.
commonMistake: Mixing up eponymous results: Bayes' theorem (Bayes) and the uncertainty principle (Heisenberg) belong to other scientists.

optionExplanations.2: The law of supply and demand is an economics principle with no connection to Gauss's mathematics.
optionExplanations.3: Bayes' theorem is named after the English statistician Thomas Bayes, not Gauss.
optionExplanations.4: The uncertainty principle is a quantum mechanics result due to Werner Heisenberg.

shortExplanation: The sharing economy is built on using idle assets (unused value is wasted value), trusting strangers via reputation systems, preferring access over ownership, and open data driving innovation. 'Competition is dangerous' is not one of its principles.
solutionSteps: Recall the core principles popularised in sharing-economy literature: idle capacity should be used (unused value is wasted value).
Platforms overcome 'stranger danger' through ratings, reviews and trust systems.
Consumers increasingly prefer access to goods and services over owning them outright.
Transparent and open data is held to increase innovation and trust across platforms.
'Competition is dangerous' is not part of this framework — sharing-economy thinking generally embraces open markets — so it is the statement that is NOT a principle.
keyConcept: Sharing-economy principles: use idle capacity, build trust between strangers, favour access over ownership, and open data.
commonMistake: Reading 'stranger danger can be overcome' as negative when it is actually a core sharing-economy claim about trust systems.

optionExplanations.0: Putting idle assets to use — 'unused value is wasted value' — is a founding principle of the sharing economy.
optionExplanations.3: Preferring access to ownership (renting, sharing, subscribing) is central to the sharing-economy model.
optionExplanations.4: Open, transparent data enabling innovation and trust is one of the movement's stated principles.

shortExplanation: Amarcord (1973), the nostalgic portrait of life in a 1930s Italian seaside town, was directed by Federico Fellini and won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film.
solutionSteps: Amarcord is a 1973 Italian film whose title comes from the Romagnol dialect for 'I remember'.
It depicts adolescence in a small Italian town (modelled on Rimini) during the Fascist era.
Rimini was the hometown of Federico Fellini, and the film is his semi-autobiographical work.
Fellini directed it, earning the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film.
Kubrick, Coppola, Truffaut and Hitchcock are directors of other traditions and never made Amarcord.
keyConcept: Amarcord (1973) is Federico Fellini's semi-autobiographical film about his youth in Rimini.
commonMistake: Attributing famous European art films generically to Truffaut — Amarcord is Italian, not French New Wave.

optionExplanations.0: Stanley Kubrick directed films such as 2001: A Space Odyssey, not this Italian memoir film.
optionExplanations.1: Francis Ford Coppola is known for The Godfather series, not for Amarcord.
optionExplanations.2: François Truffaut was a French New Wave director (The 400 Blows); Amarcord is an Italian film by another director.

shortExplanation: Spanish, Romanian, Catalan and French all descend from Latin and are Romance languages; Bulgarian is a South Slavic language, so it does not belong to the Romance family.
solutionSteps: Romance languages are those that evolved from Vulgar Latin.
Spanish, French and Catalan are classic Western Romance languages.
Romanian, despite its Balkan location, is an Eastern Romance language descended from Latin.
Bulgarian belongs to the Slavic branch of Indo-European (South Slavic, related to Serbian and Macedonian) and uses the Cyrillic alphabet.
Therefore Bulgarian is the language that is not Romance.
keyConcept: Romance languages descend from Latin; Bulgarian is South Slavic, a separate Indo-European branch.
commonMistake: Assuming Romanian's Slavic-region neighbours share its family — Romanian is Romance, while neighbouring Bulgarian is Slavic.

optionExplanations.1: Spanish is one of the most widely spoken Romance languages, descended from Vulgar Latin.
optionExplanations.2: Romanian is an Eastern Romance language directly descended from Latin, despite being surrounded by Slavic languages.
optionExplanations.3: Catalan, spoken in northeastern Spain, evolved from Latin and is a Romance language.

shortExplanation: Hungary is an EU member but has kept its own currency, the forint; it does not use the euro. All the other currency-country pairs are correct.
solutionSteps: Peso is the currency of Argentina — correct pair.
Baht is the currency of Thailand — correct pair.
Rand is the currency of South Africa — correct pair.
Rupee is the currency of India — correct pair.
Hungary uses the forint, not the euro, so 'Euro - Hungary' is the incorrect pair.
keyConcept: EU membership does not imply euro adoption: Hungary retains the forint.
commonMistake: Assuming every European Union country uses the euro — several members (Hungary, Poland, Czechia, Denmark, Sweden and others) keep national currencies.

optionExplanations.0: Argentina's currency is indeed the Argentine peso, so this pair is correct.
optionExplanations.1: Thailand's currency is the baht, so this pair is correct.
optionExplanations.4: India's currency is the rupee, so this pair is correct.

shortExplanation: The Fields Medal is the most prestigious award in mathematics, given every four years to outstanding mathematicians under 40.
solutionSteps: The Fields Medal is awarded by the International Mathematical Union at its congress every four years.
It honours mathematicians under the age of 40 for outstanding mathematical achievement.
It is often described as the mathematics equivalent of a Nobel Prize, since there is no Nobel Prize in mathematics.
Economics has the Nobel Memorial Prize, and music, psychology and biology have their own distinct honours.
Hence the field is mathematics.
keyConcept: The Fields Medal is mathematics' highest honour, awarded quadrennially to mathematicians under 40.
commonMistake: Assuming every major discipline has a Nobel Prize — mathematics does not, which is why the Fields Medal fills that role.

optionExplanations.0: Economics is recognised by the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, not by the Fields Medal.
optionExplanations.3: Psychology has no connection to the Fields Medal, which is strictly mathematical.
optionExplanations.4: Biology achievements fall under prizes such as the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, not the Fields Medal.

shortExplanation: Charles Dickens died in 1870, three decades before the Nobel Prizes were first awarded in 1901, so he could never have won the Nobel Prize in Literature. Neruda, Dylan, Mann and Pinter are all laureates.
solutionSteps: The Nobel Prizes were first awarded in 1901 and are never given posthumously to earlier figures.
Charles Dickens died in 1870, before the prize existed, so he cannot be a laureate.
Pablo Neruda won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1971.
Thomas Mann won in 1929, Harold Pinter in 2005, and Bob Dylan in 2016.
Therefore Dickens is the one who did not win.
keyConcept: Nobel Prizes began in 1901, so 19th-century authors like Dickens (d. 1870) were never eligible.
commonMistake: Doubting Bob Dylan because he is a songwriter — he genuinely received the 2016 Nobel Prize in Literature.

optionExplanations.0: Pablo Neruda received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1971.
optionExplanations.1: Bob Dylan won the 2016 Nobel Prize in Literature for creating new poetic expressions within song.
optionExplanations.2: Thomas Mann received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1929.

shortExplanation: Beyond Good and Evil is a philosophical work by Friedrich Nietzsche. The Truce, If This Is a Man, The Drowned and the Saved, and If Not Now, When? are all by Primo Levi.
solutionSteps: Primo Levi was an Italian chemist and Holocaust survivor whose writing centres on his Auschwitz experience.
If This Is a Man is his memoir of Auschwitz, and The Truce recounts his journey home after liberation.
The Drowned and the Saved is his late collection of essays on the camps, and If Not Now, When? is his novel about Jewish partisans.
Beyond Good and Evil (1886) is a philosophy book by Friedrich Nietzsche, unrelated to Levi.
So Beyond Good and Evil is the work not written by Primo Levi.
keyConcept: Primo Levi's core works are Holocaust testimony (If This Is a Man, The Truce, The Drowned and the Saved); Beyond Good and Evil is Nietzsche.
commonMistake: Confusing similar-sounding moral-philosophy titles with Levi's ethical reflections on the camps.

optionExplanations.0: The Truce is Levi's account of his long journey home from Auschwitz.
optionExplanations.1: If This Is a Man is Levi's famous Auschwitz memoir, his best-known book.
optionExplanations.2: The Drowned and the Saved is Levi's final essay collection on the Holocaust.

shortExplanation: Cape Verde is an independent island republic in the Atlantic off West Africa (a former Portuguese colony), not part of Brazil. The other archipelago-country pairs are all correct.
solutionSteps: Hawaii is a state of the United States of America — correct pair.
The Azores are an autonomous Portuguese archipelago in the Atlantic — correct pair.
The Canary Islands are a Spanish autonomous community off northwest Africa — correct pair.
The Galapagos Islands belong to Ecuador — correct pair.
Cape Verde has been an independent country since 1975 (previously Portuguese, never Brazilian), so pairing it with Brazil is incorrect.
keyConcept: Cape Verde is a sovereign African island nation; its colonial link was to Portugal, not Brazil.
commonMistake: Linking Cape Verde to Brazil because both are Portuguese-speaking Atlantic nations — shared language does not mean shared sovereignty.

optionExplanations.1: The Azores really are Portuguese, an autonomous region of Portugal in the mid-Atlantic.
optionExplanations.3: The Canary Islands really are Spanish territory off the coast of Morocco.
optionExplanations.4: The Galapagos Islands really do belong to Ecuador, lying about 1000 km off its coast.

shortExplanation: In Italy only Parliament is chosen directly by the voters: the Senate of the Republic is elected by direct universal suffrage. The President of the Republic is elected by Parliament, and the Government and its President of the Council are appointed, not directly elected.
solutionSteps: Under the Italian Constitution, the two chambers of Parliament — the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate of the Republic — are elected directly by universal suffrage.
The President of the Republic is elected indirectly, by Parliament in joint session together with regional delegates.
The President of the Council of Ministers (prime minister) is appointed by the President of the Republic and must win parliamentary confidence; citizens never vote for this office directly.

The Government (Council of Ministers) is likewise appointed, and the High Council of the Judiciary is composed partly of magistrates elected by their peers and partly of members elected by Parliament.
Therefore the only institution listed that is chosen by direct universal suffrage is the Senate of the Republic.
keyConcept: In Italy direct universal suffrage elects Parliament (Chamber and Senate); the Head of State and the Government are chosen indirectly.
commonMistake: Assuming the President of the Republic is elected by the people — Italy's president is chosen by Parliament plus regional delegates.

optionExplanations.0: The President of the Council of Ministers is appointed by the Head of State and confirmed by parliamentary confidence, never elected directly.
optionExplanations.2: The Government is formed by appointment and confidence votes; citizens do not elect it directly.
optionExplanations.4: The President of the Republic is elected by Parliament in joint session with regional delegates, not by direct popular vote.

shortExplanation: The World Heritage List of sites of outstanding cultural or natural importance is maintained by UNESCO, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization.
solutionSteps: The World Heritage Sites programme stems from the 1972 World Heritage Convention.
That convention is administered by UNESCO, whose World Heritage Committee inscribes and monitors the sites.
WTO deals with trade rules, WHO with public health, OECD with economic policy, and UNICEF with children's welfare.
None of those four bodies has any mandate over heritage sites.
Hence the organisation is UNESCO.
keyConcept: UNESCO administers the World Heritage Convention and maintains the World Heritage List.
commonMistake: Confusing the various UN-family acronyms — UNICEF protects children, while UNESCO covers education, science and culture, including heritage.

optionExplanations.0: WTO is the World Trade Organization, which regulates international trade.
optionExplanations.1: WHO is the World Health Organization, concerned with global public health.
optionExplanations.3: UNICEF is the UN agency for children's rights and welfare, not cultural heritage.

shortExplanation: Rationalise 2/(2+sqrt(3)) by multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate (2-sqrt(3)). The denominator becomes 4-3 = 1, leaving 4 - 2*sqrt(3).
solutionSteps: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate (2 - sqrt(3)).
Denominator: (2 + sqrt(3))(2 - sqrt(3)) = 2^2 - (sqrt(3))^2 = 4 - 3 = 1.
Numerator: 2*(2 - sqrt(3)) = 4 - 2*sqrt(3).
Result = (4 - 2*sqrt(3)) / 1 = 4 - 2*sqrt(3).
keyConcept: Rationalising a denominator uses the conjugate and the difference-of-squares identity.
commonMistake: Multiplying by (2 + sqrt(3)) instead of the conjugate, which does not remove the surd.

optionExplanations.0: 1 - sqrt(3)/2 is roughly 0.13; the true value 2/(2+sqrt(3)) is about 0.54, so this is too small.
optionExplanations.2: 4 + 2*sqrt(3) comes from using the wrong sign in the conjugate; the denominator would not simplify to 1.
optionExplanations.3: 4/7 + 2*sqrt(3)/7 wrongly keeps a denominator of 7, but (2+sqrt(3))(2-sqrt(3)) equals 1, not 7.

figureExplanation: The figure shows the expression 2/(2+sqrt(3)) and five candidate simplified forms; the algebra selects 4 - 2*sqrt(3).

shortExplanation: For y = 2x^2 + 5x - 2 the turning point x-coordinate is -b/(2a) = -5/4; substituting gives y = -41/8, so the vertex is (-5/4, -41/8).
solutionSteps: Identify a = 2, b = 5, c = -2.
x of turning point = -b/(2a) = -5/(2*2) = -5/4.
Convert to eighths: 25/8 - 50/8 - 16/8 = -41/8.
Turning point = (-5/4, -41/8).
keyConcept: The vertex of y = ax^2 + bx + c lies at x = -b/(2a).
commonMistake: Using x = -b/a (giving -5/2) instead of -b/(2a).

optionExplanations.0: (-5/4, -41/16) has the correct x but the y-value is halved; substituting -5/4 gives -41/8, not -41/16.
optionExplanations.3: (-5/2, -41/8) uses x = -b/a = -5/2, which is not the vertex formula.
optionExplanations.4: (-5/2, -41/16) has both coordinates wrong, mixing the -b/a error with a halved y.

figureExplanation: The figure gives y = 2x^2 + 5x - 2 and five coordinate pairs; the vertex formula picks (-5/4, -41/8).
formulaNotes: Vertex x = -b/(2a); then y is found by substitution.

shortExplanation: Write every base as a power of 2: 8^(2x+3) = 2^(6x+9) and 1/4^(3x) = 2^(-6x). The left side collapses to 2^9, so 9 = x + 3 and x = 6.
solutionSteps: Set equal to right side: 2^9 = 2^(x+3), so 9 = x + 3.
Solve: x = 6.
keyConcept: Express all terms with a common base, then equate exponents.
commonMistake: Forgetting the reciprocal makes the 4-term exponent negative, or not tripling the 8-exponent.

optionExplanations.0: x = 0 gives 2^9 on the left but 2^3 on the right, which are not equal.
optionExplanations.1: x = 3 gives 2^9 on the left and 2^6 on the right, so it fails.
optionExplanations.3: x = 1/2 does not satisfy 9 = x + 3, which requires x = 6.

figureExplanation: The figure shows 8^(2x+3) * (1/4^(3x)) = 2^(x+3); converting to base 2 yields x = 6.

shortExplanation: Total meals = 75 students * 3.2 mean = 240. Males ate 39*2 = 78, so females ate 162, giving x = 162/36 = 4.5 = 4 1/2.
solutionSteps: Overall mean 3 1/5 = 3.2, with 39 + 36 = 75 students.
Total meals for all students = 75 * 3.2 = 240.
Total meals for males = 39 * 2 = 78.
Total meals for females = 240 - 78 = 162.
keyConcept: A weighted (combined) mean equals total sum divided by total count.
commonMistake: Averaging the two group means directly (i.e. treating (2 + x)/2 = 3.2) ignores the unequal group sizes.

optionExplanations.1: 4 2/5 (4.4) would give female total 36*4.4 = 158.4, so overall total 236.4, not 240.
optionExplanations.2: 2 3/5 is far too low; females must average well above the overall 3.2 to lift the males' 2.
optionExplanations.4: 3 4/5 (3.8) gives female total 136.8 and overall 214.8, well below 240.

figureExplanation: The table gives male mean 2, female mean x, and overall mean 3 1/5; the weighted-mean equation yields x = 4 1/2.
formulaNotes: Combined mean = (n1*mean1 + n2*mean2) / (n1 + n2).

shortExplanation: The net upward force is thrust minus weight, T - mg. By Newton's second law a = (T - mg)/m = T/m - g.
solutionSteps: Two vertical forces act: thrust T up and weight mg down.
Net upward force F = T - mg.
Apply Newton's second law: a = F/m = (T - mg)/m.
Simplify: a = T/m - g.
keyConcept: Acceleration equals net force divided by mass (Newton's second law).
commonMistake: Forgetting to divide the whole net force by m, or subtracting g before dividing thrust by m.

optionExplanations.2: T/m ignores gravity, which still acts downward as the rocket leaves the pad.
optionExplanations.3: T/m - mg is dimensionally inconsistent: T/m is an acceleration but mg is a force.
optionExplanations.4: T - mg is the net force, not the acceleration; it must still be divided by m.

figureExplanation: The free-body sketch shows thrust T upward and weight mg downward on mass m; the net force T - mg divided by m gives T/m - g.
formulaNotes: Newton's second law: a = F_net/m, with F_net = T - mg.

shortExplanation: The heater delivers 100 W for 1600 s, and all of that energy vaporises 200 g of liquid, so the specific latent heat is the energy divided by the mass vaporised, giving 800 J/g.
solutionSteps: Energy supplied = power * time = 100 W * 1600 s = 160000 J.
All energy goes into evaporation since the liquid is already at boiling point and no heat is lost.
Specific latent heat L = energy / mass = 160000 J / 200 g = 800 J/g.
keyConcept: At boiling point, added energy converts liquid to vapour without raising temperature: Q = m*L.
commonMistake: Dividing by the total 1000 g in the beaker instead of the 200 g that actually vaporised.

optionExplanations.0: 12.5 J/g comes from dividing by 1600 s and the full mass, mixing up quantities.
optionExplanations.1: 160 J/g uses 1000 g (total liquid) instead of the 200 g vaporised.
optionExplanations.2: 3200 J/g uses only a fraction of the energy or a wrong mass, not 160000 J / 200 g.

formulaNotes: Q = m*L, so L = Q/m; here Q = P*t = 160000 J and m = 200 g.

shortExplanation: For a parabolic concave mirror, rays parallel to the axis reflect through F and, by reversibility, rays through F reflect parallel to the axis; the image type depends on object position, so it is not always inverted, real, or magnified.
solutionSteps: Statement 1: parallel incident rays converge at F after reflection - true for a parabolic mirror.
Statement 2: by the reversibility of light, rays passing through F emerge parallel to the axis - true.
Statement 3: an object inside the focal length gives an upright virtual image, so 'always inverted' is false.
Statement 4: that same case gives a virtual image, so 'always real' is false.
Statement 5: image size varies with object distance, so 'always larger' is false.
Only statements 1 and 2 are correct.
keyConcept: The focus and parallel-ray properties are fixed for a concave mirror, but image orientation, nature, and size depend on object position relative to F.
commonMistake: Assuming a concave mirror always produces a real, inverted image, forgetting the magnifying-mirror case when the object is inside F.

optionExplanations.0: '1 and 3 only' wrongly keeps statement 3, since an object inside F gives an upright image.
optionExplanations.2: '2 and 4 only' includes statement 4, but the image is not always real.
optionExplanations.4: '1, 3 and 4 only' adds the false 'always inverted' and 'always real' claims.

shortExplanation: The boat's 4.0 m/s across and the river's 3.0 m/s downstream are perpendicular, giving a resultant of sqrt(4^2+3^2) = 5.0 m/s. Measured from the straight-across line, cos(angle) = 4.0/5.0.
solutionSteps: The boat velocity (4.0 m/s) points straight across; the river velocity (3.0 m/s) points along the bank, so they are at right angles.
Resultant speed = sqrt(4.0^2 + 3.0^2) = sqrt(16 + 9) = sqrt(25) = 5.0 m/s.
The angle is measured from the line at 90 degrees to the bank (the straight-across direction).
The across component (4.0) is adjacent to this angle and the resultant (5.0) is the hypotenuse, so cos(angle) = 4.0/5.0.
Hence angle = cos^-1(4.0/5.0).
keyConcept: Perpendicular velocity components add as a right-angled vector triangle (Pythagoras and trigonometry).
commonMistake: Measuring the angle from the bank instead of from the perpendicular, which swaps the 3.0 and 4.0 in the ratio.

optionExplanations.1: 7.0 m/s adds the speeds arithmetically (4.0 + 3.0) instead of combining perpendicular vectors.
optionExplanations.2: 7.0 m/s again wrongly sums the magnitudes; the resultant is 5.0 m/s.
optionExplanations.4: cos^-1(3.0/4.0) uses component/component rather than adjacent/hypotenuse; here cos uses 4.0/5.0.

figureExplanation: The options show speed-and-angle pairs; the right-angled 3-4-5 triangle gives 5.0 m/s and angle cos^-1(4.0/5.0) from the perpendicular.
formulaNotes: Resultant = sqrt(vx^2 + vy^2); cos(angle) = adjacent/hypotenuse = 4.0/5.0.

shortExplanation: Different viruses use single-stranded DNA, double-stranded DNA, or RNA as their genetic material, so all three types occur among viruses.
solutionSteps: Viruses are classified partly by their genome type.
Examples exist for single-stranded DNA (e.g. parvoviruses), double-stranded DNA (e.g. herpesviruses), and RNA (e.g. influenza).
Therefore all three nucleic acid types are found in viruses.
keyConcept: Viral genomes are diverse and can be DNA or RNA, single- or double-stranded.
commonMistake: Assuming all viruses store information only as double-stranded DNA like cellular organisms.

optionExplanations.1: '1 and 2 only' excludes RNA viruses, which are extremely common.
optionExplanations.2: '2 only' wrongly limits viruses to double-stranded DNA alone.
optionExplanations.4: '2 and 3 only' omits single-stranded DNA viruses, which also exist.

shortExplanation: Only the eukaryotic cell (irregular membrane enclosing a nucleus with chromosomes) is produced by mitosis; the bacterium, mitochondrion, chloroplast and virus are not.
solutionSteps: Mitosis is nuclear division of eukaryotic cells that produces genetically identical daughter cells.
The first diagram shows a eukaryotic cell with a nucleus and chromosome material, i.e. a product of mitosis.
The rod-shaped cell with flagella and free DNA/ribosomes is a bacterium, which divides by binary fission, not mitosis.
The double-membraned organelle with cristae is a mitochondrion, and the one with internal stacked membranes is a chloroplast; both replicate by their own fission of existing organelles.
The particle with an outer envelope, surface spikes and internal genetic material is a virus, which is assembled inside a host, not by mitosis.
keyConcept: Mitosis produces eukaryotic cells; prokaryotes and organelles use binary fission and viruses self-assemble.
commonMistake: Assuming any dividing structure uses mitosis, when bacteria and organelles use binary fission.

optionExplanations.1: The rod cell with flagella and no true nucleus is a bacterium; it divides by binary fission.
optionExplanations.2: The organelle with folded inner membrane (cristae) is a mitochondrion, formed by division of existing mitochondria.
optionExplanations.4: The enveloped, spiked particle is a virus, produced by assembly in a host cell, not mitosis.

figureExplanation: Diagram A is a eukaryotic cell/nucleus with chromosomes; the others are a bacterium, mitochondrion, chloroplast and virus, none of which arise by mitosis.

shortExplanation: Esterifying three C8H16O2 fatty acids with glycerol releases three water molecules; summing atoms and subtracting 3 H2O gives C27H50O6.
solutionSteps: Three fatty acids: 3 * C8H16O2 = C24H48O6.
Add glycerol C3H8O3: total = C27H56O9.
Ester formation releases 3 water molecules: subtract 3 H2O = -H6O3.
keyConcept: Each ester bond in a triglyceride forms by condensation, removing one water molecule per fatty acid.
commonMistake: Forgetting to remove three water molecules (one per ester bond) when combining the fragments.

optionExplanations.2: C27H48O6 removes too many hydrogens for the three condensations.
optionExplanations.3: C27H52O7 removes too few atoms, keeping extra oxygen and hydrogen.
optionExplanations.4: C27H56O9 is the simple sum with no water removed at all.

formulaNotes: Triglyceride = glycerol + 3 fatty acids - 3 H2O.

shortExplanation: Cholesterol sits between phospholipids in the cell membrane and regulates its fluidity, keeping it stable across temperature changes.
solutionSteps: Cholesterol is a lipid embedded among membrane phospholipids.
It restricts phospholipid movement at high temperature and prevents tight packing at low temperature.
This buffering role maintains an appropriate membrane fluidity.
keyConcept: Cholesterol is a membrane fluidity buffer, not an energy store or transport molecule.
commonMistake: Confusing cholesterol's structural membrane role with the transport and energy roles of other lipids.

optionExplanations.1: Cholesterol is a precursor for steroid hormones only, not all hormones (e.g. not protein hormones).
optionExplanations.2: Cholesterol is not used as an energy source; fats and carbohydrates provide energy.
optionExplanations.4: Cholesterol is largely hydrophobic and does not stabilise membranes via hydrogen bonds to water.

shortExplanation: Label T points to the dense body inside the nucleus, the nucleolus, whose function is forming ribosomal sub-units; that is the row with a correct name-and-function match.
solutionSteps: P points to a stack of flattened membrane sacs (Golgi apparatus), not a mitochondrion, so calling it 'mitochondrion / protein synthesis' is wrong.
Q points to a small paired rod-like structure (centrioles); their role is spindle formation, not holding sister chromatids together.
R points to membranes studded with dots (rough endoplasmic reticulum); a lone ribosome does not form lysosomes.
S points to an oval organelle with cristae (mitochondrion); Golgi apparatus and 'anaerobic respiration' do not describe it.
T points to the dense sphere within the nucleus (nucleolus), which forms ribosomal sub-units, so that row is fully correct.
keyConcept: The nucleolus, inside the nucleus, assembles ribosomal sub-units.
commonMistake: Confusing the nucleolus (ribosome sub-unit assembly) with the whole nucleus or with ribosomes themselves.

optionExplanations.1: The row matching Q to centrioles with 'holds sister chromatids together' is wrong; the centromere/cohesin does that, and centrioles organise the spindle.
optionExplanations.2: The row matching R (rough ER) to ribosome with 'formation of lysosomes' misnames the structure and its function.
optionExplanations.3: The row matching S (a mitochondrion) to Golgi apparatus with 'anaerobic respiration' is doubly wrong.

figureExplanation: T's leader line ends at the dark body within the stippled nucleus, identifying the nucleolus, which makes ribosomal sub-units.

shortExplanation: Enzymes (biological catalysts) operate in the cytoplasm, in the nucleus (e.g. DNA and RNA polymerases), and in mitochondria (respiratory enzymes), so all three contain them.
solutionSteps: Cytoplasm hosts many metabolic enzymes, e.g. those of glycolysis.
The nucleus contains enzymes for replication and transcription such as polymerases.
Mitochondria contain enzymes of the Krebs cycle and electron transport.
All three locations contain biological catalysts.
keyConcept: Enzymes are distributed throughout the cell wherever chemical reactions are catalysed.
commonMistake: Thinking enzymes are confined to the cytoplasm and ignoring nuclear and mitochondrial enzymes.

optionExplanations.1: '2 only' ignores the abundant enzymes in cytoplasm and mitochondria.
optionExplanations.2: '3 only' overlooks nuclear and cytoplasmic enzymes.
optionExplanations.3: '2 and 3 only' leaves out the many cytoplasmic enzymes.

shortExplanation: Converting NAD+ to NADH is a reduction in which NAD+ gains electrons (as hydrogen), making it a redox reaction; the other options involve no change in oxidation state.
solutionSteps: In NAD+ + H2 to NADH + H+, NAD+ accepts a hydride and is reduced.
Reduction of NAD+ is coupled to oxidation of the hydrogen source, so electrons transfer.
The other listed processes (condensation, base pairing, peptide bonding, membrane depolarisation) do not transfer electrons between species.
keyConcept: A redox reaction requires transfer of electrons, changing oxidation states.
commonMistake: Assuming any reaction involving hydrogen or charge (like depolarisation) is automatically redox.

optionExplanations.1: Maltose formation from glucose is a condensation reaction with no electron transfer.
optionExplanations.2: Cytosine-guanine pairing is hydrogen bonding, not oxidation or reduction.
optionExplanations.4: Neuron depolarisation is ion movement across a membrane, not electron transfer between molecules.

formulaNotes: NAD+ + 2H (2e- + 2H+) -> NADH + H+ shows electron gain (reduction).

shortExplanation: A functional SRY gene triggers male development wherever it lands, so inserting it into an X of a female zygote (1) or moving it onto an X sperm by crossing over (3) both cause male characteristics; statement 2 is wrong because an SRY-carrying sperm produces a male, not a female.
solutionSteps: Statement 1: SRY inserted into an X chromosome would still initiate male development, so true.
Statement 3: crossing over can transfer SRY to an X-bearing sperm, producing an XX male, so true.
Statement 2: a sperm carrying functional SRY fertilising a normal ovum would drive male development, not produce a female, so false.
Correct combination is 1 and 3 only.
keyConcept: It is the presence of a functional SRY gene, not the chromosome carrying it, that initiates male development.
commonMistake: Assuming male characteristics require an intact Y chromosome rather than just the SRY gene.

optionExplanations.1: '2 only' selects the one false statement while rejecting the two correct ones.
optionExplanations.3: '1 and 2 only' wrongly includes statement 2, which describes a female outcome from an SRY sperm.
optionExplanations.4: '1 only' omits the valid crossing-over mechanism in statement 3.

shortExplanation: Four pairs of homologous chromosomes means 2n = 8. Meiosis I halves this to two cells of 4 chromosomes each, and meiosis II gives four cells of 4 chromosomes each.
solutionSteps: Four pairs of homologous chromosomes = 8 chromosomes in the parent cell (2n = 8).
Meiosis I separates homologous pairs, producing two cells each with 4 chromosomes (n = 4, each still with two chromatids).
Meiosis II separates the sister chromatids, producing four cells.
Each final cell still has 4 chromosomes, so the counts are 4, 4, 4, 4.
This matches parent 8, meiosis I 4 and 4, meiosis II 4, 4, 4, 4.
keyConcept: Meiosis halves chromosome number at meiosis I; meiosis II separates chromatids without changing chromosome number.
commonMistake: Thinking meiosis II halves the chromosome number again (to 2), when it only separates chromatids.

optionExplanations.1: The row with a parent of 4 is wrong; four pairs means 8 chromosomes, not 4.
optionExplanations.2: The row keeping 8 at the end of meiosis I fails to halve the number during meiosis I.
optionExplanations.4: The row ending with cells of 8 does not reduce the chromosome number at all, contradicting meiosis.

figureExplanation: The table row with parent 8, end of meiosis I 4 and 4, and after meiosis II four cells of 4 is the only one consistent with 2n = 8 undergoing meiosis.
formulaNotes: Diploid 2n = 8 -> meiosis I gives n = 4 per cell -> meiosis II keeps n = 4 in four cells.

shortExplanation: Transcribing the template TATGATCTTAGGCAACAT gives mRNA with A=6, U=6, G=3, C=3, so A and U are each about one third and G and C each about one sixth of the chart.
solutionSteps: mRNA is complementary to the template, pairing A-U, T-A, G-C, C-G (U replaces T).
Template TATGATCTTAGGCAACAT transcribes to mRNA AUACUAGAAUCCGUUGUA.
Count the mRNA bases: A = 6, U = 6, C = 3, G = 3 (total 18).
So A and U are equal and largest (each 1/3), while C and G are equal and smaller (each 1/6).
The correct chart shows U present (not T), with A and U as the two large equal slices and C and G as the two small equal slices.
keyConcept: mRNA is complementary to the DNA template and uses uracil instead of thymine.
commonMistake: Copying the template directly (keeping T and the template proportions) instead of taking the complement with U.

optionExplanations.1: This chart makes U and C the large equal slices, but the correct large pair is A and U.
optionExplanations.2: This chart contains thymine (T), which does not occur in mRNA.
optionExplanations.3: This chart also contains T and uses three equal thirds, matching neither the base set nor the proportions.

figureExplanation: Chart A shows U (not T) with A and U as the two large equal sectors and C and G as the two small equal sectors, matching A=U=6 and C=G=3.
formulaNotes: Base pairing for transcription: A-U, T-A, G-C, C-G.

shortExplanation: In pedigree 2 two affected parents have an unaffected child. Under an autosomal recessive model both affected parents are homozygous recessive and could only have affected children, so this pattern requires the dominant model.
solutionSteps: Under autosomal recessive inheritance, affected individuals are homozygous recessive (aa).
Two affected (aa x aa) parents can produce only aa (affected) offspring.
In pedigree 2, the affected male and affected female who marry have an unaffected daughter.
That unaffected child from two affected parents is impossible if the allele is recessive.
Under autosomal dominant inheritance, affected parents can be heterozygous (Aa x Aa) and can produce an unaffected (aa) child, so pedigree 2 fits only the dominant model.
keyConcept: Two affected recessive parents cannot have an unaffected child; two affected dominant heterozygotes can.
commonMistake: Overlooking that two affected parents producing an unaffected child rules out recessive inheritance.

optionExplanations.1: In pedigree 1 the affected-by-affected crosses give only affected children, which is fully consistent with a recessive model too.
optionExplanations.2: Pedigree 3 has no two-affected-parents-to-unaffected-child event, so a recessive model can explain it.
optionExplanations.3: Pedigree 4's crosses (unaffected x affected) are possible under recessive inheritance as well.

figureExplanation: In pedigree 2 an affected male married to an affected female produces an unaffected daughter, an outcome impossible for a recessive allele but allowed for a dominant one.

shortExplanation: The proton pumps of photosynthesis sit within the thylakoid membrane, which is the membrane of the granum; the stroma and the space between thylakoid membranes are where protons collect, not where the pumps are located.
solutionSteps: During the light reactions, protons are pumped across the thylakoid membrane into the thylakoid space (lumen).
The pump proteins, such as the cytochrome complex, are embedded in the thylakoid membrane itself.
Grana are stacks of thylakoids, so 'the membrane of the granum' is the thylakoid membrane that contains the pumps.
Only the statement naming the membrane of the granum correctly locates the proton pumps.
keyConcept: Membrane transport proteins reside within a membrane, while the ions they move accumulate in the adjacent compartment.
commonMistake: Placing the pumps in the space or the stroma where protons collect, rather than in the membrane that spans them.

optionExplanations.1: The gap between the thylakoid membranes stores the pumped protons but does not house the pump proteins.
optionExplanations.2: The chloroplast stroma receives protons flowing back through ATP synthase but contains no proton pumps.
optionExplanations.3: Combining the stroma with the inter-membrane gap names two compartments where protons gather, neither of which holds the pumps.

shortExplanation: Directional selection can favour an initially low-frequency extreme phenotype, can be driven by a predator, and can raise a recessive allele's frequency if that allele gives the favoured phenotype, so all three statements can be true.
solutionSteps: Directional selection shifts the population toward one extreme phenotype.
The favoured extreme is often initially at low frequency, so 'a low-frequency phenotype is selected' can be true.
A predator removing the previously common phenotype is a valid cause of directional selection, so 'a predator could be the cause' can be true.
If the favoured extreme is expressed by a recessive allele, that allele's frequency rises, so 'the frequency of a recessive allele increases' can be true.
Only the row marking all three as possible (yes/yes/yes) is consistent with directional selection.
keyConcept: Directional selection favours one extreme phenotype, which may be rare, predator-driven, and recessive.
commonMistake: Assuming directional selection cannot increase a recessive allele or cannot start from a rare phenotype.

optionExplanations.1: The row denying that a low-frequency phenotype can be selected is wrong, since directional selection typically favours a rare extreme.
optionExplanations.2: The row denying that a predator could cause it is wrong, since predation is a classic selective pressure.
optionExplanations.3: Rows marking any of the three as impossible are wrong, because each can genuinely occur under directional selection.

figureExplanation: The correct table row marks all three columns as 'yes', matching that a rare, predator-driven, recessive-based phenotype can all feature in directional selection.

shortExplanation: When the left ventricle relaxes, its pressure falls below aortic pressure, so the aortic valve snaps shut to prevent backflow.
solutionSteps: During ventricular systole the aortic valve is open and blood leaves the ventricle.
As the left ventricle relaxes, ventricular pressure drops below aortic pressure.
The pressure reversal forces the aortic (semilunar) valve to close.
keyConcept: Heart valves open and close passively according to the pressure difference across them.
commonMistake: Thinking the aortic valve opens during atrial contraction rather than during ventricular contraction.

optionExplanations.1: The aortic valve opens during ventricular contraction, not when the atrium contracts.
optionExplanations.2: The two atrioventricular valves open and close together, not in opposition.
optionExplanations.3: Both atria contract essentially simultaneously; right atrial contraction does not drive left ventricular contraction.

shortExplanation: The graph shows blood cell count rising after a delay and then plateauing at a higher level. All three proposed causes are mechanisms that raise the number of blood cells, so any of them could produce this rise.
solutionSteps: Read the graph: cell count is steady and low, then climbs steeply, then levels off higher — a net increase in blood cells.
Low atmospheric oxygen causes hypoxia; the kidney releases erythropoietin, stimulating more red blood cell production — count rises.
A bacterial infection triggers proliferation of white blood cells to fight it — count rises.
Increased differentiation of bone marrow stem cells directly yields more blood cells — count rises.
Every statement is a valid cause of an increased count, so all three fit.
keyConcept: Blood cell numbers rise when production is stimulated (hypoxia -> EPO, infection -> leucocytes, or greater stem-cell differentiation).
commonMistake: Assuming only infection can raise blood cell count and overlooking that low oxygen and stem-cell differentiation also increase it.

optionExplanations.1: This excludes valid causes; all three mechanisms raise blood cell numbers, not just two.
optionExplanations.3: Low atmospheric oxygen also raises red cell count via erythropoietin, so it cannot be left out.
optionExplanations.4: Infection and stem-cell differentiation both raise cell count too, so oxygen reduction alone is too narrow.

figureExplanation: The sigmoid curve of number of blood cells per mL versus time shows a clear net increase, which is the effect each listed mechanism would produce.

shortExplanation: The cornea is avascular and gets its glucose and oxygen by diffusion from the aqueous humour, so the note stating that glucose in the aqueous humour diffuses into the cornea is correct.
solutionSteps: The cornea has no blood vessels, so it must obtain nutrients by diffusion from the aqueous humour behind it — this note is true.
The note that the cornea adjusts refraction for fine focusing is wrong: the lens performs accommodation; the cornea's refraction is fixed.
The note that the pupil closes in the dark is wrong: in dim light the pupil dilates to admit more light.
The note that the retina contains motor neurons is wrong: the retina holds photoreceptors and sensory neurons.
The note that the labelled area contains mostly rods for colour vision is wrong: rods give monochrome low-light vision; cones give colour.
keyConcept: The avascular cornea is nourished by diffusion from the aqueous humour, while the lens (not cornea) does fine focusing and cones (not rods) give colour vision.
commonMistake: Crediting the cornea with fine focusing; that role belongs to the lens through accommodation.

optionExplanations.1: The retina contains photoreceptors and sensory (not motor) neurons.
optionExplanations.2: Rods provide black-and-white low-light vision, not colour vision, which relies on cones.
optionExplanations.4: The pupil dilates rather than closes in the dark to let in more light.

figureExplanation: Label 4 points to the front chamber/cornea region, where nutrient diffusion from the aqueous humour into the avascular cornea genuinely occurs.

shortExplanation: The cornea is avascular and immune-privileged, so corneal transplants rarely trigger rejection and generally need no antigen matching.
solutionSteps: Rejection depends on immune cells reaching the graft via blood vessels.
The cornea has no blood supply and is an immune-privileged site.
Consequently corneal grafts can usually succeed without matching donor and recipient antigens.
keyConcept: Immune-privileged, avascular tissues like the cornea are largely shielded from immune rejection.
commonMistake: Assuming every transplanted tissue requires close antigen matching like heart or kidney.

optionExplanations.1: The liver is highly vascular and requires immunological matching and immunosuppression.
optionExplanations.3: The lung is vascularised and strongly rejected without matching.
optionExplanations.4: The heart is a vascular organ that demands careful matching and lifelong immunosuppression.

shortExplanation: In the Venn diagram X is bile only, Z is amylase only, and Y is the shared feature. Bile emulsifies lipid, amylase digests starch, and both act in the small intestine, matching the row that reads emulsifies lipid / works in the small intestine / digests starch.
solutionSteps: X (bile only): bile physically emulsifies fats into droplets; it does not chemically digest them.
Z (amylase only): amylase is an enzyme that digests starch into maltose.
Y (shared by bile and amylase): both are active in the small intestine.
Reject 'produced by the pancreas' as the shared feature: amylase can be, but bile is made by the liver.
The row emulsifies lipid / works in the small intestine / digests starch fits all three.
keyConcept: Bile emulsifies (not digests) lipids and is made by the liver; amylase digests starch; both operate in the small intestine.
commonMistake: Writing that bile 'digests' lipid — bile only emulsifies; lipase carries out the chemical digestion.

optionExplanations.1: Says X digests lipid, but bile emulsifies rather than digests, so this row is wrong.
optionExplanations.2: Says X digests lipid; bile emulsifies lipid instead.
optionExplanations.4: Gives the shared feature as 'produced by the pancreas', but bile comes from the liver, and calls Z 'digests maltose' rather than starch.

figureExplanation: The overlapping region Y must hold a property common to both bile and amylase; only 'works in the small intestine' qualifies, since bile is not pancreatic.

shortExplanation: Going down Group VII, atoms get larger, so electronegativity and first ionisation energy decrease, while melting points increase because of stronger van der Waals forces between larger molecules.
solutionSteps: Electronegativity (property 2) decreases down the group as atomic radius grows and nuclear pull on bonding electrons weakens.
First ionisation energy (property 3) decreases down the group as the outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded.
Melting point (property 1) increases down the group because larger molecules have stronger van der Waals attractions.
So only properties 2 and 3 decrease.
keyConcept: Down a group, atomic size increases, lowering electronegativity and ionisation energy, but intermolecular forces (and melting points) grow.
commonMistake: Assuming melting point follows the same downward trend as electronegativity and ionisation energy.

optionExplanations.1: '2 only' omits the decreasing first ionisation energy.
optionExplanations.2: '1 only' is backwards, since melting points actually increase down Group VII.
optionExplanations.4: '1, 2 and 3' wrongly includes the increasing melting point.

shortExplanation: Mass number 18 with 10 neutrons means 8 protons (oxygen); the O2- ion has 10 electrons, giving the configuration 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6.
solutionSteps: Protons = mass number - neutrons = 18 - 10 = 8, so the element is oxygen.
A -2 charge means the atom gained 2 electrons: 8 + 2 = 10 electrons.
Ten electrons fill 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 (the neon configuration).
keyConcept: An ion's electron configuration is built from its electron count, found by adjusting the proton number for the charge.
commonMistake: Using the neutral atom's 8 electrons instead of adding the 2 electrons gained by the -2 ion.

optionExplanations.1: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^4 is neutral oxygen (8 electrons), not the -2 ion.
optionExplanations.3: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 corresponds to 12 electrons, too many.
optionExplanations.4: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^4 corresponds to 16 electrons, far too many.

shortExplanation: Only raising the surrounding pressure raises water's boiling point; dissolving salt lowers the freezing point, and cooling from 150 to 120 C lowers average kinetic energy.
solutionSteps: Statement 1: dissolving salt causes freezing-point depression, so the freezing point falls, not rises - false.
Statement 2: lowering temperature from 150 C to 120 C decreases average kinetic energy - false.
Statement 3: higher external pressure raises the boiling point of water - true.
Only statement 3 is correct.
keyConcept: Average kinetic energy depends on temperature, and boiling point rises with external pressure while dissolved solute lowers freezing point.
commonMistake: Confusing freezing-point depression (added solute lowers freezing point) with an increase.

optionExplanations.1: '2 only' picks a false claim, since cooling reduces kinetic energy.
optionExplanations.2: '1 only' is wrong because salt lowers, not raises, the freezing point.
optionExplanations.4: '1 and 3 only' incorrectly retains the false freezing-point statement.

shortExplanation: Hexane is C6H14, so a structural isomer must also be C6H14. Only the branched five-carbon chain with a methyl branch (2-methylpentane) has that formula; the ring is C6H12 and the straight chain shown is C5H12.
solutionSteps: Hexane has formula C6H14.
Structure 1 is a six-carbon ring (cyclohexane), C6H12 — not an isomer of hexane.
Structure 2 is a five-carbon chain carrying a CH3 branch: 6 carbons and 14 hydrogens, C6H14 — this is 2-methylpentane, an isomer of hexane.
Structure 3 is a straight five-carbon chain (pentane), C5H12 — wrong number of carbons.
Only structure 2 matches C6H14.
keyConcept: Structural isomers share the same molecular formula; for hexane that is C6H14, ruling out rings (fewer H) and shorter chains.
commonMistake: Counting the branched carbon but ignoring formula, or treating the six-membered ring as hexane despite it being C6H12.

optionExplanations.1: Structure 1 alone is cyclohexane (C6H12), not an isomer of hexane.
optionExplanations.2: Structure 3 is a five-carbon straight chain (pentane, C5H12), so it is not included.
optionExplanations.3: Structure 1 is a ring with formula C6H12, so it cannot be paired as an isomer of hexane.

figureExplanation: Counting carbons: structure 1 is a 6-carbon ring (C6H12), structure 2 is a 5-carbon chain plus a CH3 branch (C6H14), and structure 3 is a 5-carbon straight chain (C5H12); only structure 2 equals C6H14.
formulaNotes: Hexane = C6H14; cyclohexane = C6H12; pentane = C5H12.

shortExplanation: The first electron affinity is the energy change when one mole of gaseous atoms each gain one electron: Cl(g) + e^- -> Cl^-(g).
solutionSteps: First electron affinity involves a single gaseous atom gaining one electron.
Both species must be gaseous, and exactly one electron is added per atom.
This matches Cl(g) + e^- -> Cl^-(g).
keyConcept: First electron affinity: one mole of gaseous atoms each acquire one electron to form gaseous 1- ions.
commonMistake: Using molecular Cl2 or losing an electron instead of a single gaseous atom gaining one.

optionExplanations.1: Cl(g) -> Cl^-(g) + e^- shows electron loss, which is not electron affinity.
optionExplanations.2: Cl2(g) + 2e^- -> 2Cl^-(g) starts from a molecule, not a single atom.
optionExplanations.4: Cl^-(g) + e^- -> Cl(g) is not even balanced or physically an affinity step.

formulaNotes: First electron affinity: X(g) + e^- -> X^-(g).

shortExplanation: Vitamin B5 contains hydroxyl groups (alcohol), a C(=O)-NH linkage (amide), and a terminal COOH (carboxylic acid). It has no aldehyde, no free amine, and no ketone.
solutionSteps: Identify the -CH2OH and the -CH(OH)- groups: both are alcohols.
Identify the C(=O)-N-H group joining the two halves: this is an amide.
Identify the terminal -C(=O)-OH: this is a carboxylic acid.
The nitrogen is bonded to a carbonyl (amide N), so there is no free amine; there is no terminal CHO (no aldehyde) and no C=O between two carbons (no ketone).
Groups present are alcohol, amide, and carboxylic acid.
keyConcept: A nitrogen adjacent to a carbonyl is an amide, not an amine; a C=O bearing an -OH is a carboxylic acid, not a ketone or aldehyde.
commonMistake: Calling the N-H an amine — because it sits next to a carbonyl it is part of an amide.

optionExplanations.2: There is no aldehyde (no terminal CHO) and the N is amide-bound, not a free amine.
optionExplanations.3: The right-hand C=O bears an OH (carboxylic acid), not a ketone (no C=O between two carbons).
optionExplanations.4: No free amine and no ketone are present; the N is in an amide and both C=O groups are amide/acid.

figureExplanation: The drawn structure shows CH2OH and CH(OH) (alcohols), a central C(=O)-N-H (amide), and a terminal C(=O)-OH (carboxylic acid), with no isolated CHO, N-only amine, or C-C=O-C ketone.

shortExplanation: X (HNO3) gives [H+] = 0.050 M and Y (H2SO4) gives [H+] = 0.100 M, so Y is only twice X (not four times); both acids are strong, so statement 2 is wrong; Y's pH is 1, which is below 2.
solutionSteps: For X: HNO3 is monoprotic, so [H+] = 0.050 M.
For Y: H2SO4 provides 2 H+ per molecule, so [H+] = 2 * 0.050 = 0.100 M.
Statement 1: 0.100 / 0.050 = 2, not four times, so false.
Statement 2: HNO3 is also a strong acid that dissociates fully, so 'only Y' is false.
Statement 3: pH of Y = -log(0.100) = 1, which is less than 2, so true.
Only statement 3 is correct.
keyConcept: Both nitric and sulfuric acid are strong acids; sulfuric is diprotic, doubling its hydrogen ion concentration at equal molarity.
commonMistake: Treating HNO3 as weak, or forgetting that H2SO4 releases two protons when comparing concentrations.

optionExplanations.1: 'none of them' is wrong because statement 3 (pH < 2) is correct.
optionExplanations.2: '1 only' overstates the ratio; Y's [H+] is twice, not four times, that of X.
optionExplanations.3: '1 and 3 only' incorrectly keeps the false factor-of-four claim.

formulaNotes: pH = -log10[H+]; for Y, [H+] = 0.100 M gives pH = 1.

shortExplanation: In AlCl3 the aluminium has three bonding pairs and no lone pair, giving a trigonal planar shape. In the dimer Al2Cl6 each aluminium bonds to four chlorines (two bridging, two terminal), giving a tetrahedral shape.
solutionSteps: AlCl3: Al forms three Al-Cl bonds and has no lone pairs, so three electron domains arrange trigonal planar (120 degrees).
Al2Cl6: two AlCl3 units dimerise via two bridging chlorines, so each Al now bonds to four Cl atoms.
Four bonding pairs around each Al give four electron domains: tetrahedral geometry.
So AlCl3 is trigonal planar and Al2Cl6 has tetrahedral Al centres.
keyConcept: Electron-deficient AlCl3 (3 domains) is trigonal planar; on dimerising to Al2Cl6 each Al becomes 4-coordinate and tetrahedral.
commonMistake: Treating AlCl3 as trigonal pyramidal — unlike NH3 it has no lone pair, so it is planar.

optionExplanations.1: The dimer is not square planar; four bonds with no lone pairs around each Al are tetrahedral.
optionExplanations.2: AlCl3 has no lone pair, so it is trigonal planar, not trigonal pyramidal.
optionExplanations.3: AlCl3 is 3-coordinate and planar, not tetrahedral.

figureExplanation: The AlCl3 drawing shows three Cl around one Al in a flat arrangement (trigonal planar); the Al2Cl6 drawing shows each Al surrounded by four Cl including two bridges, i.e. tetrahedral.

shortExplanation: Ethanoic acid has O-H groups and forms strong hydrogen-bonded dimers, giving the strongest intermolecular hydrogen bonds among the options.
solutionSteps: Hydrogen bonding requires H bonded to N, O, or F.
Ethanoic acid (CH3COOH) has an O-H group and forms double hydrogen-bonded dimers.
Propanal, fluoromethane, trimethylamine, and H2S have weaker or no true O/N-H hydrogen bonding, so ethanoic acid has the strongest.
keyConcept: Strong hydrogen bonds need H directly bonded to a highly electronegative O, N, or F atom.
commonMistake: Assuming any molecule containing fluorine or nitrogen automatically hydrogen bonds strongly, even without an H on that atom.

optionExplanations.1: Propanal's H atoms are on carbon, so it only accepts, and cannot donate, hydrogen bonds.
optionExplanations.2: Fluoromethane has C-F, not H-F, so it forms only weak dipole interactions.
optionExplanations.3: Trimethylamine has no N-H bond, so it cannot donate hydrogen bonds.

shortExplanation: The original solution is 32 g/L; diluting 25 mL to 250 mL reduces it tenfold to 3.2 g/L, and merely transferring 25 mL of that does not change the concentration.
solutionSteps: Original concentration = 3.2 g / 0.100 L = 32 g/L.
Dilution 25 mL to 250 mL is a factor of 10: 32 / 10 = 3.2 g/L.
Transferring 25 mL of this solution to a conical flask does not change its concentration.
So the concentration in the conical flask is 3.20 g/L.
keyConcept: Dilution scales concentration by the volume ratio; simply moving a solution leaves its concentration unchanged.
commonMistake: Applying a second dilution when the final 25 mL is just transferred, not diluted.

optionExplanations.1: 0.80 g/L wrongly applies an extra factor to the transfer step.
optionExplanations.2: 0.32 g/L applies a hundredfold dilution instead of tenfold.
optionExplanations.3: 8.00 g/L uses an incorrect volume ratio for the dilution.

shortExplanation: Setting the sum of oxidation states of H (+1 each) and O (-2 each) plus X to zero gives X = 2n - m.
solutionSteps: In H_m X O_n the molecule is neutral, so oxidation states sum to zero.
Hydrogen contributes m(+1) and oxygen contributes n(-2).
Let X have oxidation state x: m(+1) + x + n(-2) = 0.
Solving: x = 2n - m.
keyConcept: In a neutral compound the oxidation states of all atoms sum to zero, with H = +1 and O = -2.
commonMistake: Swapping the signs and writing m - 2n instead of 2n - m.

optionExplanations.1: m - 2n reverses the correct sign of the expression.
optionExplanations.2: m + 2n uses the wrong sign for oxygen's contribution.
optionExplanations.3: 2m - n mixes up the coefficients of hydrogen and oxygen.

formulaNotes: m(+1) + x + n(-2) = 0 gives x = 2n - m.

shortExplanation: Iron gives 1.68/56 = 0.03 mol and oxygen gives 0.64/16 = 0.04 mol, a 3:4 ratio, so the formula is Fe3O4.
solutionSteps: Moles of Fe = 1.68 / 56 = 0.03 mol.
Moles of O = 0.64 / 16 = 0.04 mol.
Empirical formula = Fe3O4.
keyConcept: Empirical formulae come from the simplest whole-number mole ratio of the elements.
commonMistake: Dividing masses by the wrong atomic mass or not simplifying the ratio, giving the wrong subscripts.

optionExplanations.1: Fe4O3 inverts the ratio, giving more iron than oxygen.
optionExplanations.2: Fe2O3 corresponds to a 2:3 mole ratio, not the 3:4 found here.
optionExplanations.4: FeO is a 1:1 ratio, inconsistent with 0.03 : 0.04 mol.

formulaNotes: moles = mass / Ar; ratio 0.03 : 0.04 = 3 : 4.

shortExplanation: The committee insisted on following the waiting list, which ranks recipients by urgency of medical need, so its principle is that transplant decisions should be based on the recipient's medical need.
solutionSteps: The committee gave the kidney to C because his medical need was more urgent (higher on the list).
It said it must act solely by the rationale behind the waiting list.
That rationale is prioritising recipients by medical need, so that is the principle behind the decision.
keyConcept: Identify the principle a decision applies by finding the criterion it actually used to choose.
commonMistake: Choosing an option describing what the committee rejected (emotions, family, donor wishes) rather than the criterion it applied.

optionExplanations.1: 'cannot be influenced by emotions' describes the committee's stance loosely but not the positive principle it used to allocate the organ.
optionExplanations.3: 'should include social considerations' is the opposite of the committee's reasoning, which excluded social factors.
optionExplanations.4: 'donor's wishes should not be considered' is a consequence, not the guiding principle of prioritising medical need.

shortExplanation: The argument treats a correlation between outdoor activity and self-esteem as proof that activity raises self-esteem, ignoring that higher self-esteem may instead lead people to do more outdoor activity.
solutionSteps: The evidence is that people who do lots of outdoor activity tend to have high self-esteem (a correlation).
The argument concludes that going for a run or walk will raise self-esteem (causation).
It overlooks reverse causation: confident people may be more likely to go outside in the first place.
That reverse-causation gap is the flaw.
keyConcept: A correlation does not establish the direction of causation; the effect could drive the supposed cause.
commonMistake: Accepting the leap from 'active people have high self-esteem' to 'activity causes high self-esteem' without questioning direction.

optionExplanations.1: Assuming self-confidence alone guarantees good mental health is not what the argument claims.
optionExplanations.2: That not everyone with low self-esteem wants to exercise does not undermine the causal inference itself.
optionExplanations.4: Suggesting professional help would benefit people is a separate recommendation, not the reasoning flaw.

shortExplanation: All the points about stress, lost childhood, and keenly felt rejection are reasons supporting the final claim that young performers need further legal protection, which is the main conclusion.
solutionSteps: Identify the claim the other statements are meant to support.
The passage lists pressures and harms of young performing as reasons.
It ends by stating these factors indicate young performers need further protection by law.
That final statement is the conclusion the reasons lead to.
keyConcept: The main conclusion is the claim all the supporting reasons are working towards.
commonMistake: Mistaking a supporting reason (such as being robbed of childhood) for the overall conclusion.

optionExplanations.2: 'can be suddenly thrust into the limelight' is background context, not the conclusion.
optionExplanations.3: 'robbed of their childhood' is a supporting reason for the conclusion, not the conclusion itself.
optionExplanations.4: 'feel rejection more because they lack experience' is another premise, not the main claim.

shortExplanation: The original argument says a qualifying condition (being from our school) guarantees an offer, then denies you the guarantee because you lack that condition. The over-60 bus-pass argument uses exactly the same 'you lack the qualifying condition, so you do not get the benefit' structure.
solutionSteps: Identify the original structure: being from our school is a sufficient condition for a guaranteed offer; you are not from that school, so you are not guaranteed an offer.
Look for the option that denies a benefit on the grounds that the person lacks the stated qualifying condition.
The over-60 argument: being over 60 grants free bus travel; you are under 60, so you are not entitled to free travel, matching the structure exactly.
That option parallels the original reasoning.
keyConcept: Parallel-reasoning questions are answered by matching the logical form, not the subject matter.
commonMistake: Selecting an option merely because it shares a topic, or one that uses valid necessary-condition logic rather than the original's structure.

optionExplanations.1: The high-score-college option affirms a condition to guarantee a positive outcome, the opposite move from denying a benefit.
optionExplanations.2: The bus-pass-after-9:30 option applies a rule to conclude a specific case holds, rather than denying a benefit for lacking a condition.
optionExplanations.3: The teacher-degree option uses a genuine necessary condition (valid reasoning), unlike the original's flawed treatment of a sufficient condition.

shortExplanation: The argument uses waste percentages to conclude how much we 'value' each food, which only works if the assumption holds that we throw food away mainly because we do not value it much.
solutionSteps: The argument equates a low waste percentage with valuing a food more.
This link requires that valuing is the main driver of whether food is wasted.
So it assumes the main reason we throw food away is that we do not value it much.
Without that assumption, waste figures would not indicate value.
keyConcept: An underlying assumption is the unstated link the argument needs to connect its evidence to its conclusion.
commonMistake: Picking a plausible real-world fact (like bread going stale) that actually undermines the value-based link rather than being assumed by it.

optionExplanations.1: 'bread is a low-quality food' is not needed for the argument's value reasoning.
optionExplanations.2: 'we should buy less bread' is a recommendation, not an assumption the argument depends on.
optionExplanations.3: 'more expensive foods are less wasted' is a possible alternative explanation, not the assumption the argument relies on.

shortExplanation: The three named preferences account for 70% of the cats, so the remaining 30% consists of the 6 indifferent plus the 27 refusing cats, which is 33. Since 30% = 33 cats, the whole survey is 33 / 0.30 = 110 cats.
solutionSteps: Add the named preference percentages: 10% + 20% + 40% = 70%.
The remaining fraction is 100% - 70% = 30% of the cats.
That 30% equals the leftover cats: 6 (did not care) + 27 (would not touch any) = 33 cats.
Total = 33 / 0.30 = 110 cats.
keyConcept: When a known count corresponds to a known percentage, divide the count by that percentage (as a decimal) to scale up to the whole.
commonMistake: Treating the 33 leftover cats as the entire survey instead of as only the 30% not covered by a named preference.

optionExplanations.1: 33 is just the leftover cats making up the 30%, not the whole survey.
optionExplanations.2: 63 does not match any correct combination of the data; it corresponds to no consistent total for which 30% equals 33 cats.
optionExplanations.3: 90 comes from using only the 27 refusing cats as the 30% (27 / 0.30 = 90) and forgetting the 6 indifferent cats.

formulaNotes: total = known_count / (known_percentage as a decimal) = 33 / 0.30 = 110.

shortExplanation: Each of the 6 men can sit next to at most 2 different women, so at most 12 women can have a male neighbour, leaving at least 2 of the 14 women without one.
solutionSteps: There are 20 seats: 14 women and 6 men around a circle.
A single man has only two neighbours, so each man can 'cover' at most 2 women.
Maximum women adjacent to some man = 6 x 2 = 12 (achieved when no two men are adjacent and no woman is shared).
Arrange as repeated blocks M W W around the circle so each man's two neighbouring women are both covered.
That covers 12 women; the remaining 14 - 12 = 2 women sit together with no male neighbour.
keyConcept: Maximising coverage: each covering element (a man) has a fixed, limited number of neighbours.
commonMistake: Placing men adjacent to each other, which wastes coverage and leaves more women isolated.

optionExplanations.1: 4 uncovered women occurs only with a wasteful arrangement, not the optimal one.
optionExplanations.2: 6 corresponds to leaving many women in unbroken all-female runs, far from optimal.
optionExplanations.4: 8 would require most men clustered together, the worst case rather than the best.

shortExplanation: The single design must be non-glitter and 2-fold, leaving only the religious and father xmas packs. Buying whole father xmas packs (10 each at 3.10) needs 4 packs for 35 cards, costing 12.40, cheaper than 7 religious packs at 12.60.
solutionSteps: Constraints: one design for all 35 cards, no glitter, and it must be 2-fold (needed for the 5 letters).
Eliminate glitter (village scene) and 1-fold (robins, cartoon).
Remaining valid types: religious (5 per pack, 1.80) and father xmas (10 per pack, 3.10), both no-glitter 2-fold.
Religious: 35/5 = 7 packs, 7 x 1.80 = 12.60.
Father xmas: need at least 35, so 4 packs (40 cards), 4 x 3.10 = 12.40.
Lowest cost is 12.40.
keyConcept: Filter options by every stated condition first, then minimise cost by buying the fewest whole packs that meet the quantity.
commonMistake: Forgetting the design must be 2-fold for all cards (not just five), which wrongly admits the cheaper 1-fold cartoon or robins packs.

optionExplanations.1: 12.60 is the religious option (7 packs); the father xmas option is cheaper at 12.40.
optionExplanations.2: 5.00 and similar small figures ignore that 35 cards are needed, not one pack.
optionExplanations.3: 6.00 undercounts the number of packs required to reach 35 cards.

figureExplanation: The table shows only religious and father xmas are both no-glitter and 2-fold; comparing full-pack totals (7 x 1.80 = 12.60 vs 4 x 3.10 = 12.40) makes father xmas the cheaper valid choice.

shortExplanation: The clock is upside down, so the first reading of 20:50 corresponds to a real time of 05:02. Ninety minutes later the real time is 06:32, whose upside-down display reads 2E:90.
solutionSteps: The clock is inverted, so a displayed 20:50 is the upside-down view; rotating it back gives the true time 05:02 (early morning, which is why 20:50 seemed 'faulty').
Add the 1 hour 30 minutes elapsed: 05:02 + 01:30 = 06:32 real time.
To find what she saw, invert 06:32: reverse the character order to 23:60 and rotate each digit 180 degrees.
Rotated digits: 2 stays 2, 3 becomes E, 6 becomes 9, 0 stays 0.
The inverted display therefore reads 2E:90.
keyConcept: Inverting a 7-segment display reverses left-to-right order and rotates each digit 180 degrees (2->2, 3->E, 6->9, 9->6, 0/5/8 unchanged).
commonMistake: Rotating each digit in place but forgetting to reverse the order of the four digits.

optionExplanations.1: This shows a different inverted string not equal to the 180-degree rotation of 06:32.
optionExplanations.2: This corresponds to a different real time, not 05:02 plus 90 minutes.
optionExplanations.3: This inverted reading does not correspond to real time 06:32.

figureExplanation: Reading 20:50 upside down gives real time 05:02; ninety minutes on is 06:32, and inverting that display (reverse to 23:60, then rotate each digit) yields the 2E:90 option.

shortExplanation: Vertical text spun to be read from the back is mirrored left-to-right, so every letter must be symmetric about a vertical axis. Only HAWAII uses solely such letters.
solutionSteps: Reading the vertical sign from front and back means each letter must look the same after a left-right mirror flip.
Letters with vertical-axis symmetry include A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y.
HAWAII = H, A, W, A, I, I: every letter is vertically symmetric, so it works.
Each other state contains at least one non-symmetric letter (L, B, D, N, K).
keyConcept: Mirror symmetry about a vertical axis is what lets a letter read the same from front and back.
commonMistake: Confusing left-right (vertical-axis) symmetry with top-bottom symmetry.

optionExplanations.1: ALABAMA contains L and B, which are not symmetric under a left-right flip.
optionExplanations.2: IDAHO contains D, which is not vertically symmetric.
optionExplanations.3: MONTANA contains N, which reverses under a mirror flip.

shortExplanation: Hans Jonas was a philosopher known for ethics and bioethics, not a scholar of medicine, so that pairing is incorrect.
solutionSteps: Check each pairing against the scholar's actual field.
Hans Jonas: philosopher (philosophy of technology, bioethics), not medicine.
Keynes/economics, Montessori/pedagogy, Planck/physics, Skinner/psychology are all correct.
keyConcept: Matching thinkers to their primary academic discipline.
commonMistake: Assuming Jonas worked in medicine because his ethics touched on biomedical questions.

optionExplanations.1: Keynes is correctly the founder of modern macroeconomics.
optionExplanations.2: Montessori correctly pioneered a method in pedagogy.
optionExplanations.3: Planck correctly founded quantum theory in physics.

shortExplanation: My Brilliant Friend is the first of the Neapolitan Novels written by Elena Ferrante.
solutionSteps: Recall the author of the Neapolitan quartet beginning with My Brilliant Friend.
It is the pseudonymous Italian author Elena Ferrante.
keyConcept: Identifying authors of major contemporary novels.
commonMistake: Confusing it with other international bestsellers by the other listed authors.

optionExplanations.1: Khaled Hosseini wrote The Kite Runner, not My Brilliant Friend.
optionExplanations.2: Ian McEwan wrote works such as Atonement.
optionExplanations.4: Kazuo Ishiguro wrote The Remains of the Day and Never Let Me Go.

shortExplanation: FAO stands for the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, so A is Agriculture.
solutionSteps: Expand the acronym FAO.
Food and Agriculture Organization: the A is Agriculture.
keyConcept: Names of major UN specialized agencies.
commonMistake: Guessing an unrelated 'A' word instead of recalling the full name.

optionExplanations.1: Architecture is not part of the FAO's name or mandate.
optionExplanations.2: Aerospace has no connection to the FAO.
optionExplanations.3: Automotive is unrelated to a food and agriculture body.

shortExplanation: The Metropolitan Opera House is in New York; the other theatre-city pairings are all mismatched.
solutionSteps: Match each theatre to its true city.
Metropolitan Opera House is indeed in New York.
San Carlo is in Naples, the Bolshoi in Moscow, La Fenice in Venice, and the Palais Garnier in Paris.
keyConcept: Locations of famous opera houses and theatres.
commonMistake: Mixing up Italian opera houses (San Carlo, La Fenice) with the wrong cities.

optionExplanations.1: San Carlo is in Naples, not Venice.
optionExplanations.2: The Bolshoi Theatre is in Moscow, not Saint Petersburg.
optionExplanations.3: La Fenice is in Venice, not Florence.

shortExplanation: The Rosetta Stone's parallel Greek, Demotic and hieroglyphic text allowed Champollion to decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs.
solutionSteps: Recall what the Rosetta Stone contained: the same decree in three scripts.
The known Greek text served as the key to the unknown Egyptian hieroglyphs.
keyConcept: The Rosetta Stone unlocked ancient Egyptian writing.
commonMistake: Associating it with other ancient scripts like cuneiform or Phoenician.

optionExplanations.1: The Phoenician alphabet was not the subject of the Rosetta Stone.
optionExplanations.3: Ancient Greek was already readable and served as the key, not the target.
optionExplanations.4: The Code of Hammurabi is a separate Babylonian legal text in cuneiform.

shortExplanation: Only the European Parliament's members (MEPs) are chosen directly by EU citizens through universal suffrage.
solutionSteps: Identify which EU institution's members are directly elected by voters.
The European Parliament is elected directly; the others are appointed or composed of member-state representatives.
keyConcept: Composition and selection of EU institutions.
commonMistake: Assuming the Commission or Council is directly elected rather than appointed/delegated.

optionExplanations.1: The European Commission is appointed and approved, not directly elected.
optionExplanations.2: The Court of Justice's judges are appointed by the member states.
optionExplanations.4: The Council of the European Union is made up of member-state ministers.

shortExplanation: All three Godfather films were directed by Francis Ford Coppola.
solutionSteps: Recall the director of The Godfather (1972), Part II (1974) and Part III (1990).
Francis Ford Coppola directed the entire trilogy.
keyConcept: Directors of landmark films.
commonMistake: Confusing Coppola with other prominent directors of American crime films.

optionExplanations.1: Martin Scorsese directed films like Goodfellas, not The Godfather.
optionExplanations.2: Sergio Leone directed spaghetti Westerns and Once Upon a Time in America.
optionExplanations.3: Brian De Palma directed Scarface, not The Godfather.

shortExplanation: The electron microscope was developed by Ernst Ruska, not Niels Bohr, whose work was the atomic model, so that pairing is incorrect.
solutionSteps: Check each scholar against the discovery credited to them.
Niels Bohr is known for the Bohr model of the atom, not the electron microscope.
The other four pairings (periodic table, x-rays, particle detector, mercury barometer) are correct.
keyConcept: Matching scientists to their actual discoveries.
commonMistake: Associating Bohr with electron instruments because his model involved electrons.

optionExplanations.1: Mendeleev correctly devised the periodic table.
optionExplanations.2: Roentgen correctly discovered x-rays.
optionExplanations.3: Geiger correctly developed a particle detector (the Geiger counter).

shortExplanation: The European Coal and Steel Community was established by the 1951 Treaty of Paris.
solutionSteps: Recall that the ECSC was the first of the European Communities, founded in 1951.
Its founding treaty was signed in Paris, giving the Treaty of Paris.
The later Treaties of Rome (1957) created the EEC and Euratom, not the ECSC.
keyConcept: The founding treaties of European integration: Paris (1951, ECSC) preceded Rome (1957, EEC and Euratom).
commonMistake: Confusing the Treaty of Paris (ECSC) with the Treaties of Rome (EEC/Euratom).

optionExplanations.1: The Treaty of Lisbon (2007) reformed the modern European Union rather than founding the ECSC.
optionExplanations.3: The Treaty of Nice (2001) adjusted EU institutions ahead of enlargement, long after the ECSC was founded.
optionExplanations.4: The Treaties of Rome (1957) established the EEC and Euratom, not the ECSC.

shortExplanation: The World Trade Organization (WTO) is the body that sets and enforces the rules of international trade.
solutionSteps: Identify the organisation whose specific mandate is trade rules between nations.
The WTO administers trade agreements and settles trade disputes.
keyConcept: Roles of major international economic organisations.
commonMistake: Confusing the WTO's trade-rule role with the financing roles of the World Bank or IMF.

optionExplanations.1: The World Bank provides development financing, not trade rule-making.
optionExplanations.2: The IMF focuses on monetary stability and balance-of-payments support.
optionExplanations.3: The OECD produces analysis and standards but does not enforce trade rules.

shortExplanation: Uncle Vanya was written by Anton Chekhov; Bulgakov's famous work is The Master and Margarita, so that pairing is incorrect.
solutionSteps: Check each writer against the work attributed to them.
Mikhail Bulgakov did not write Uncle Vanya (that is Chekhov's play).
Nabokov/Lolita, Dostoyevsky/Karamazov, Tolstoy/Anna Karenina, Pasternak/Zhivago are all correct.
keyConcept: Matching Russian authors to their works.
commonMistake: Assuming any famous Russian play belongs to Bulgakov rather than Chekhov.

optionExplanations.1: Nabokov correctly wrote Lolita.
optionExplanations.2: Dostoyevsky correctly wrote The Brothers Karamazov.
optionExplanations.3: Tolstoy correctly wrote Anna Karenina.

shortExplanation: A 'perfect bicameral system' is one in which both chambers of parliament hold identical legislative powers.
solutionSteps: Interpret 'bicameral' as a two-chamber legislature.
'Perfect' (equal) bicameralism means the two chambers have the same powers, as in the Italian Parliament.
keyConcept: Perfect bicameralism = two equally powerful legislative chambers.
commonMistake: Interpreting bicameralism as relating to the judiciary or to individual officeholders.

optionExplanations.1: This describes an appeals procedure in the judiciary, not a legislature.
optionExplanations.2: This concerns two individual figures, not two parliamentary chambers.
optionExplanations.3: This concerns a monarchy's balance of power, not equal chambers.

shortExplanation: Factor the denominator as (x + 2)(x - 1) and cancel one (x + 2) from the numerator's (x + 2)^2, leaving (x + 2)/(x - 1).
solutionSteps: Factor x^2 + x - 2 = (x + 2)(x - 1).
Rewrite the expression as (x + 2)^2 / ((x + 2)(x - 1)).
Cancel one common factor (x + 2).
Result: (x + 2)/(x - 1).
keyConcept: Simplify rational expressions by factoring and cancelling common factors.
commonMistake: Factoring the denominator incorrectly, e.g. as (x - 2)(x + 1).

optionExplanations.1: This uses the wrong denominator factorisation (x - 2)(x + 1).
