optionExplanations.1: There is no triplet transcribed from mRNA and translated by rRNA; rRNA is structural/catalytic, not a translator of triplets.
optionExplanations.3: A DNA triplet coding an amino acid is a DNA codon, not the tRNA anticodon.
optionExplanations.4: rRNA does not carry a terminal amino-acid-binding triplet; the amino acid attaches to tRNA.

shortExplanation: Ribosomes are ribonucleoprotein particles built from ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and ribosomal proteins.
solutionSteps: Recall the composition of ribosomal subunits.
Each subunit contains rRNA molecules folded together with numerous proteins.
No DNA or lipid is part of ribosome structure.
Therefore ribosomes are made of RNA and proteins.
keyConcept: Ribosomes = rRNA + proteins (ribonucleoprotein complexes).
commonMistake: Assuming ribosomes contain DNA because they handle genetic information.

optionExplanations.1: DNA is not a ribosome component; the genetic code is delivered by mRNA.
optionExplanations.3: Lipids belong to membranes, not to ribosomes.
optionExplanations.4: Ribosomes contain no DNA.

shortExplanation: The plasma membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with hydrophobic tails turned inward and hydrophilic heads outward, embedded with integral and associated with peripheral proteins.
solutionSteps: Recall the fluid mosaic model.
Phospholipids form two layers with polar heads facing the aqueous sides and nonpolar tails facing each other.
Proteins are integral (spanning/embedded) or peripheral (surface-associated).
This matches a double phospholipid layer with tails inward plus integral and peripheral proteins.
keyConcept: The membrane is a phospholipid bilayer studded with integral and peripheral proteins.
commonMistake: Describing the membrane as triglycerides or as proteins sandwiched between lipids (outdated sandwich model).

optionExplanations.1: The bilayer is phospholipids, not a protein layer enclosed by lipids.
optionExplanations.2: Triglycerides are storage fats, not the structural lipid of membranes.
optionExplanations.3: The framework is a bilayer, not a glycoprotein layer.

shortExplanation: Translation is the ribosomal reading of mRNA codons to assemble a specific sequence of amino acids into a polypeptide.
solutionSteps: Distinguish transcription (DNA to RNA) from translation (RNA to protein).
In translation, ribosomes read mRNA codons.
tRNAs deliver matching amino acids in order.
The result is a specific amino acid sequence, i.e., a protein.
keyConcept: Translation converts mRNA sequence into an amino acid sequence.
commonMistake: Mixing up translation with transcription (making mRNA from DNA).

optionExplanations.1: Transcribing mRNA into DNA is reverse transcription, not translation.
optionExplanations.3: Amino acids do not recognize rRNA; codon-anticodon pairing drives selection.
optionExplanations.4: Reading DNA to make mRNA is transcription.

shortExplanation: The cytoskeleton is built from three filament systems: microtubules, microfilaments (actin), and intermediate filaments.
solutionSteps: Recall the three main cytoskeletal elements by diameter.
Microtubules (tubulin) are the thickest.
Microfilaments (actin) are the thinnest.
Intermediate filaments are of middle diameter; together these three define the cytoskeleton.
keyConcept: Cytoskeleton = microtubules + microfilaments + intermediate filaments.
commonMistake: Listing motor proteins (myosin, dynein) as structural filaments instead of the three filament classes.

optionExplanations.1: Myosin and filamin are associated proteins, not the three defining filament types.
optionExplanations.2: Dynein and myosin are motor proteins, not filament classes.
optionExplanations.4: Collagen and reticular fibres are extracellular matrix components, not cytoskeleton.

shortExplanation: An allele is one of the alternative versions of a gene occupying the same locus.
solutionSteps: Recall that a gene can exist in variant forms.
Each variant sequence at that locus is an allele.
Alleles determine different versions of a trait.
So an allele is one of several alternative forms of a gene.
keyConcept: Allele = an alternative form of a gene at a given locus.
commonMistake: Confusing an allele with a codon, a trait, or the phenotype it produces.

optionExplanations.1: A single coding base is a nucleotide, not an allele.
optionExplanations.3: Alleles occur in diploid cells too, not only haploid.
optionExplanations.4: The phenotypic manifestation is the trait, not the allele itself.

shortExplanation: In a heterozygote the two alleles differ, and the one that is expressed in the phenotype is the dominant allele.
solutionSteps: Heterozygous means two different alleles are present.
A dominant allele masks the recessive one in the phenotype.
Thus the dominant allele is certainly expressed.
The recessive is expressed only when homozygous.
keyConcept: In heterozygotes the dominant allele determines the phenotype.
commonMistake: Thinking a recessive allele shows in a heterozygote (it is masked).

optionExplanations.1: A recessive allele is masked in the heterozygous state.
optionExplanations.2: Being mutated does not guarantee expression; dominance does.
optionExplanations.4: Multiple refers to allele number in a population, not to expression in one individual.

shortExplanation: Mutations are heritable or somatic changes in the genetic information (DNA sequence) of a cell.
solutionSteps: Recall that genetic information is stored in DNA.
Any alteration of that sequence or its organization is a mutation.
Mutations range from single-base changes to large chromosomal changes.
So mutations are alterations in the cell's genetic information.
keyConcept: A mutation is a change in a cell's genetic (DNA) information.
commonMistake: Confusing genetic alterations with metabolic or transport changes.

optionExplanations.1: Energy-metabolism changes are physiological, not genetic mutations.
optionExplanations.3: Enzyme malfunction is a consequence, not the definition of a mutation.
optionExplanations.4: Changes in cell division are outcomes, not the definition of a mutation.

shortExplanation: Translation is the process that synthesizes polypeptide chains using mRNA as the template read by ribosomes.
solutionSteps: Translation is protein synthesis at the ribosome.
mRNA codons are read and matched by tRNA anticodons.
Amino acids are joined into a polypeptide.
So translation yields polypeptide chains from mRNA.
keyConcept: Translation builds polypeptides from an mRNA template.
commonMistake: Confusing translation with transcription or restricting it to eukaryotes.

optionExplanations.1: Translation occurs in the cytoplasm; only transcription in eukaryotes is nuclear.
optionExplanations.2: Synthesizing RNA from DNA is transcription, not translation.
optionExplanations.4: Translation differs fundamentally from transcription and occurs in prokaryotes too.

shortExplanation: Applying antiparallel complementary base pairing (A-T, G-C) to CCGTTATTGA gives GGCAATAACT.
solutionSteps: Write the given strand: C C G T T A T T G A.
Pair each base: C->G, C->G, G->C, T->A, T->A, A->T, T->A, T->A, G->C, A->T.
Read the complementary bases in the same alignment: G G C A A T A A C T.
The complementary strand is GGCAATAACT.
keyConcept: DNA strands are complementary: A pairs with T, G pairs with C.
commonMistake: Substituting U for T (that would be RNA) or mispairing G with A.

optionExplanations.2: AGTTATTGCC does not follow correct complementary pairing of the sequence.
optionExplanations.3: GGACATCCCT contains incorrect pairings for several bases.
optionExplanations.4: GGCAATTAAT reverses two internal bases, breaking the A-T/G-C matches.

formulaNotes: Base pairing: A-T, T-A, G-C, C-G.

shortExplanation: Replication uses existing DNA as a template to synthesize new DNA molecules (semiconservatively).
solutionSteps: Recall DNA replication precedes cell division.
Each parental strand serves as a template.
DNA polymerase adds complementary nucleotides to build new strands.
The product is new DNA molecules, so replication makes DNA from DNA.
keyConcept: Replication: DNA templates the synthesis of new DNA.
commonMistake: Confusing replication with transcription (DNA to RNA) or with cell division itself.

optionExplanations.1: Making RNA from DNA is transcription, not replication.
optionExplanations.2: Daughter cells forming is cell division, a later event, not replication.
optionExplanations.3: RNA templating protein is translation.

shortExplanation: A prokaryotic operon is a functional unit of adjacent, coordinately controlled genes together with regulatory DNA sequences (promoter and operator).
solutionSteps: Recall the operon model (e.g., lac operon).
Structural genes lie adjacent and are transcribed together.
Regulatory DNA (promoter, operator) controls their coordinated expression.
Thus the operon is a unit of adjacent genes plus regulatory sequences.
keyConcept: An operon groups coordinately regulated genes with their control sequences.
commonMistake: Thinking operon genes are independent, or confusing the operon with the ribosome/replication machinery.

optionExplanations.1: Operon genes are coordinately controlled, not independent.
optionExplanations.2: The protein complex catalyzing protein synthesis is the ribosome.
optionExplanations.4: An operon includes regulatory function, so a sequence without regulation is not one.

shortExplanation: By Dalton's law the partial pressure of N2 equals its mole fraction times total pressure: (0.3/1.2)*2.4 = 0.6 atm.
solutionSteps: Total moles = 0.3 + 0.5 + 0.4 = 1.2 mol.
Mole fraction of N2 = 0.3/1.2 = 0.25.
Partial pressure of N2 = mole fraction * total pressure.
keyConcept: Partial pressure = mole fraction x total pressure (Dalton's law).
commonMistake: Dividing total pressure by number of gases instead of using mole fractions.

optionExplanations.1: 0.8 atm is the CO2 partial pressure (0.5/1.2 * 2.4), not N2.
optionExplanations.2: 0.5 atm ignores the correct mole fraction.
optionExplanations.3: 0.3 atm mistakes moles for pressure directly.

formulaNotes: P_i = x_i * P_total, x_i = n_i / n_total.

shortExplanation: At constant volume, P/T is constant (Gay-Lussac). Converting to kelvin, P2 = 9 * 300/270 = 10 atm.
solutionSteps: Convert temperatures to kelvin: -3 C = 270 K, 27 C = 300 K.
Gay-Lussac: P1/T1 = P2/T2 at constant volume.
keyConcept: At fixed volume, pressure is proportional to absolute (kelvin) temperature.
commonMistake: Using Celsius directly instead of kelvin, which gives nonsense (e.g., negative pressure).

optionExplanations.1: -81 atm comes from using Celsius values in the ratio.
optionExplanations.2: 8.1 atm inverts the temperature ratio.
optionExplanations.3: 9.6 atm uses an incorrect temperature conversion.

formulaNotes: P1/T1 = P2/T2 (T in kelvin).

shortExplanation: BaO is a basic (metal) oxide; with water it forms Ba(OH)2, a hydroxide. The others are non-metal (acidic) oxides that form oxoacids.
solutionSteps: Identify metal vs non-metal oxides.
BaO is a metal oxide: BaO + H2O -> Ba(OH)2.
Cl2O, SO3, SiO2, N2O3 are non-metal oxides that form acids (HClO, H2SO4, etc.).
Therefore only BaO yields a hydroxide.
keyConcept: Metal oxides + water -> hydroxides (bases); non-metal oxides + water -> acids.
commonMistake: Assuming any oxide plus water gives a hydroxide, ignoring acidic non-metal oxides.

optionExplanations.1: Cl2O is an acidic oxide, forming hypochlorous acid, not a hydroxide.
optionExplanations.2: SO3 forms sulfuric acid (H2SO4), an acid.
optionExplanations.3: SiO2 is a poorly reactive acidic oxide, not a hydroxide former.

shortExplanation: With 2 mol FeS2 (needing 5.5 mol O2) and 11 mol O2 present, FeS2 is limiting and 2 FeS2 -> 1 Fe2O3, giving 1 mol Fe2O3.
solutionSteps: Use the balanced ratios: 4 FeS2 : 11 O2 : 2 Fe2O3 : 8 SO2.
Scale down: 2 FeS2 : 5.5 O2 : 1 Fe2O3 : 4 SO2.
With 2 mol FeS2 and 11 mol O2, O2 is in excess and FeS2 limits.
So 1 mol Fe2O3 is produced, matching the correct statement.
keyConcept: Use the balanced coefficients and identify the limiting reagent.
commonMistake: Ignoring the limiting reagent or misreading the 4:11:2:8 stoichiometric ratios.

optionExplanations.1: 4 mol O2 limits and yields only about 2.9 mol SO2, not 8 mol.
optionExplanations.2: 1 mol Fe2O3 needs 5.5 mol O2, not 5 mol.
optionExplanations.3: 1 mol FeS2 gives only 2 mol SO2, not 3 mol.

formulaNotes: Ratios from 4 FeS2 + 11 O2 -> 2 Fe2O3 + 8 SO2.

shortExplanation: Dilution: C1V1 = C2V2 gives final volume 75 mL, so 75 - 15 = 60 mL of water must be added.
solutionSteps: V2 = 3.75 / 0.05 = 75 mL final volume.
Water added = final volume - initial volume = 75 - 15.
= 60 mL of water.
keyConcept: Dilution conserves moles: C1V1 = C2V2; added water = V_final - V_initial.
commonMistake: Reporting the final volume (75 mL) instead of the water added (60 mL).

optionExplanations.1: 30 mL uses an incorrect concentration ratio.
optionExplanations.2: 120 mL overestimates the required dilution.
optionExplanations.3: 75 mL is the final total volume, not the water added.

formulaNotes: C1V1 = C2V2.

shortExplanation: Moles Na2SO4 = 0.250 L * 1.2 M = 0.3 mol; each yields 2 Na+, so 0.6 mol Na+.
solutionSteps: Moles of Na2SO4 = 0.250 L * 1.2 mol/L = 0.3 mol.
Each Na2SO4 dissociates into 2 Na+ ions.
Moles Na+ = 2 * 0.3 = 0.6 mol.
So 0.6 mol of Na+ are present.
keyConcept: Account for the 2:1 dissociation ratio of Na2SO4 into Na+.
commonMistake: Forgetting the factor of 2 and reporting 0.3 mol.

optionExplanations.1: 1.2 mol ignores the volume and uses concentration directly.
optionExplanations.3: 0.3 mol counts Na2SO4 moles, not the doubled Na+.
optionExplanations.4: 0.4 mol does not follow from the calculation.

formulaNotes: n = C * V; Na2SO4 -> 2 Na+ + SO4^2-.

shortExplanation: NH3 donates its nitrogen lone pair to the electron-deficient boron of BF3, so ammonia acts as a Lewis base (electron-pair donor).
solutionSteps: BF3 has an empty orbital on boron (electron-pair acceptor = Lewis acid).
NH3 has a lone pair on nitrogen.
NH3 donates the lone pair to form the N-B dative bond.
Donating an electron pair defines a Lewis base.
keyConcept: A Lewis base donates an electron pair; here NH3 donates to BF3.
commonMistake: Calling it a Bronsted base, but no proton is transferred in this adduct reaction.

optionExplanations.1: A Bronsted base accepts a proton; no proton transfer occurs here.
optionExplanations.2: It is not donating a proton, so not a Bronsted acid.
optionExplanations.3: BF3, not NH3, is the electron-pair acceptor (Lewis acid).

shortExplanation: Metallic zinc goes from oxidation state 0 to +2, losing electrons; the species that is oxidized is the reducing agent, so Zn(s) is the reducing species.
solutionSteps: Assign oxidation states: Zn(s) is 0, becomes Zn^2+ in Zn(NO3)2.
Zinc loses electrons (oxidized).
Nitrogen in HNO3 (+5) is reduced to +4 in NO2.
The oxidized species (electron donor) is the reducing agent: Zn(s).
keyConcept: The reducing agent is the species that is oxidized (loses electrons).
commonMistake: Confusing the reducing agent with the oxidizing agent (HNO3 is the oxidizer here).

optionExplanations.2: Zn^2+ is the oxidized product, not the reducing species itself.
optionExplanations.4: Zn(NO3)2 contains already-oxidized zinc, not the reductant.
optionExplanations.5: HNO3 is reduced (nitrogen +5 to +4), so it is the oxidizing agent.

shortExplanation: 2,3-Dimethylpentane is a saturated C7 alkane (C7H16) with 16 hydrogens, more than the C6 rings/alkene (12 H) or the C6 alcohol (14 H).
solutionSteps: 2,3-Dimethylpentane: C7 alkane, formula C7H16 -> 16 H.
Cyclohexane: C6H12 -> 12 H (one ring).
1,2-Dimethylcyclobutane: C6H12 -> 12 H (one ring).
2,3-Dimethyl-2-butene: C6H12 -> 12 H (one double bond); 2-Hexanol: C6H14O -> 14 H. Maximum is 16 H.
keyConcept: Saturated acyclic alkanes (CnH2n+2) carry the most hydrogens for a given carbon count; rings and double bonds each remove 2 H.
commonMistake: Judging by molecular size instead of counting hydrogens from degrees of unsaturation.

optionExplanations.1: Cyclohexane (C6H12) has only 12 H due to its ring.
optionExplanations.3: 2,3-Dimethyl-2-butene (C6H12) has 12 H because of the double bond.
optionExplanations.4: 2-Hexanol (C6H14O) has 14 H, fewer than 16.

formulaNotes: Alkane CnH2n+2; each ring or double bond removes 2 H.

shortExplanation: Dimethyl ether (CH3-O-CH3) has only C-O single bonds; the other molecules all contain a carbonyl (C=O) group.
solutionSteps: Dimethyl ether: two C-O single bonds, no C=O.
Acetaldehyde and acetone contain a carbonyl (C=O).
Acetic acid and methyl acetate contain a C=O in their carboxyl/ester group.
Only dimethyl ether lacks a carbon-oxygen double bond.
keyConcept: Ethers have C-O-C single bonds; aldehydes, ketones, acids, and esters all contain C=O.
commonMistake: Assuming any oxygen-containing molecule has a double bond, overlooking ether single bonds.

optionExplanations.1: Acetaldehyde has an aldehyde carbonyl C=O.
optionExplanations.2: Acetone has a ketone carbonyl C=O.
optionExplanations.3: Acetic acid has a carboxyl group containing C=O.

shortExplanation: 1 atm equals 101.325 kPa, not 1013.25 kPa; the other listed values (101325 Pa, ~1013 mbar, 760 mmHg, 760 torr) all equal 1 atm.
solutionSteps: The value 1013.25 kPa is ten times too large.
1 atm = 1013.25 mbar (approximately 1013), = 760 mmHg = 760 torr.
So 1013.25 kPa does NOT equal 1 atm.
commonMistake: Misplacing the decimal between Pa and kPa (a factor of 1000) or kPa and mbar.

optionExplanations.1: 101325 Pa is exactly 1 atm.
optionExplanations.2: 1013 millibar approximates 1 atm correctly.
optionExplanations.3: 760 mmHg equals 1 atm.

shortExplanation: 0.7 g of nitrogen contains 0.7/14 = 0.05 mol of N atoms, so 0.05 * 6.02*10^23 = 3.01*10^22 atoms.
solutionSteps: Moles of N atoms = mass / atomic mass = 0.7 g / 14 g/mol = 0.05 mol.
Multiply by Avogadro's number: 0.05 * 6.02*10^23.
(Same result if computed as 0.025 mol N2 times 2 atoms each.)
keyConcept: Number of atoms = (mass / atomic mass) * Avogadro's number.
commonMistake: Using the wrong power of ten or forgetting that N2 has 2 atoms per molecule (both routes give 3.01*10^22).

optionExplanations.1: 6.02*10^22 is twice the correct atom count.
optionExplanations.2: 3.01*10^23 is off by a factor of ten.
optionExplanations.3: 1.51*10^22 halves the correct value.

shortExplanation: C + O2 -> CO2: 9 g C = 0.75 mol is limiting, producing 0.75 mol CO2 = 33 g, and 12 g of O2 remain unreacted.
solutionSteps: Moles C = 9/12 = 0.75 mol; moles O2 = 36/32 = 1.125 mol.
Reaction ratio C:O2 is 1:1, so 0.75 mol C needs 0.75 mol O2; carbon is limiting.
CO2 formed = 0.75 mol * 44 g/mol = 33 g.
So 33 g of CO2 are produced (leftover O2 = 0.375 mol = 12 g).
keyConcept: Identify the limiting reagent, then compute product mass from its moles.
commonMistake: Adding all reactant masses (assuming 45 g CO2) despite excess unreacted oxygen.

optionExplanations.1: 45 g assumes all oxygen reacts, but O2 is in excess.
optionExplanations.2: 9 g O2 remaining is incorrect; 12 g remain.
optionExplanations.3: 4 g of oxygen remaining is not the calculated leftover (12 g).

formulaNotes: C + O2 -> CO2; M(CO2) = 44 g/mol.

shortExplanation: pH 2 means [H+] = 0.01 M and pH 4 means [H+] = 0.0001 M, so the acid must be diluted 100-fold. Starting from 1 mL, the final volume is 100 mL, meaning 99 mL of water is added.
solutionSteps: Dilution factor = 0.01 / 0.0001 = 100.
Final volume = 1 mL * 100 = 100 mL.
Water to add = 100 mL - 1 mL = 99 mL.
keyConcept: A change of one pH unit corresponds to a 10-fold change in [H+]; two units means 100-fold dilution.
commonMistake: Forgetting to subtract the original 1 mL and answering 100 mL instead of 99 mL.

optionExplanations.1: 1 mL of water would only double the volume, changing pH by about 0.3, not 2 units.
optionExplanations.3: 2 mL gives a threefold total volume, far from the 100-fold dilution required.
optionExplanations.4: 24 mL gives a 25-fold dilution, changing pH by only ~1.4 units.

formulaNotes: C1*V1 = C2*V2, with C proportional to 10^-pH.

shortExplanation: In Bronsted-Lowry theory the strength of an acid is inversely related to that of its conjugate base, so a strong acid corresponds to a weak conjugate base.
solutionSteps: A Bronsted acid donates H+; a base accepts H+.
Removing H+ from an acid gives its conjugate base.
The stronger the acid, the more stable and weaker its conjugate base.
Therefore a strong acid pairs with a weak conjugate base.
keyConcept: Bronsted-Lowry acids donate protons and bases accept protons; strong acid implies weak conjugate base.
commonMistake: Confusing the Bronsted definition with Arrhenius (OH- release) or Lewis (electron-pair) definitions.

optionExplanations.1: A conjugate base forms when an acid donates H+, not when it acquires OH-.
optionExplanations.3: A conjugate acid forms when a base accepts H+, not by bonding to OH-.
optionExplanations.4: Donating OH- ions is the Arrhenius definition of a base, not the Bronsted one.

shortExplanation: Marks above 5 are 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 with frequencies 1+2+2+1+0 = 6, out of a total of 24 candidates, giving 25%.
solutionSteps: Passing means mark > 5, i.e. marks 6, 7, 8, 9, 10.
Passing count = 1 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 6.
Percentage = 6/24 = 0.25 = 25%.
keyConcept: Percentage passing = (candidates above threshold) / (total candidates) * 100.
commonMistake: Including mark 5 as a pass; the condition is strictly higher than 5.

optionExplanations.2: 24% would require the totals or counts to differ slightly; the exact ratio is 6/24 = 25%.
optionExplanations.3: 20% would correspond to a passing count of about 4.8, which does not match the data.
optionExplanations.4: 30% corresponds to a passing count of about 7.2, more than the actual 6.

shortExplanation: 12% of 1500 is 180 pens; with silver twice gold, gold pens = 60, so Shelly's chance of a gold pen is 60/1500 = 4%.
solutionSteps: Total pens = 12% of 1500 = 180.
Let gold = g, silver = 2g, so g + 2g = 180, g = 60.
Probability of gold for one participant = 60 / 1500.
keyConcept: Probability equals favorable outcomes over total participants.
commonMistake: Computing gold as a fraction of the 180 prize winners (33%) instead of all 1500 participants.

optionExplanations.1: 33% is the gold share among prize winners (60/180), not the chance over all participants.
optionExplanations.2: 8% would be the silver share over all participants (120/1500), not gold.
optionExplanations.3: 67% is the silver share among prize winners (120/180).

shortExplanation: Applying 10% then 20% leaves 0.9 * 0.8 = 0.72 of the price, which is a single discount of 28%.
solutionSteps: After 10% off, price factor = 0.90.
After a further 20% off, factor = 0.90 * 0.80 = 0.72.
Remaining fraction 0.72 means total discount = 1 - 0.72 = 0.28 = 28%.
keyConcept: Successive discounts multiply the remaining fractions; they do not simply add.
commonMistake: Adding 10% + 20% = 30% instead of multiplying the surviving fractions.

optionExplanations.1: 25% does not match the product 0.9*0.8.
optionExplanations.2: 30% is the result of incorrectly adding the two percentages.
optionExplanations.3: 18% would be 0.9*0.2 misapplied and is not the combined discount.

shortExplanation: 343 = 7^3, so the cube is 7x7x7; only the fully interior blocks are unpainted, and there are (7-2)^3 = 125 of them, leaving 343 - 125 = 218 painted blocks.
solutionSteps: 343 = 7^3, so each edge has 7 blocks.
Unpainted blocks are strictly inside: a 5x5x5 core.
Interior count = 5^3 = 125.
Blocks with at least one painted face = 343 - 125 = 218.
keyConcept: For an n-cube, interior unpainted cubes number (n-2)^3.
commonMistake: Reporting the interior count (125) instead of the painted outer shell (218).

optionExplanations.1: 125 is the number of unpainted interior blocks, not the painted ones.
optionExplanations.2: 245 does not correspond to any correct shell or core count for a 7-cube.
optionExplanations.3: 238 miscounts the interior core.

shortExplanation: The statement is 'train implies on time'; its only valid deduction is the contrapositive: if not on time (late), then not by train.
solutionSteps: Given: takes train -> arrives on time.
Valid contrapositive: not on time -> not by train.
'Marco arrived late; therefore he did not take the train' matches the contrapositive.
keyConcept: From 'P implies Q', only the contrapositive 'not Q implies not P' is guaranteed.
commonMistake: Affirming the consequent or denying the antecedent, which are logically invalid.

optionExplanations.1: Being late does not imply taking the train; the train guarantees punctuality, not lateness.
optionExplanations.2: Arriving on time does not prove he missed the train; other causes of punctuality exist.
optionExplanations.3: Not taking the train does not force lateness; he could still be on time by other means.

shortExplanation: To the Lighthouse (1927) is a modernist novel written by Virginia Woolf.
solutionSteps: Recall the modernist author of To the Lighthouse.
It is Virginia Woolf, part of the Bloomsbury Group.
The matching option names Virginia Woolf.
keyConcept: Virginia Woolf is a central English modernist known for stream-of-consciousness novels.
commonMistake: Confusing Woolf with other British women writers of different eras.

optionExplanations.1: Mary Shelley wrote Frankenstein, a Gothic novel, not To the Lighthouse.
optionExplanations.2: Jane Austen wrote early 19th-century social novels like Pride and Prejudice.
optionExplanations.4: Emily Dickinson was an American poet, not a novelist.

shortExplanation: The passage states that only with the Greeks did mathematics become abstract and general, so claiming it was abstract and general 'since antiquity' contradicts the text and cannot be inferred.
solutionSteps: The text says abstraction and generality arose specifically with Greek civilisation.
Pre-Greek documents show only concrete, case-specific solutions.
Therefore 'characterized by abstractness and generality since antiquity' contradicts the passage.
This is the statement that cannot be inferred.
keyConcept: An inference must be supported by the text; a claim contradicting it cannot be inferred.
commonMistake: Overlooking that the passage restricts abstraction to the Greek period, not all antiquity.

optionExplanations.1: The text explicitly says notions were communicated sporadically and non-methodically.
optionExplanations.2: The text confirms ancient societies devised symbols to represent numbers.
optionExplanations.3: The text states early solutions were geared toward practical outcomes.

shortExplanation: The Hundred Years' War (1337-1453) was fought principally between the Kingdom of France and the Kingdom of England over succession and territory.
solutionSteps: Recall the belligerents of the Hundred Years' War.
It was a dynastic conflict over the French crown and lands.
The two principal kingdoms were France and England.
keyConcept: The Hundred Years' War was an Anglo-French dynastic and territorial conflict.
commonMistake: Confusing it with Iberian conflicts involving Aragon, Castile, or Portugal.

optionExplanations.1: Aragon and France were not the principal opponents of this war.
optionExplanations.2: Aragon and Castile were Iberian kingdoms not central to this conflict.
optionExplanations.3: Castile and Portugal fought their own wars, not the Hundred Years' War.

shortExplanation: 'The deeds of Aeneas were sung by Virgil' uses 'were sung' with a by-agent, the hallmark of the passive voice.
solutionSteps: Passive voice = form of 'to be' + past participle, subject receives the action.
'were sung by Virgil' fits this pattern: the deeds receive the action.
The other sentences use active verbs with the subject performing the action.
keyConcept: Passive voice makes the receiver of the action the grammatical subject, often with a 'by' agent.
commonMistake: Mistaking descriptive active sentences for passive because they mention a doer.

optionExplanations.1: 'read' is active; the students perform the reading.
optionExplanations.2: 'described' is active; Caesar performs the action.
optionExplanations.4: 'sings' is active; Homer performs the action.

keyConcept: Nested powers multiply exponents; convert the base to a prime power to simplify.
commonMistake: Mishandling the fractional exponent and losing the factor of 2 outside the root.

optionExplanations.1: sqrt(2) = 2^(1/2), too small by a factor of 2.
optionExplanations.2: cube root of 4 = 2^(2/3), the wrong exponent.
optionExplanations.3: sixth root of 2 = 2^(1/6), far smaller than 2^(3/2).

shortExplanation: f(2) = log_2(2^2 + 12) = log_2(16) = 4, so its reciprocal is 1/4.
solutionSteps: Compute the argument: 2^2 + 12 = 4 + 12 = 16.
Reciprocal of 4 = 1/4.
keyConcept: log_2(16) = 4 because 2^4 = 16; the reciprocal of x is 1/x.
commonMistake: Reporting f(2) = 4 instead of its reciprocal 1/4.

optionExplanations.1: 4 is the value of f(2) itself, not its reciprocal.
optionExplanations.2: 2 would be log_2 of the argument only if the argument were 4.
optionExplanations.3: 1/2 is the reciprocal of 2, not of 4.

formulaNotes: log_2(16) = 4; reciprocal = 1/f(2).

shortExplanation: With replacement, P(green) = 7/10 each time, so P(two greens) = (7/10)^2 = 49/100.
solutionSteps: Total balls = 3 + 7 = 10.
P(green on one draw) = 7/10.
With replacement the draws are independent.
keyConcept: With replacement, draws are independent so probabilities multiply and stay constant.
commonMistake: Using 7/10 * 6/9 (without replacement) instead of keeping 7/10 both times.

optionExplanations.1: 42/90 is the without-replacement result (7/10 * 6/9).
optionExplanations.2: 7/10 is the probability for a single draw, not two.
optionExplanations.4: 9/100 would be the probability of two red draws (3/10)^2.

formulaNotes: Independent events: P(A and B) = P(A)*P(B).

shortExplanation: The numerator x^2 + |4x+3| is always strictly positive, so the fraction is non-negative only where the denominator 4 - 3x is positive, i.e. x < 4/3.
solutionSteps: Numerator = x^2 + |4x+3|; both terms are >= 0.
They cannot be zero simultaneously (x=0 vs x=-3/4), so numerator > 0 for all x.
A positive numerator over a denominator is >= 0 only when the denominator > 0.
4 - 3x > 0 gives x < 4/3.
keyConcept: A fraction with a strictly positive numerator is non-negative exactly where its denominator is positive.
commonMistake: Including x = 4/3, which makes the denominator zero and the expression undefined.

optionExplanations.2: Excluding only -3/4 and 0 ignores the denominator's sign restriction.
optionExplanations.3: x >= 4/3 makes the denominator zero or negative, giving an undefined or negative value.
optionExplanations.4: x > 4/3 gives a negative denominator, so the fraction is negative.

formulaNotes: Sign of A/B with A > 0 follows the sign of B.

shortExplanation: By the tangent-chord angle theorem, the angle between the tangent and chord AB equals the inscribed angle subtending AB from the alternate segment, so phi = theta.
solutionSteps: The tangent-chord angle theta equals half the intercepted arc AB.
An inscribed angle phi from point D subtends the same chord AB.
For D on the larger arc, phi subtends the minor arc, equal to half that arc.
Both equal half the same arc, so phi = theta.
keyConcept: Tangent-chord angle equals the inscribed angle in the alternate segment.
commonMistake: Assuming the two angles are supplementary or complementary instead of equal.

optionExplanations.1: Explementary (summing to 360 degrees) does not describe these two acute angles.
optionExplanations.3: There is a definite relationship: the tangent-chord theorem links them.
optionExplanations.4: They are equal, not complementary (summing to 90 degrees).

formulaNotes: theta = (1/2)*arc AB = inscribed angle phi in the alternate segment.

shortExplanation: The cylinder volume is pi*r^2*h = pi*5^2*7 = 175*pi cm^3.
solutionSteps: Volume of a cylinder = pi * r^2 * h.
r = 5 cm so r^2 = 25.
keyConcept: Cylinder volume equals base area (pi*r^2) times height.
commonMistake: Using diameter or forgetting to square the radius.

optionExplanations.1: 245*pi would use r^2 = 35, which is incorrect.
optionExplanations.2: 70*pi treats the base as 2*pi*r (circumference) times height, not area.
optionExplanations.3: 105*pi uses r = 3 or another wrong radius.

formulaNotes: V = pi*r^2*h.

shortExplanation: The sine of angle alpha equals opposite over hypotenuse, sin(alpha) = a/c, so a = c*sin(alpha).
solutionSteps: alpha is opposite leg a; hypotenuse is c.
sin(alpha) = opposite/hypotenuse = a/c.
Rearranging gives a = c*sin(alpha).
keyConcept: In a right triangle, the leg opposite an angle equals the hypotenuse times the sine of that angle.
commonMistake: Swapping sine and cosine, or putting the hypotenuse on the wrong side of the equation.

optionExplanations.1: a = c*cos(alpha) uses the adjacent-leg relation, which fits leg b, not a.
optionExplanations.2: c = a*sin(alpha) inverts the ratio; the hypotenuse is longer than a leg.
optionExplanations.4: a = b*cos(alpha) is not a standard right-triangle identity here.

formulaNotes: sin(alpha) = a/c, so a = c*sin(alpha).

shortExplanation: At constant temperature Boyle's law gives P*V = constant, so tripling the volume divides the pressure by 3, yielding P/3.
solutionSteps: Isothermal process: P*V = constant (Boyle's law).
New volume = 3V.
P_new = P*V / (3V) = P/3.
keyConcept: For an ideal gas at constant T, pressure is inversely proportional to volume.
commonMistake: Thinking pressure scales directly with volume, giving 3P.

optionExplanations.1: Pressure must change since volume changes at constant T.
optionExplanations.2: 3P would apply if pressure rose with volume, which is the opposite of Boyle's law.
optionExplanations.3: P/2 would correspond to doubling the volume, not tripling it.

formulaNotes: P1*V1 = P2*V2 at constant T.

solutionSteps: Power dissipated: P = I^2 * R.
Solve for R: R = P / I^2.
keyConcept: Joule heating in a resistor is P = I^2*R.
commonMistake: Dividing by I instead of I^2, giving 292.2 ohm.

optionExplanations.1: 2922 ohm would ignore the current entirely.
optionExplanations.2: 2.922 ohm divides by I^3 or misplaces the decimal.
optionExplanations.3: 292.2 ohm results from dividing by I instead of I^2.

shortExplanation: A magnetic force is always perpendicular to velocity, so it changes the direction (hence the velocity vector) while keeping speed constant; saying the velocity vector stays constant is false.
solutionSteps: The magnetic force F = e*v*B is perpendicular to v.
This keeps the speed constant but continually changes the direction.
A changing direction means the velocity vector is not constant.
So the statement that velocity vector v stays constant is false.
keyConcept: A magnetic force does no work and only changes the direction of motion, producing uniform circular motion.
commonMistake: Confusing constant speed with constant velocity vector; direction change alters the vector.

optionExplanations.1: The radius r = m*v/(e*B) is the correct cyclotron radius, so this is true.
optionExplanations.2: The period T = 2*pi*m/(e*B) is correct for circular motion, so this is true.
optionExplanations.4: The frequency f = e*B/(2*pi*m) is the correct cyclotron frequency, so this is true.

formulaNotes: r = m*v/(e*B); T = 2*pi*m/(e*B); the magnetic force is always perpendicular to v.

shortExplanation: v(t) = -4*omega*sin(omega*t) = -8*pi*sin(2*pi*t); at t = 1/2 s, sin(pi) = 0, so the velocity is 0 m/s.
solutionSteps: x(t) = 4*cos(omega*t), so v(t) = dx/dt = -4*omega*sin(omega*t).
With omega = 2*pi, v(t) = -8*pi*sin(2*pi*t).
At t = 1/2: 2*pi*(1/2) = pi, and sin(pi) = 0.
Therefore v = 0 m/s.
keyConcept: Velocity in SHM is the derivative of position; it is zero at the turning points.
commonMistake: Evaluating the amplitude 8*pi without noting sin(pi) = 0.

optionExplanations.1: Approximately -4 m/s ignores that sin(pi) = 0.
optionExplanations.2: 8.5 m/s is roughly the speed amplitude 8*pi/... but not the value at t = 1/2.
optionExplanations.4: 25.1 m/s is about 8*pi, the maximum speed, not the value at this instant.

formulaNotes: v(t) = -A*omega*sin(omega*t); at t=1/2, sin(pi)=0.

shortExplanation: Without friction there is no energy loss, so an ideal pendulum oscillates indefinitely; claiming it comes to a stop after some time is false.
solutionSteps: In the absence of friction, mechanical energy is conserved.
With no energy dissipation the amplitude never decays.
So the pendulum keeps oscillating forever, never stopping.
The statement that it stops after a certain time is false.
keyConcept: A frictionless pendulum undergoes undamped oscillation with conserved energy.
commonMistake: Assuming any oscillator eventually stops, forgetting the frictionless idealization.

optionExplanations.1: For small swings the frictionless pendulum is indeed simple harmonic, so this is true.
optionExplanations.2: Friction does damp real oscillations, so this statement is true.
optionExplanations.3: At each extreme the pendulum momentarily stops and swings back, which is true.

formulaNotes: Undamped SHM conserves energy; amplitude stays constant without friction.

shortExplanation: In lactic fermentation pyruvate accepts electrons from NADH and is converted to lactate, so pyruvic acid is reduced.
solutionSteps: Fermentation regenerates NAD+ from NADH after glycolysis.
Pyruvate gains electrons (and H) from NADH.
Gaining electrons is reduction.
Pyruvate is reduced to lactate.
keyConcept: Reduction is a gain of electrons; pyruvate is the electron acceptor that becomes lactate.
commonMistake: Confusing lactic fermentation with alcoholic fermentation, where pyruvate is first decarboxylated.

optionExplanations.1: Oxidation is loss of electrons; here NADH is oxidised, not pyruvate.
optionExplanations.2: Decarboxylation (loss of CO2) occurs in alcoholic fermentation, not lactic.
optionExplanations.3: Pyruvate is not phosphorylated during lactic fermentation.

shortExplanation: During glycolysis, the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step reduces 2 NAD+ to 2 NADH per glucose molecule.
solutionSteps: One glucose is split into two triose phosphate molecules.
Each triose (glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate) is oxidized, transferring electrons to NAD+.
This gives 2 NADH (2 NAD+ reduced) per glucose.
No CO2, no FADH2, and no decarboxylation occur in glycolysis.
keyConcept: Glycolysis reduces 2 NAD+ to 2 NADH per glucose and produces no CO2.
commonMistake: Confusing glycolytic enzyme roles or thinking CO2 is released during glycolysis.

optionExplanations.1: Triose phosphate isomerase interconverts dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, not 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate.
optionExplanations.2: Aldolase splits fructose 1,6-bisphosphate into two trioses; phosphofructokinase acts on fructose 6-phosphate.
optionExplanations.3: No decarboxylation occurs in glycolysis, so no CO2 is produced.
optionExplanations.4: FADH2 is not generated in glycolysis; it appears later in the Krebs cycle.

shortExplanation: One turn of the Krebs cycle per acetyl-CoA yields 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP, and 2 CO2.
solutionSteps: Acetyl-CoA (2 carbons) enters and combines with oxaloacetate.
Two decarboxylation steps release 2 CO2.
Three dehydrogenase steps produce 3 NADH.
The succinate dehydrogenase step produces 1 FADH2, and substrate-level phosphorylation gives 1 GTP.
keyConcept: Per acetyl-CoA the citric acid cycle gives 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP, and 2 CO2.
commonMistake: Miscounting CO2 as 3 (which is per pyruvate, not per acetyl-CoA) or swapping NADH/FADH2 counts.

optionExplanations.1: Only one FADH2 (not three) and three NADH (not one) are made per turn.
optionExplanations.2: Only 2 CO2 leave per acetyl-CoA, not 3.
optionExplanations.4: Two NADH and two FADH2 do not match the actual 3 NADH and 1 FADH2.

shortExplanation: Oxidative phosphorylation uses the energy from reoxidizing NADH and FADH2 to drive ATP synthesis.
solutionSteps: Electrons from reduced coenzymes pass along the electron transport chain.
This pumps protons and builds an electrochemical gradient.
ATP synthase uses the gradient to synthesize ATP.
keyConcept: Oxidative phosphorylation converts the energy of reduced coenzymes into ATP.
commonMistake: Confusing oxidative phosphorylation with catabolic pathways like beta-oxidation or the urea cycle.

optionExplanations.1: Elimination of amino groups describes the urea cycle, not oxidative phosphorylation.
optionExplanations.2: Removing two carbons at a time describes beta-oxidation of fatty acids.
optionExplanations.3: Oxidative phosphorylation is catabolic, not the final stage of anabolism.
optionExplanations.4: It does not synthesize fatty acids; that is a separate anabolic pathway.

shortExplanation: Cytochromes are heme-containing electron carriers embedded in the respiratory (electron transport) chain.
solutionSteps: Cytochromes contain an iron-heme group that cycles between Fe2+ and Fe3+.
They pass electrons (not whole hydrogen atoms) down the chain.
Thus they are components present in the respiratory chain.
keyConcept: Cytochromes are electron carriers of the respiratory chain.
commonMistake: Calling cytochromes hydrogen-atom carriers; they transfer electrons only.

optionExplanations.1: Cytochromes carry electrons, not whole hydrogen atoms.
optionExplanations.2: ATP synthesis is done by ATP synthase, not cytochromes.
optionExplanations.3: They facilitate, not inhibit, oxidative phosphorylation.
optionExplanations.4: They are not glycolytic cofactors; glycolysis occurs in the cytosol.

shortExplanation: Collagen is the main structural protein of the extracellular matrix, secreted by cells into the space around them.
solutionSteps: Fibroblasts synthesize procollagen and secrete it.
It assembles into fibrils outside the cell.
Collagen therefore functions in the extracellular matrix.
keyConcept: Collagen is the principal extracellular matrix protein.
commonMistake: Confusing collagen with intracellular contractile proteins like actin or myosin.

optionExplanations.1: Collagen is not an integral membrane protein.
optionExplanations.2: It is secreted and functions outside the cell, not intracellularly.
optionExplanations.3: The thick filament contains myosin, not collagen.
optionExplanations.4: Collagen is not a nuclear protein.

shortExplanation: Calcium ions bind troponin, causing tropomyosin to shift and expose actin's myosin-binding sites.
solutionSteps: An action potential releases Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
Ca2+ binds troponin C.
Troponin changes shape and moves tropomyosin off the actin binding sites, allowing contraction.
keyConcept: Ca2+ binds troponin to initiate the sliding-filament mechanism.
commonMistake: Thinking calcium binds directly to actin or tropomyosin rather than to troponin.

optionExplanations.1: Myosin binds ATP and actin, but calcium does not bind myosin to trigger contraction.
optionExplanations.2: Tropomyosin is moved by troponin; it does not directly bind the triggering calcium.
optionExplanations.3: Actin is the target of exposed binding sites but does not bind the regulatory calcium.
optionExplanations.4: Vimentin is a cytoskeletal intermediate filament unrelated to muscle triggering.

shortExplanation: ATP binding to the myosin head weakens its affinity for actin, causing the actin-myosin cross-bridge to dissociate.
solutionSteps: Myosin heads bound to actin form the rigor complex.
ATP binds the myosin head.
This lowers myosin's affinity for actin, releasing the cross-bridge; ATP hydrolysis then re-cocks the head.
keyConcept: ATP binding dissociates the actin-myosin cross-bridge.
commonMistake: Believing ATP binding forms the complex; it actually causes detachment.

optionExplanations.1: ATP binding promotes dissociation, not formation, of the complex.
optionExplanations.2: Calcium binding troponin exposes binding sites to promote attachment, not dissociation.
optionExplanations.3: Myosin, not actin, has the ATPase activity.
optionExplanations.4: Tropomyosin is regulatory and has no ATPase activity.

shortExplanation: The Bohr effect: high CO2 and H+ (low pH) lower hemoglobin's oxygen affinity, so oxygenated hemoglobin decreases as O2 is released to tissues.
solutionSteps: Active tissues produce CO2 and H+ ions.
These bind hemoglobin and stabilize its low-affinity (T) state.
Hemoglobin releases O2, so the amount of oxygenated hemoglobin falls.
keyConcept: Lower pH and higher CO2 reduce hemoglobin oxygen affinity, promoting O2 unloading.
commonMistake: Assuming acidosis increases oxygen binding; it actually decreases affinity.

optionExplanations.1: Oxygenated hemoglobin decreases, not increases, under Bohr conditions.
optionExplanations.2: The Bohr effect changes affinity, not the number of red blood cells.
optionExplanations.3: Hemoglobin is not denatured; it reversibly shifts conformation.
optionExplanations.4: It affects oxygen release, not protein synthesis rates.

shortExplanation: A catalyst speeds up a reaction while being recovered unchanged at the end.
solutionSteps: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of a reaction.
It participates but is regenerated by the end.
This matches the definition given.
keyConcept: A catalyst accelerates a reaction and is not consumed.
commonMistake: Confusing catalysts with cofactors or modulators, which have narrower regulatory roles.

optionExplanations.1: An effector modulates activity but is not defined as an unchanged rate-increaser.
optionExplanations.2: A cofactor assists an enzyme but is not the general term for the described substance.
optionExplanations.3: A modulator adjusts activity rather than simply speeding a reaction while staying unchanged.
optionExplanations.4: Cholesterol is a lipid, not a catalytic agent.

shortExplanation: In competitive inhibition the inhibitor resembles the substrate and competes with it for the enzyme's active site.
solutionSteps: The inhibitor is structurally similar to the substrate.
It binds the active site, blocking substrate access.
Increasing substrate concentration can outcompete the inhibitor.
keyConcept: Competitive inhibitors bind the active site and compete with substrate.
commonMistake: Confusing competitive with allosteric (non-competitive) inhibition, which binds a different site.

optionExplanations.1: Binding the substrate itself is not competitive inhibition of the enzyme.
optionExplanations.2: Binding an allosteric site describes non-competitive/allosteric inhibition.
optionExplanations.3: Blocking product release is not the mechanism of competitive inhibition.
optionExplanations.4: There is no enzyme-cholesterol complex involved here.

shortExplanation: Peptidases (proteases) hydrolyze the peptide bonds of proteins.
solutionSteps: Proteins are chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.
Peptidases cleave these peptide bonds.
Thus peptidases digest proteins.
keyConcept: Peptidases/proteases digest proteins by cleaving peptide bonds.
commonMistake: Matching enzyme classes to the wrong substrate (e.g., amylase to protein).

optionExplanations.1: Amylase digests starch (carbohydrates), not proteins.
optionExplanations.2: Lipase digests fats, not proteins.
optionExplanations.3: Isomerases rearrange molecules and are not digestive protein enzymes.
optionExplanations.4: Transaminases move amino groups; they are not digestive enzymes.

shortExplanation: Oxidative phosphorylation uses fixed membrane protein complexes plus mobile carriers like ubiquinone and cytochrome c.
solutionSteps: Complexes I-IV and ATP synthase are integral proteins of the inner mitochondrial membrane.
Ubiquinone (a lipid) and cytochrome c (a peripheral protein) shuttle electrons between complexes.
So both membrane proteins and mobile molecules are involved.
keyConcept: The electron transport chain combines fixed membrane complexes with mobile electron carriers.
commonMistake: Assuming all components are fixed integral proteins and forgetting the mobile carriers.

optionExplanations.1: It is not confined to matrix proteins; it is membrane-associated.
optionExplanations.2: Mobile carriers such as ubiquinone are not integral membrane proteins.
optionExplanations.3: The complexes are integral, so it is not exclusively peripheral proteins.
optionExplanations.4: It uses mitochondrially/nuclearly encoded proteins acting in the membrane, not only nuclear proteins.

shortExplanation: NADH and FADH2 are reoxidized by donating electrons to the respiratory chain (electron transport chain).
solutionSteps: Reduced coenzymes carry high-energy electrons.
They deliver these electrons to complexes of the respiratory chain.
This regenerates NAD+ and FAD, with oxygen as the final electron acceptor.
keyConcept: The respiratory chain reoxidizes NADH and FADH2.
commonMistake: Thinking oxygen directly oxidizes the coenzymes rather than acting at the chain's end.

optionExplanations.1: Beta-oxidation generates reduced coenzymes; it does not reoxidize them.
optionExplanations.2: Oxygen acts only at the chain's terminus, not by directly oxidizing the coenzymes.
optionExplanations.3: ATP synthase pumps protons through, not electrons; electron flow is through the chain complexes.
optionExplanations.4: Hormone synthesis is unrelated to coenzyme reoxidation.

shortExplanation: Creatine phosphate (phosphocreatine) is the muscle's high-energy phosphate reserve, rapidly regenerating ATP.
solutionSteps: During short bursts of activity ATP is depleted quickly.
Creatine phosphate donates its phosphate to ADP via creatine kinase.
This rapidly regenerates ATP in muscle.
keyConcept: Creatine phosphate is the rapid phosphate energy reserve in muscle.
commonMistake: Confusing creatine phosphate with creatinine (its waste product) or carnitine.

optionExplanations.1: Carnitine transports fatty acids; carnitine phosphate is not a muscle energy reserve.
optionExplanations.2: Creatinine is the metabolic waste product, not an energy store.
optionExplanations.3: Glucose 1-phosphate is a glycogen-metabolism intermediate, not the muscle phosphate reserve.
optionExplanations.4: Phosphofructokinase is a glycolytic enzyme, not an energy-storage compound.

shortExplanation: The urea cycle occurs mainly in the liver, which detoxifies ammonia into urea.
solutionSteps: Amino acid breakdown releases toxic ammonia.
Hepatocytes convert ammonia to urea via the urea cycle.
This pathway is essentially liver-specific.
keyConcept: The urea cycle is a liver-specific pathway for ammonia detoxification.
commonMistake: Assuming any listed pathway is liver-specific; most occur in many tissues.

optionExplanations.1: Glycolysis occurs in essentially all cells, not mainly the liver.
optionExplanations.2: Beta-oxidation occurs in many tissues (e.g., muscle, heart), not chiefly the liver.
optionExplanations.3: The Krebs cycle operates in mitochondria of virtually all aerobic cells.
optionExplanations.4: Transamination occurs widely in many tissues, not mainly the liver.

shortExplanation: Triglycerides store more energy per gram and are anhydrous, whereas protein/glycogen bind large amounts of water.
solutionSteps: Fats are highly reduced, yielding about 9 kcal/g versus about 4 kcal/g for protein.
Adipose fat is stored without associated water.
So triglycerides pack more calories and less water per unit mass.
keyConcept: Fat is a compact, water-free, energy-dense storage form.
commonMistake: Overlooking that hydration weight makes protein storage far less energy-dense.

optionExplanations.1: Triglycerides have more, not fewer, calories per gram.
optionExplanations.2: They contain fewer, not more, associated water molecules.
optionExplanations.3: They have more calories and less water, not more water.
optionExplanations.4: The advantage is energy density and low water, not oxygen/nitrogen content.

shortExplanation: Lysosomes bud from the Golgi apparatus and contain acid hydrolases that work best at low pH.
solutionSteps: The Golgi packages hydrolytic enzymes into vesicles.
These vesicles become lysosomes.
Their enzymes function optimally at acidic pH (around 5).
keyConcept: Lysosomes originate from the Golgi and contain acid hydrolases.
commonMistake: Thinking lysosomal enzymes work best at neutral/alkaline pH or that lysosomes make secretory proteins.

optionExplanations.1: Lysosomal enzymes work best at acidic pH (below 7), not above 7.
optionExplanations.2: Lysosomes derive from the Golgi, not by budding from smooth ER.
optionExplanations.3: Lysosomal malfunction causes storage diseases (e.g., Tay-Sachs).
optionExplanations.4: Protein synthesis occurs at ribosomes/ER, not in lysosomes.

shortExplanation: The nucleus, mitochondria, and chloroplasts each contain their own DNA, reflecting the endosymbiotic origin of the latter two.
solutionSteps: The nucleus holds the main genome.
Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own circular DNA.
So all three contain DNA.
keyConcept: Mitochondria and chloroplasts are semi-autonomous organelles with their own DNA.
commonMistake: Assuming only the nucleus contains DNA, or that prokaryotes have a true nucleus.

optionExplanations.1: Mitochondria and chloroplasts contain DNA, not only RNA.
optionExplanations.2: Not all organelles have DNA; for example, lysosomes and the ER do not.
optionExplanations.3: The rough ER contains ribosomes for protein synthesis, not DNA.
optionExplanations.4: Prokaryotes lack a membrane-bound nucleus; their DNA lies in the nucleoid.

shortExplanation: The plasma membrane's main role is selective control of what enters and leaves the cell.
solutionSteps: The membrane is a selectively permeable phospholipid bilayer.
Transport proteins and channels regulate passage of substances.
This controls exchange between the cell interior and exterior.
keyConcept: The plasma membrane selectively regulates exchange with the environment.
commonMistake: Assigning to the membrane functions performed by other structures (mitochondria, ribosomes, nucleus).

optionExplanations.1: Energy is chiefly produced by mitochondria, not the membrane.
optionExplanations.2: Protein synthesis is carried out by ribosomes.
optionExplanations.3: Genetic material is stored in the nucleus.
optionExplanations.4: Cell movement involves cytoskeletal structures, not the membrane's main role.

shortExplanation: Exergonic reactions release free energy (negative delta G) and can proceed spontaneously.
solutionSteps: Exergonic means net energy is released.
A negative free-energy change makes the reaction thermodynamically favorable.
Such reactions occur spontaneously.
keyConcept: Exergonic reactions have negative delta G and release energy spontaneously.
commonMistake: Confusing 'spontaneous' with 'instantaneous'; spontaneity refers to energetics, not speed.

optionExplanations.1: Requiring heat input describes endergonic/endothermic reactions.
optionExplanations.2: Light dependence is specific to photochemical reactions, not exergonic ones in general.
optionExplanations.3: Energy cannot be produced without consuming reactants; this violates conservation.
optionExplanations.4: Exergonic reactions can be catabolic (breakdown), not always synthesis.

shortExplanation: Osteoblasts build bone by secreting collagen (osteoid) and depositing mineral into the matrix.
solutionSteps: Osteoblasts synthesize and secrete the organic collagen matrix.
They promote deposition of calcium phosphate minerals.
This forms new bone tissue.
keyConcept: Osteoblasts form bone matrix; osteoclasts resorb it.
commonMistake: Swapping osteoblast (build) and osteoclast (resorb) functions.

optionExplanations.1: Resorbing minerals is the job of osteoclasts.
optionExplanations.2: Blood pH regulation is not the osteoblast's main role.
optionExplanations.3: Breaking down damaged bone is done by osteoclasts.
optionExplanations.4: Nutrient transport in marrow is not an osteoblast function.

shortExplanation: Insulin promotes glucose uptake by muscle (and fat) via GLUT4 translocation, lowering blood glucose.
solutionSteps: Insulin is released when blood glucose is high.
It signals muscle and fat cells to insert GLUT4 transporters.
Glucose enters these cells, and glycogen and fat synthesis are promoted.
keyConcept: Insulin is an anabolic peptide hormone that lowers blood glucose.
commonMistake: Confusing insulin's actions with glucagon's or misclassifying it as a steroid.

optionExplanations.1: Insulin promotes glycogen synthesis; glycogen breakdown is stimulated by glucagon.
optionExplanations.2: Insulin is a peptide/protein hormone, not a steroid.
optionExplanations.3: Insulin promotes fat synthesis rather than inhibiting it.
optionExplanations.4: Insulin is secreted by pancreatic beta cells, not the adrenal gland.

shortExplanation: The ideal gas law is PV = nRT, relating pressure, volume, moles, the gas constant, and temperature.
solutionSteps: State the ideal gas law: PV = nRT.
Check dimensions: pressure times volume equals moles times R times absolute temperature.
The other forms rearrange the variables incorrectly.
keyConcept: Ideal gas law: PV = nRT.
commonMistake: Rearranging the variables into physically inconsistent forms.

optionExplanations.1: nV = PRT is not a valid rearrangement of the gas law.
optionExplanations.2: V = RT/(Pn) inverts n incorrectly; correct is V = nRT/P.
optionExplanations.3: V = Pn/(RT) has pressure in the numerator, which is wrong.

formulaNotes: PV = nRT; equivalently V = nRT/P.

shortExplanation: In HClO2 (chlorous acid), H is +1 and each O is -2, so chlorine must be +3 for a neutral molecule.
solutionSteps: Assign H = +1 and O = -2 each; two O give -4.
Sum of oxidation numbers is zero: (+1) + Cl + (-4) = 0.
Solve: Cl = +3.
keyConcept: Oxidation numbers in a neutral compound sum to zero.
commonMistake: Miscounting oxygen atoms or their -2 contribution.

optionExplanations.1: In Cl2 elemental chlorine has oxidation number 0.
optionExplanations.2: In HCl chlorine is -1.
optionExplanations.3: In HClO chlorine is +1.
optionExplanations.4: In HClO3 chlorine is +5.

formulaNotes: For HClO2: (+1) + Cl + 2(-2) = 0 gives Cl = +3.

shortExplanation: Oxidation numbers are whole numbers (or simple fractions in special cases) but never irrational; they can be negative, positive, zero, or fractional.
solutionSteps: Oxidation numbers are determined by integer electron assignments.
They may be negative, positive, or zero, and occasionally fractional averages (e.g., +8/3 in Fe3O4).
They can never be irrational (like sqrt(2) or pi).
keyConcept: Oxidation numbers are rational (usually integer) values, never irrational.
commonMistake: Thinking oxidation numbers must be integers and forgetting fractional averages exist, so the excluded case is irrational values.

optionExplanations.1: Negative oxidation numbers are common (e.g., -2 for oxygen).
optionExplanations.2: Positive oxidation numbers are common (e.g., +1 for hydrogen).
optionExplanations.3: Fractional (decimal) values occur as averages, such as +8/3 in Fe3O4.
optionExplanations.4: Zero is a valid oxidation number for elements in their standard state.

shortExplanation: Sodium chloride is built from Na+ and Cl- ions held in a repeating lattice by electrostatic attraction, so it is an ionic solid.
solutionSteps: Na is a metal that loses one electron to form Na+; Cl is a non-metal that gains one electron to form Cl-.
The oppositely charged ions arrange into a regular 3D lattice held together by ionic bonds.
This is the definition of an ionic solid.
keyConcept: Metal + non-metal with electron transfer produces an ionic lattice solid.
commonMistake: Confusing an ionic lattice with a covalent network like diamond or quartz.

optionExplanations.1: Molecular solids are made of discrete neutral molecules held by weak forces, not ions.
optionExplanations.2: Metallic solids consist of metal cations in a sea of delocalised electrons, not Na+ and Cl-.
optionExplanations.3: A covalent network (e.g. diamond) has atoms bonded by shared electrons throughout, unlike an ionic array.

shortExplanation: Atomic radius grows down a group (added shells) and grows toward the left of a period (less nuclear pull), i.e. from right to left and from top to bottom.
solutionSteps: Down a group a new electron shell is added each period, so radius increases from top to bottom.
Across a period left to right the nuclear charge rises while shielding stays similar, pulling electrons in, so radius decreases left to right (increases right to left).
Combine: radius increases going right to left and top to bottom.
keyConcept: Atomic radius increases down a group and toward the left of a period.
commonMistake: Reversing the horizontal trend and assuming radius grows left to right.

optionExplanations.1: Left to right the radius decreases, not increases.
optionExplanations.2: Bottom to top the radius decreases because shells are removed.
optionExplanations.3: Both directions given here are wrong for increasing radius.

shortExplanation: A purely covalent (nonpolar) bond has zero electronegativity difference, which only happens between two atoms of the same element.
solutionSteps: Bond polarity is set by the electronegativity difference between the bonded atoms.
A pure covalent bond means the shared pair is equally attracted, so the difference must be exactly zero.
Only two atoms of the same element have identical electronegativity, e.g. H-H or Cl-Cl.
keyConcept: Pure (nonpolar) covalent bonding requires identical electronegativity, i.e. the same element.
commonMistake: Treating 'similar' electronegativity as 'pure'; similar values give a slightly polar bond, not a pure one.

optionExplanations.1: Quite similar (but not identical) electronegativities give a weakly polar covalent bond, not a pure one.
optionExplanations.2: A very large electronegativity difference produces an ionic bond, not a covalent one.
optionExplanations.4: Two identical ions carry like charges and repel; they do not form a covalent bond.

shortExplanation: For a weak monoprotic acid, [H+] = sqrt(Ka*C) = sqrt(1.0*10^-5 * 1.0*10^-3) = 1.0*10^-4 M, so pH = 4.
solutionSteps: Weak acid dissociation: HA <-> H+ + A-, with Ka = [H+][A-]/[HA].
Approximate [H+] = sqrt(Ka*C) since dissociation is small.
keyConcept: For a dilute weak monoprotic acid, [H+] approximately equals sqrt(Ka*C).
commonMistake: Treating it as a strong acid and taking pH = -log(C) = 3.

optionExplanations.1: pH 3 would follow only if the acid were strong (fully dissociated at 0.001 M).
optionExplanations.2: 10^-8 is a concentration value, not a pH, and is far too small.
optionExplanations.3: pH 8 would be basic, impossible for an acidic solution.

formulaNotes: [H+] = sqrt(Ka*C); pH = -log[H+].

shortExplanation: KBr is the salt of a strong base (KOH) and a strong acid (HBr), so neither ion hydrolyses and the solution stays neutral at pH 7.
solutionSteps: Identify parent acid and base: K+ comes from strong base KOH, Br- comes from strong acid HBr.
Neither the K+ nor the Br- ion reacts with water (no hydrolysis).
The solution is therefore neutral regardless of concentration, so pH = 7.
keyConcept: Salts of a strong acid and a strong base give neutral (pH 7) solutions.
commonMistake: Assuming the 0.7 M concentration changes the pH; a neutral salt does not shift pH from 7.

optionExplanations.1: 0.7 is the molarity, not a pH.
optionExplanations.2: 13.3 would require a strongly basic solution, which KBr does not create.
optionExplanations.3: 10^-7 is the H+ concentration, not the pH.

shortExplanation: Cl2 is the only gaseous product; increasing its concentration by Le Chatelier shifts the equilibrium back toward the reactants (to the left).
solutionSteps: Only species with variable concentration matter: pure solids (FeCl3, FeCl2) do not appear in the equilibrium expression.
Cl2 is a gaseous product, so adding Cl2 opposes the forward reaction.
By Le Chatelier's principle the system shifts left to consume the added Cl2.
keyConcept: Adding a product shifts equilibrium toward reactants; pure solids do not affect the position.
commonMistake: Thinking changing the amount of a pure solid shifts the equilibrium.

optionExplanations.1: Changing the amount of solid FeCl2 does not shift the equilibrium.
optionExplanations.2: Removing solid FeCl3 does not change its (constant) activity, so no shift occurs.
optionExplanations.3: The reaction is endothermic (heat is a reactant), so cooling shifts it left, not right.

shortExplanation: Activation energy is the minimum energy barrier reactants must overcome to reach the transition state and form products.
solutionSteps: Reactions proceed through a high-energy transition state.
The activation energy is the energy gap from reactants up to that transition state.
Only molecules with at least this energy can react.
keyConcept: Activation energy is the energy barrier between reactants and the transition state.
commonMistake: Confusing activation energy with the overall reaction enthalpy (products minus reactants).

optionExplanations.1: The difference between product and reactant energy is the reaction enthalpy, not the activation energy.
optionExplanations.3: Activation energy is not the kinetic-minus-potential energy of reactants.
optionExplanations.4: Activation energy is absorbed to start the reaction, not energy released during it.

shortExplanation: Each carbon in benzene forms three sigma bonds using sp2 hybrid orbitals, leaving a p orbital for the delocalised pi ring, giving a flat planar molecule.
solutionSteps: Every carbon bonds to two carbons and one hydrogen: three sigma bonds means sp2 hybridisation.
The unhybridised p orbitals overlap side-on to form a delocalised pi system above and below the ring.
sp2 geometry (120 degrees) forces all atoms into one plane.
keyConcept: Aromatic benzene has all carbons sp2 hybridised and is planar.
commonMistake: Assigning sp3 or a chair/boat shape as in cyclohexane; benzene is flat, not puckered.

optionExplanations.1: sp3 carbons would be tetrahedral and could not give a planar aromatic ring.
optionExplanations.2: Chair/boat shapes belong to saturated cyclohexane, not planar benzene.
optionExplanations.3: sp hybridisation would imply linear geometry, which benzene does not have.

shortExplanation: Glycogen is a branched polymer built entirely from glucose units, making it a homopolysaccharide.
solutionSteps: A homopolysaccharide is a polysaccharide made of one repeating monosaccharide.
Glycogen consists only of alpha-glucose units linked 1,4 with 1,6 branches.
Therefore it is a homopolysaccharide.
keyConcept: Glycogen is a glucose-only (homo) polysaccharide used for energy storage in animals.
commonMistake: Calling it a storage molecule of plants; plants store starch, while glycogen is the animal store.

optionExplanations.1: A heteropolysaccharide needs more than one type of sugar; glycogen has only glucose.
optionExplanations.2: A disaccharide has two units; glycogen is a large polymer.
optionExplanations.3: Glycogen stores energy in animals (and fungi), not in plant cells.

shortExplanation: Carbonate is CO3 with charge -2, so iron must be Fe2+ (the ferrous ion), making FeCO3 ferrous carbonate.
solutionSteps: Carbonate ion is CO3^2-.
For a neutral formula FeCO3, iron must supply +2 charge, i.e. Fe2+.
Fe2+ is the ferrous (iron II) ion, so the compound is ferrous carbonate.
keyConcept: Charge balance fixes the oxidation state: CO3^2- forces Fe(II), the ferrous ion.
commonMistake: Calling it ferric carbonate, which would require Fe3+ and the formula Fe2(CO3)3.

optionExplanations.1: Ferric carbonate contains Fe3+, giving Fe2(CO3)3, not FeCO3.
optionExplanations.2: Iron oxide contains oxide (O2-), not carbonate.
optionExplanations.3: Iron pentacarbonyl is Fe(CO)5, a carbonyl complex, not a carbonate salt.

shortExplanation: By the Pauli exclusion principle each orbital holds at most two electrons, and they must have opposite (antiparallel) spins.
solutionSteps: An orbital is defined by three quantum numbers; the fourth (spin) can be +1/2 or -1/2.
The Pauli exclusion principle forbids two electrons from having all four quantum numbers equal.
So one orbital holds two electrons only if their spins are opposite (antiparallel).
keyConcept: Each orbital holds a maximum of two electrons with opposite spins (Pauli principle).
commonMistake: Allowing two electrons with parallel spins in the same orbital, which Pauli forbids.

optionExplanations.1: Two electrons in one orbital cannot have parallel spins; they must be antiparallel.
optionExplanations.2: Three electrons would violate the Pauli exclusion principle.
optionExplanations.4: Four electrons per orbital is impossible; four is the capacity of nothing standard here.

shortExplanation: Every amino acid has a basic amine group (-NH2) and an acidic carboxyl group (-COOH) attached to the same central carbon.
solutionSteps: The general amino acid structure is H2N-CHR-COOH.
It carries both an amine (-NH2) and a carboxyl (-COOH) functional group.
These groups make amino acids water soluble and amphoteric (both acidic and basic).
keyConcept: Amino acids are amphoteric molecules bearing both an amine and a carboxyl group.
commonMistake: Thinking amino acids lack acid/base activity; their two ionisable groups make them zwitterions.

optionExplanations.1: The polar/ionic groups make amino acids generally well soluble in water, not poorly.
optionExplanations.2: Nonpolar solvents like hexane do not dissolve the polar amino acids well.
optionExplanations.3: Amino acids build proteins, not carbohydrates.

shortExplanation: If two is a prime number, then a prime number exists, so 'at least one prime number exists' follows directly.
solutionSteps: The statement asserts that a specific number (two) is prime.
If a particular thing has property P, then something with property P exists.
Therefore at least one prime number exists.
keyConcept: Existential generalisation: a specific instance guarantees existence.
commonMistake: Over-generalising to claims about all numbers, which the single fact cannot support.

optionExplanations.1: That no primes exist directly contradicts the statement.
optionExplanations.2: The statement says nothing about non-prime numbers, so this is not deducible from it alone.
optionExplanations.4: Claiming all numbers are prime cannot be inferred from one example.

shortExplanation: By modus tollens, 'if Saturday then philosopher' plus 'not a philosopher' forces the conclusion 'today is not Saturday'.
solutionSteps: Given: Saturday implies philosopher.
Given: not a philosopher (the consequent is false).
Modus tollens: if the consequent is false, the antecedent must be false, so it is not Saturday.
keyConcept: Modus tollens: from (P implies Q) and (not Q) infer (not P).
commonMistake: Concluding a specific alternative day (like Friday), which the premises do not fix.

optionExplanations.1: Today being Saturday would make the person a philosopher, contradicting the premise.
optionExplanations.2: Friday is not derivable; only 'not Saturday' follows.
optionExplanations.3: The person is stated not to be a philosopher, so this is false.

shortExplanation: Placing people so Alberto is immediately left of Beatrice and not to Carlo's right fixes the clockwise order Beatrice, Alberto, Daniela, Carlo, which puts Daniela to Carlo's right.
solutionSteps: At a square table each person faces the centre; 'to the left of' means the next seat clockwise.
Set Alberto immediately clockwise from Beatrice (Alberto to Beatrice's left).
The remaining seats hold Carlo and Daniela; 'Alberto not to the right of Carlo' means Alberto is not immediately counterclockwise of Carlo.
This forces the clockwise order Beatrice, Alberto, Daniela, Carlo.
Then Daniela sits immediately to Carlo's right (counterclockwise from Carlo).
keyConcept: Fixing one adjacency plus a negative constraint uniquely orders four people at a table.
commonMistake: Mixing up left and right relative to a person facing the table centre.

optionExplanations.1: Carlo ends up next to (not across from) Beatrice in the forced arrangement.
optionExplanations.2: Alberto, not Daniela, sits immediately to Beatrice's left.
optionExplanations.3: Beatrice sits across from Daniela, not Alberto.

shortExplanation: No pill in its own colour box is a derangement; ruling out blue-in-green leaves the unique solution green pill in blue box, red pill in green box, blue pill in red box.
solutionSteps: No pill in its own-colour box means a derangement of three items, of which only two exist.
The two derangements are: (blue->red, red->green, green->blue) and (blue->green, green->red, red->blue).
The blue pill is not in the green box, which eliminates the second derangement.
So blue pill in red box, red pill in green box, green pill in blue box.
keyConcept: A derangement of three objects has exactly two arrangements; one extra constraint picks one.
commonMistake: Allowing a pill to stay in its own-colour box, which the rules forbid.

optionExplanations.1: Two pills cannot share the blue box; this places both green and red pills there.
optionExplanations.2: This is the other derangement, which puts the blue pill in the green box (forbidden).
optionExplanations.4: This leaves green in green and red in red, violating the no-own-colour rule.

shortExplanation: 1.75 rotations of the minute hand equals 105 minutes; adding 1 hour 45 minutes to 3:00 PM gives 4:45 PM.
solutionSteps: One full rotation of the minute hand is 60 minutes.
1.75 rotations = 1.75 * 60 = 105 minutes = 1 hour 45 minutes.
keyConcept: Minute-hand rotations convert to time as rotations times 60 minutes.
commonMistake: Treating 1.75 rotations as 1 hour 75 minutes handled incorrectly, or as 45 minutes only.

optionExplanations.1: 1:25 PM would move the clock backward, not forward.
optionExplanations.2: 3:35 PM corresponds to only 35 minutes, not 105.
optionExplanations.3: 4:30 PM corresponds to 1.5 rotations (90 minutes), not 1.75.

formulaNotes: elapsed minutes = rotations * 60.

shortExplanation: The excerpt lists severe kidney inflammation possibly progressing to kidney failure as a rare adverse effect, so the drug could lead to serious kidney problems.
solutionSteps: The text describes severe kidney inflammation as a possible serious condition.
It notes this can potentially progress to kidney failure.
So a correct reading is that the medication could lead to serious kidney problems.
keyConcept: Adverse-effect leaflets describe possible (not certain) risks.
commonMistake: Reading 'could' or 'sometimes' as 'always' or 'never'.

optionExplanations.1: Skin yellowing is only a possible effect, not something that always happens.
optionExplanations.2: The excerpt discusses kidney and liver effects, not pancreatic problems.
optionExplanations.3: It mentions painful urination as a possible sign, so urinary problems are not ruled out.

shortExplanation: The text credits recovery to companies revising and digitalising their processes, not to sector firms 'transforming into digital companies'; that overstatement is the incorrect interpretation.
solutionSteps: The article attributes growth to firms revising processes and increasing digitalisation.
It does not say the ICT firms 'transformed into digital companies' as the cause of growth.
That claim misreads the passage, so it is the statement that is not correct.
keyConcept: Identify the option that misrepresents the stated cause-effect relationship in the text.
commonMistake: Picking a statement that merely paraphrases the text instead of the one that distorts it.

optionExplanations.1: Growth from revising company processes is explicitly stated, so this is correct.
optionExplanations.2: Increased profitability despite a professional shortage is stated, so this is correct.
optionExplanations.3: The pandemic driving digitalisation of processes is supported by the 'great lesson' remark.

shortExplanation: An animal that weeps over its victim before devouring it is the classic 'crocodile tears' image, so the passage describes a crocodile.
solutionSteps: The animal kills a man, then weeps with tears before devouring him.
This matches the legendary 'crocodile tears' motif used as a symbol of hypocrisy.
Therefore the animal is the crocodile.
keyConcept: The 'crocodile tears' allegory links false weeping to hypocrisy.
commonMistake: Choosing tiger because the text mentions 'the heart of a tiger', which is only a comparison, not the animal described.

optionExplanations.1: The lion is not associated with weeping over prey.
optionExplanations.3: The panther legend involves sweet breath, not weeping.
optionExplanations.4: Tiger appears only as a metaphor for the cruel heart, not the animal that weeps.

shortExplanation: The text says kuru resembles Creutzfeldt-Jakob and that Creutzfeldt-Jakob is sometimes confused with Alzheimer's, so all three can be confused in diagnosis.
solutionSteps: The excerpt states Creutzfeldt-Jakob resembles kuru.
It also states Creutzfeldt-Jakob is sometimes confused with diseases like Alzheimer's.
So the three diseases' diagnoses can be confused with one another.
keyConcept: Select the statement fully consistent with the diagnostic links stated in the passage.
commonMistake: Confusing kuru (spread by cannibalism) with Creutzfeldt-Jakob (rare, not tied to that rite).

optionExplanations.1: The text does not say Alzheimer's develops from Creutzfeldt-Jakob.
optionExplanations.2: Zigas discovered the cause of kuru, not a cure for prion effects.
optionExplanations.4: It is kuru, not Creutzfeldt-Jakob, that was linked to eating relatives' brains in New Guinea.

shortExplanation: The domain requires x >= 0, and squaring gives 2x < 1 + 2x + x^2, i.e. 0 < 1 + x^2, which always holds, so every x >= 0 is a solution.
solutionSteps: Domain: 2x >= 0 requires x >= 0.
For x >= 0 both sides are non-negative, so squaring is valid: 2x < (1 + x)^2.
Expand: 2x < 1 + 2x + x^2, which reduces to 0 < 1 + x^2.
Since 1 + x^2 > 0 for all x, the inequality holds for every x in the domain, i.e. all x >= 0.
keyConcept: Solve a radical inequality by enforcing the domain, then squaring where both sides are non-negative.
commonMistake: Forgetting the domain restriction x >= 0 and claiming the solution is all real numbers.

optionExplanations.1: All of R is wrong because 2x under the root demands x >= 0.
optionExplanations.2: x > 0 wrongly excludes x = 0, where sqrt(0)=0 < 1 also holds.
optionExplanations.3: The empty set is wrong; many values satisfy the inequality.

formulaNotes: For x >= 0: sqrt(2x) < 1 + x  <=>  2x < (1+x)^2  <=>  0 < 1 + x^2 (always true).

shortExplanation: Writing sin x = s in [-1,1], sin^2 x + sin x - 2 = (s+2)(s-1) which is <= 0 for all s in [-1,1], so this inequality holds for every real x.
solutionSteps: Let s = sin x, so s ranges over [-1, 1].
For s in [-1,1], (s + 2) > 0 and (s - 1) <= 0, so the product is <= 0.
Thus sin^2 x + sin x - 2 <= 0 for every real x.
keyConcept: Substitute the bounded range of sin/cos and analyse the resulting quadratic sign.
commonMistake: Testing only one value of x instead of checking the whole range of sin x or cos x.

optionExplanations.1: cos^2 x - cos x - 2 = (c-2)(c+1) <= 0 on [-1,1], so it is not >= 0 for all x.
optionExplanations.2: (tan x - 1)^2 > 0 fails whenever tan x = 1.
optionExplanations.3: 2sin^2 x - sin x - 1 is negative at sin x = 0, so not always > 0.

shortExplanation: The Cartesian product A x B is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) with a in A and b in B.
solutionSteps: By definition A x B = {(a, b) : a in A, b in B}.
Each element is an ordered pair with the first component from A and the second from B.
This matches the option describing all such ordered pairs.
keyConcept: Cartesian product = set of all ordered pairs pairing each element of A with each element of B.
commonMistake: Confusing the Cartesian product with set operations like union, intersection, or difference.

optionExplanations.1: Intersection collects common elements, not ordered pairs.
