optionExplanations.2: Union collects all elements of both sets, not pairs.
optionExplanations.3: Element-wise numeric products are not the set-theoretic Cartesian product.

shortExplanation: a^2 - 4ab + 4b^2 is the perfect square (a - 2b)^2 since (a - 2b)^2 = a^2 - 4ab + 4b^2.
solutionSteps: Recognise the form A^2 - 2AB + B^2 with A = a and B = 2b.
keyConcept: Perfect-square trinomial: A^2 - 2AB + B^2 = (A - B)^2.
commonMistake: Dropping the cross term and wrongly reducing to a^2 + b^2 or a^2 - b^2.

optionExplanations.1: a^2 + b^2 ignores the -4ab middle term.
optionExplanations.2: a^2 - b^2 is a difference of squares, not this trinomial.
optionExplanations.3: 2(a + b)^2 expands to 2a^2 + 4ab + 2b^2, which is not equal.

shortExplanation: With AB = (5/4)BC and perimeter 72, the semi-perimeter gives AB + BC = 36, so BC = 16 and AB = 20.
solutionSteps: Let the height BC = h. Then the base AB = (5/4)h.
Perimeter of a rectangle: 2(AB + BC) = 72, so AB + BC = 36.
Substitute: (5/4)h + h = 36, i.e. (9/4)h = 36.
Check: 2(20 + 16) = 72, and 20/16 = 5/4. Both conditions hold.
keyConcept: Perimeter of a rectangle: P = 2(base + height); use the given ratio to set up one equation in one unknown.
commonMistake: Setting AB + BC = 72 instead of 36 — forgetting that the perimeter counts each side twice.

optionExplanations.1: AB = 10 and BC = 8 have the correct 5/4 ratio but give perimeter 2(10+8) = 36, only half the required 72.
optionExplanations.2: AB = 12 and BC = 10 give ratio 12/10 = 6/5, not 5/4, and perimeter 44, not 72.
optionExplanations.3: AB = 18 and BC = 16 give perimeter 68, not 72, and the ratio 18/16 = 9/8 is not 5/4.

formulaNotes: P = 2(AB + BC); with AB = (5/4)BC this becomes 2 * (9/4)BC = 72.

shortExplanation: The coefficient of x is 3, which is never zero, so the equation always has exactly one solution regardless of a.
solutionSteps: A linear equation is determined (has exactly one solution) when the coefficient of x is nonzero.
Rewrite 3x + a = 3 as 3x = 3 - a.
The coefficient of x is 3, a fixed nonzero number; a only appears in the constant term.
So x = (3 - a)/3 exists and is unique for every value of a.
keyConcept: A first-degree equation ax = b is determined exactly when the coefficient a of x is nonzero.
commonMistake: Confusing the parameter in the constant term with the coefficient of x and excluding a = 3 or a = -3 for no reason.

optionExplanations.1: The equation is never impossible or indeterminate here, since the x-coefficient 3 can never vanish.
optionExplanations.2: Excluding a = -3 is wrong: a = -3 gives 3x = 6, so x = 2, again a unique solution.
optionExplanations.3: Excluding a = 3 is wrong: a = 3 simply gives 3x = 0, so x = 0, a perfectly determined solution.

shortExplanation: If a = -3 the equation becomes 0*x = 5, which no value of x can satisfy, so the equation is impossible.
solutionSteps: The equation (a + 3)x = 5 has the single solution x = 5/(a + 3) whenever a + 3 is nonzero.
Set the coefficient to zero: a + 3 = 0 gives a = -3.
With a = -3 the equation reads 0*x = 5, i.e. 0 = 5, which is false for every x.
Therefore the equation is impossible exactly when a = -3.
keyConcept: ax = b with a = 0 and b different from 0 is an impossible equation (no solutions).
commonMistake: Solving a + 3 = 5 or picking the sign-flipped value a = 3, which actually gives the valid solution x = 5/6.

optionExplanations.1: With a = 3 the equation is 6x = 5, solved by x = 5/6, so it is not impossible.
optionExplanations.2: With a = 5 the equation is 8x = 5, solved by x = 5/8.
optionExplanations.4: With a = 0 the equation is 3x = 5, solved by x = 5/3.

shortExplanation: A gains on B at 40 km/h, about 11.1 m/s, so in 60 s it gains about 667 m — more than the 500 m gap, meaning A has already overtaken B.
solutionSteps: Work in the reference frame of B: the relative speed of A is 120 - 80 = 40 km/h.
Convert to SI: 40 km/h = 40000/3600 m/s, approximately 11.1 m/s.
Distance closed in one minute: 11.1 m/s * 60 s, approximately 667 m.
Since 667 m > 500 m, A has covered the initial gap with room to spare, so after one minute A has overtaken B.
Cross-check: overtaking time = 500 m / 11.1 m/s, approximately 45 s, which is less than one minute.
keyConcept: For two bodies moving the same way, use the relative speed (difference of speeds) to find catch-up time: t = gap/relative speed.
commonMistake: Forgetting to convert km/h to m/s (dividing by 3.6), which distorts the comparison between distance gained and the 500 m gap.

optionExplanations.1: A has already passed B: the 500 m gap is closed in about 45 s, which is inside the one-minute window.
optionExplanations.2: A reaches B at about 45 s, not exactly at 60 s, and by one minute it is already ahead.
optionExplanations.3: A is faster than B, so it must eventually overtake — it can never fail to do so in uniform motion.

formulaNotes: v_rel = 40 km/h = 40/3.6 m/s ≈ 11.1 m/s; distance in 60 s ≈ 667 m > 500 m.

shortExplanation: Each branch has resistance 10R in series; putting 100 identical branches in parallel divides that by 100, giving 10R/100 = R/10.
solutionSteps: Series combination inside one branch: 10 resistors of value R give R_branch = 10R.
Parallel combination of N identical resistances R_branch gives R_eq = R_branch/N.
Here N = 100, so R_eq = 10R/100 = R/10.
keyConcept: Series resistances add; N equal resistances in parallel give their value divided by N.
commonMistake: Applying the divisions in the wrong order or dividing R by 100 first, which leads to R/100 or other wrong combinations.

optionExplanations.1: 10R is just one branch's resistance; the 100 parallel branches reduce it a hundredfold.
optionExplanations.3: R/100 would be the result of 100 single resistors R in parallel, ignoring that each branch is 10R, not R.
optionExplanations.4: R would follow from mistakenly cancelling 10 series against only 10 parallel branches; there are 100 branches, not 10.

formulaNotes: Series: R_branch = 10R. Parallel (identical): R_eq = R_branch/100 = R/10.

shortExplanation: In a metal only electrons are mobile, and they drift opposite to the conventional current, so a left-to-right current means electrons moving right to left.
solutionSteps: In a metallic conductor the charge carriers are free (conduction) electrons; the positive ions and protons are locked in the lattice and do not travel along the wire.
Conventional current direction is defined as the direction of positive charge flow.
Electrons carry negative charge, so they drift opposite to the conventional current.
Current from left to right therefore means electrons drifting from right to left.
keyConcept: Metallic conduction: only electrons move, and their drift is opposite to the conventional current direction.
commonMistake: Assuming protons flow in a wire, or making electrons move in the same direction as the conventional current.

optionExplanations.1: Protons are bound in the metal's nuclei and cannot move along the wire in ordinary conduction.
optionExplanations.2: Electrons moving left to right would produce a conventional current from right to left, the opposite of what is stated.
optionExplanations.4: This describes conduction in an electrolyte or plasma with two mobile charge types; a metal wire has only mobile electrons.

shortExplanation: At height 3R above the surface the astronaut is 4R from the Earth's center, and since gravity falls off as 1/r^2, the acceleration is g/4^2 = g/16.
solutionSteps: Surface gravity: g = GM/R^2, where R is the Earth's radius.
The astronaut's distance from the Earth's CENTER is R + 3R = 4R (the 3R is measured from the surface).
Gravitational acceleration at that distance: g' = GM/(4R)^2 = GM/(16R^2).
Compare with g: g' = g/16.
keyConcept: Newtonian gravity scales as the inverse square of the distance from the planet's center, not from its surface.
commonMistake: Using 3R as the distance from the center instead of adding the Earth's radius, which gives g/9 instead of g/16.

optionExplanations.1: 1/9 comes from squaring 3R, i.e. forgetting to add the Earth's radius to get the true center distance of 4R.
optionExplanations.2: 1/3 would mean gravity decreases linearly with distance; it actually falls off with the square of distance.
optionExplanations.3: 1/4 corresponds to a center distance of 2R (height of only one radius), not the 4R here.

formulaNotes: g' = GM/r^2 with r = 4R, so g'/g = (R/4R)^2 = 1/16.

shortExplanation: At constant speed the engine only balances the 2000 N friction, so F1 = 2000 N; during the acceleration it must also provide ma = 4000 N, so F2 = 2000 + 4000 = 6000 N.
solutionSteps: First segment (constant speed): acceleration is zero, so the net force is zero by Newton's second law.
Therefore F1 must exactly cancel friction: F1 = 2000 N.
Second segment (a = 2.0 m/s^2): Newton's second law along the motion gives F2 - friction = ma.
keyConcept: Newton's second law: at constant velocity the driving force equals the resistive force; when accelerating it must exceed it by ma.
commonMistake: Setting F1 = 0 because the speed is constant — zero net force does not mean zero engine force when friction is present.

optionExplanations.1: F1 = 0 would leave the 2000 N friction unbalanced and the car would decelerate; also F2 = 4000 N supplies only ma and ignores friction.
optionExplanations.2: F2 = 6000 N is right, but F1 = 0 is wrong: the engine must match friction to keep the speed constant.
optionExplanations.4: Equal forces of 2000 N in both segments could never accelerate the car, since the net force would stay zero.

formulaNotes: Constant v: F1 = F_friction = 2000 N. Accelerating: F2 = ma + F_friction = (2000)(2.0) + 2000 = 6000 N.

shortExplanation: In a fluid at rest there are no shear stresses, so the force on any wall element can only act along the normal — perpendicular to the wall at every point.
solutionSteps: A fluid at rest cannot sustain shear (tangential) stress; any tangential force component would make the fluid flow, contradicting equilibrium.
Hence the only stress a static liquid transmits is pressure, which acts along the normal to any surface.
The force on each wall element is dF = p*dA directed perpendicular to that element.
So the liquid pushes on the container walls with forces perpendicular to the walls at every point.
keyConcept: Hydrostatics: a fluid at rest exerts only normal (perpendicular) pressure forces on surfaces; no tangential components exist.
commonMistake: Treating pressure as if it were not a force per unit area — pressure on a wall always corresponds to a real perpendicular force.

optionExplanations.1: Arbitrary directions are impossible in equilibrium: any tangential component would set the liquid in motion.
optionExplanations.2: Forces parallel to the walls would be shear forces, which a liquid at rest cannot transmit.
optionExplanations.3: Pressure is precisely force per unit area, so saying there is pressure but no force is contradictory.
